Due in part to the accessibility of vast amounts of data and the capacity to execute intricate computations, machine learning is becoming a pivotal tool in neuroscience. In this paper, we use a machine learning technique based on a fundamental principle from the Caenorhabditis elegans nervous system model to model the temporal interconnections between neural activities. This model employs a temporal neural network, specifically a Recurrent Neural Network, to retrospectively analyze data and establish connections between neural events, thereby simulating the Caenorhabditis elegans nervous system's predictive mechanisms. Recurrent Neural Networks are particularly effective at handling dynamic systems, such as neural activity over time. To assess our model, we used simulated data generated from a neurobiological model of the Caenorhabditis elegans nervous system, which resembles a graph with various nodes and connections. Recurrent Neural Networks achieved notable accuracy in predicting neural activities based on prior information, as well as identifying causal links among neural events. Importantly, we discovered that RNNs predict neural activities more precisely when focusing on the most strongly connected nodes within subgraphs related to the target neural activity. This finding suggests that neural interactions play a crucial role in the Caenorhabditis elegans nervous system's predictive mechanisms. Overall, our model provides a valuable framework for understanding the temporal interconnections within and across neural systems, consistent with the principles of systems neuroscience. This framework has significant implications for the design of artificial neural systems, specifically machine learning algorithms, which may be more effective if based on the underlying biophysics of neural activity, as demonstrated in this study. Analysis of the integrated performance of these algorithms may reveal additional insights into the functional design of neural systems at the level of individual neurons or neural populations. Importantly, our model highlights the importance of leveraging the neural interconnections, or synapses, to improve the accuracy of neural predictions and further refine the design of artificial neural systems, with synaptic connectivity as a key factor. The transfer learning research in Graph Neural Networks seeks to develop models effective on a variety of graph data sources. Graph neural networks' underlying architecture plays a crucial role in this research. In our research, we examine the influence of architectural design decisions in Graph Neural Networks on transfer learning. The study is based on experiments performed with 8 different design variations, incorporating three distinct model architectures, on 8 different graph data sources. The study examines not only the performance outcomes but also the factors contributing to these outcomes, such as representation learning and overfitting. The research findings, published in the past, are based on a limited number of model architectures and graph data sources. Our research expands on this existing knowledge by applying the same criteria to different model architectures, yielding new insights. The research findings show that certain architectural design decisions are more effective in certain model architectures and graph data sources. Specifically, the research findings show that adding a reduction layer to models using GNN autoencoders performs well in tasks involving larger graphs. On the other hand, the research findings show that incorporating attention within convolutional networks benefits models working with small graphs. Ultimately, the research recommendations based on these findings vary depending on the model architecture used. If the model is based on an attention mechanism, then the recommendation is to utilize GNNs, reverting to GCN when working with smaller graph datasets. When working with larger graph datasets, the recommendation is to use node-riemannian autoencoders over the other model architectures evaluated. Lastly, the recommendation for working with the Wikipedia graph is based on GNNs, given its distinct characteristics when compared to other graph datasets. The study outcomes and recommendations are available at a GitHub repository. The study aims to contribute valuable knowledge to the transfer learning research in Graph Neural Networks, guiding architects in making informed design decisions. The study is distinguished from existing research, including Zhang et al. (2021), by its comprehensive assessment of the factors contributing to these decisions. Specifically, the research examines not only the performance outcomes in graph data sources but also the underlying factors influencing these performance outcomes, such as the entanglement of a model and the graph data source. A similar study was conducted by Alakoye et al. (2020), focusing on the transfer learning performance of a specific model architecture, the GNN. The study by Alakoye et al. Online learning has gained immense popularity due to its flexibility, enabling students to learn at any time and anywhere. However, self-directed learning can be challenging when students are overwhelmed by an excessive number of options. To enhance their learning experience, providing relevant suggestions is a practical solution. This paper introduces an innovative suggestion model tailored for dual feature data. Specifically, we have developed a Dual Feature Distribution model that leverages two key factors: 1) a dual embedding table to retain critical semantic characteristics, and 2) a joint content-content matrix to improve relevance ranking for content-rich queries. Experimental validation on a massive dataset demonstrates our method's superiority over conventional suggestion models. Notably, our approach performs exceptionally well on datasets like Amazon Electra, and offers efficient suggestion quality even with a significantly reduced number of suggestions. To facilitate widespread adoption, we have publicly released our code and pre-trained models at https://github.com/academictools/dddm_suggestion. This research was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China, under grant number 71831003. Additional support came from the Tsinghua University Science and Technology Publications Fund, under grant number 2020TD000220. A related demonstration is available at https://github.com/zhongying-wang/dual-feature-dataset.

One of the fundamental problems in the context of data streams has been significantly transformed into a core issue within the realm of distributed computing and, more specifically, communication complexity. Researchers have discovered that achieving an approximate solution to the "exactly $k$-set" problem in data streams, where the goal is to identify the exclusive elements within a stream of $n$ items while eliminating at least $k$ elements without error, is an arduous task. Specifically, there must be a delay of $\Omega(n + \log^2 k)$ reads from the input stream to compute such an approximate solution, and this minimum threshold is accompanied by a matching upper bound proof. This evidence also suggests that any algorithm aiming to identify the exclusive $k$-element subset while removing at least $\ell$ elements without error in the stream would require, at a minimum, $\Omega(\min{n + \log^2 (k/\ell)} + n + \log^2(\ell/k))$ reads from the input stream to do so. Our research offers a new and straightforward evidence of this upper bound within the context of data streams. This approach simplifies the complex Euler equation into a linear problem with a well-conditioned matrix, particularly suitable for amplitude and phase optimization. Our analysis specifically investigates the singular values of the Euler function and truncation errors associated with it. Furthermore, we investigate under which conditions this method can accurately represent the true Euler equation and examine the effects of noise on phase restoration. Through numerical testing, we assess the effectiveness of this method using images and synthetic data, comparing its performance with other phase restoration techniques. We also demonstrate the application of this method to accommodate geometric phase constraints, illustrating its potential in contemporary X-ray imaging experiments. The goal of our research is to develop rapid techniques for solving the Boltzmann equation in the context of rarefied gas flows, with a particular focus on steady-state solutions. We are driven by recent advancements in experimental and computational methods for uncovering the steady-state behavior of gas flows, especially in kinetic models. To this end, we are evaluating the efficiency of the linearized quasilinear relaxation operator and a version of the time-dependent solution with a spectral decomposition, against the backdrop of contemporary molecular dynamics simulations and the state-of-the-art iterative time-stepping approach. Through our comparison, we find that the time-dependent solution and the state-of-the-art iterative time-stepping approach require hundreds of cycles to produce accurate results, whereas the linearized quasilinear relaxation operator is able to converge to accurate outcomes within dozens of cycles. To explain the distinction in performance, we examined the eigenvalues of the collision matrix and discovered that our fast solver only resolves eigenvalues that are relatively small in magnitude, those associated with a slow timescale, while omitting those with larger eigenvalues. Consequently, the linearized solver is effective for modeling rarefied gas flows in steady-state, but may need to be augmented with a more complete solution in the context of non-steady flow modeling or when large eigenvalues are present. Ultimately, our research highlights the trade-offs inherent in the design of rapid kinetic models, pointing to the value of additional spectral information, whereas our discovery may provide valuable insights for the development of new numerical methods for solving the Boltzmann equation. To facilitate future research, we are offering new perspectives on the structure of the collision matrix and the behavior of gas flow dynamics at the microscale. Specifically, our work is suggesting that the collision model could be improved by accounting for the magnitude of the large eigenvalues through modifications to the collision tensor, an aspect that may provide valuable insights for the development of new collision models. Furthermore, our research is indicating that the rate of relaxation to equilibrium may be accelerated by increasing the magnitude of these large eigenvalues, an insight of practical value for the design of relaxation mechanisms in the development of systematic model-reduction strategies for the modeling of rarefied gas flows. As an example of such a model-reduction strategy, we are proposing a method to derive approximations of the rate coefficients for chemical reactions represented in the context of a reactive Boltzmann equation through their correspondence with the eigenvalues of the collision matrix, with potential applications to a broader range of physical and chemical systems. This study focuses on the p-divisibility of the cusp values of the Eisenstein series for generic Siegel modular forms. Under a specific hypothesis related to the p-adic continuity of Hecke eigenvalues, we also investigate the p-adic properties of the Fourier weights of cusp forms within the symplectic and special linear groups. Our research draws from earlier work linking p-adic properties to the classical parameters of modular forms, including critical values of L-functions and the Hecke eigenvalues of cusp forms. Utilizing the general p-adic axiomatic approach, we can then determine the p-adic properties of the Fourier parameters for both Eisenstein and cusp form series. Additionally, under the same assumption regarding Hecke eigenvalues, we can derive the p-adic continuation of the analytic rank of cusp forms. This p-adic approach holds significant potential for expansion in relation to other Siegel modular forms, including those affiliated with spin groups. However, the crucial, yet as yet unresolved, challenge of characterizing the p-adic continuous Hecke action presents a significant obstacle to further progress in this area. Specifically, in the context of the special linear group, the p-adic continuous Hecke action can be specified for newforms with average weight n >= 2, whose p-adic fields are defined over p-cycle extensions of the p-adic numbers. Human visual perception relies on the intricate interplay of on-center and off-center pathways in the retina, which respond to light stimuli in a dichotomous manner within circular zones divided by abrupt intensity changes. Inspired by this biological mechanism, we've developed alternative classification networks, tailored to process visual data in a similar binary fashion. Not only do our proposals result in superior accuracy, but they also demonstrate adaptability to different activation functions and enhanced robustness to noisy inputs and data quantization. One proposed architecture, the Alternating Center-Surround Network (ACSN), replaces conventional convolutional layers with double-channel filters that alternate between on-center and off-center responses, thereby reducing communication overhead during inference and increasing memory efficiency by half. Experimental validation across multiple activation functions, such as ReLU, Sigmoid, and Softmax, shows our proposed networks significantly outperform state-of-the-art models, with a notable improvement of 1.33% in top-1 accuracy and 1.04% in top-5 accuracy on ImageNet, as well as significant resistance to noise with an increase in accuracy from 0.0% to 44.8% and against quantized input with an increase in accuracy from 0.0% to 42.9%. Additionally, we've found our proposed models exhibit data generalizability and a decrease in training divergence that indicates semi-supervised learning behavior. The ACSN data experiments reveal a significant positive correlation between the depth of the network and accuracy under both clean and noisy conditions, suggesting our proposed models are more resilient to perturbations than conventional models. Another proposed model, the Bi-Nary Vision Transformer (Bi-ViT), achieves end-to-end binary computation and improved robustness to noise and data quantization by replacing the standard transformer dots product with a binary alternative. It outperforms state-of-the-art models by a margin of 1.17% and 1.09% in top-1 and top-5 accuracy on ImageNet, respectively. Moreover, our proposed models exhibit a compact model benefit, as measured by inference latency and number of parameters, which independently contribute to their overall performance; however, the most significant effect on their performance is due to their improved robustness to noise and data quantization. Our research shows that incorporating signed length constraints for each category can significantly aid in this process. By formulating these constraints as a quadratic optimization problem, we can obtain category representatives that accurately reflect their components. Our objective function is designed not only to minimize distance between the representations and prototype, but also to maximize correlation within the category, all while incurring minimal p-norm distance between similar examples. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in learning from limited examples, particularly in complex datasets with many categories and varying sizes. In the photoproduction process occurring during ultra-peripheral collisions of heavy ions at the Large Hadron Collider, electrons and positrons with relatively low transverse momentum are produced in proximity to nuclei. The production is primarily driven by the photon-analogon factor, with additional enhancement possible through interactions with nucleons and the Coulomb interaction, as well as by the presence of vector mesons. The experimentally measured spectrum of these electrons/positrons is compared with theoretical predictions, taking into account the complex interplay of these production mechanisms and the impact of a nucleus's complex potential using a Monte Carlo approach based on a transport model. The findings indicate that the Coulomb interaction is the primary explanation for electrons/positrons produced at transverse momenta below approximately 100 MeV, as well as for their observed scaling behavior. The measurements at higher transverse momenta are consistent with the photon-analogon process. The theoretical calculations of electron/positron production are found to be in good agreement with experimental data across a range of energies. The impacts of various complex potential effects on the photon-analogon spectrum are quantified, with potential implications for LHC experiments examined. The investigation considers potential applications of these impacts to measurements of photon-stripped nuclei and the constraint of the geometric radius of such ions. The study also discusses the potential for experiments to use low-momentum electrons/positrons produced near the endplates of the LHC detectors to refine our understanding of the photon-analogon factor, with possible effects of the complex nuclear potential on this phenomenon quantified. The success of autonomous robots in diverse environments relies on their ability to adapt to unforeseen circumstances, even when encountering unexpected objects or obstacles, like slippage or unpredictable external forces. Furthermore, robotic systems in critical settings such as hospitals, law enforcement, or military facilities frequently operate in proximity to sensitive information and are exposed to potential malicious interference, necessitating safety protocols to safeguard both the robot and confidential data from cyber threats. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a novel method for autonomous mobile robots to navigate dynamically changing environments while bracing themselves for sudden impacts and protecting themselves from cyber attacks through the utilization of Control Barrier Functions. By implementing this approach, the robot's path is established and the distance between its trajectory and a safety perimeter is continuously monitored, thus maintaining a safe and resilient distance to potential hazards. The proposed strategy is versatile and can be seamlessly integrated into various motion planning paradigms with minimal alterations, as illustrated by its successful application in two fundamental motion planning frameworks: (1) local motion planning using the Probabilistic Road Map and (2) global motion planning using the Fast Marching algorithm. The experimental outcomes demonstrate the efficacy of this strategy in navigating dynamically changing environments and defending against cyber attacks, as demonstrated by both simulated and real-world experimental studies, including a live test showcasing the robot's ability to navigate and defend against cyber attacks using a Quadcopter. Our research explores the concept of resiliency in online learning communities, where members generate and engage with educational content through crowdsourcing and machine learning guidance. These communities are particularly useful for tackling complex challenges from a security perspective, as they can help neutralize hostile agents - individuals who disrupt the flow of information for personal gain. Identifying and blocking these agents at an early stage is crucial in maintaining a reliable and secure learning environment, which is essential for ensuring the accuracy and safety of information shared within the community. To this end, we have developed and published a set of synthetic benchmark tests that assess the ability of crowd-sourced information systems to distinguish between friendly and hostile contributors. Our analysis examines the challenges associated with detecting malicious actors in these communities, particularly in cases where hostile agents feign incompetence but manage to fool the classification system, as seen in our findings. This investigation ultimately highlights the need for organic resiliency mechanisms in online learning communities, where contributors engage in ongoing learning and self-improvement, as a means of mitigating hostile influence and maintaining a secure environment. Our results from testing this concept over a 14-day period showed a significant decrease in hostile agents' effectiveness over time, as the community co-opted the hostile strategy and became increasingly resilient against further attacks. Our research demonstrated that organic resiliency can be employed to counter hostile instances in online learning communities. However, we also identified potential limitations to this approach, such as relying on human complexity for defense and potentially allowing hostile agents to further manipulate the information landscape through targeted propaganda efforts. Our analysis of the trade-offs between resiliency and information accuracy also shed light on the potential drawbacks of adopting this organic defense strategy. Our research ultimately aims to contribute to the development of more robust and adaptive online learning communities, capable of evolving and growing in response to hostile influences. To this end, we have also explored the potential for the community to self-reflect on its own resiliency and develop innovative solutions to counter hostilities that may have been overlooked. Our results from a 14-day experiment revealed that organic resiliency can be employed to counter hostile instances in online learning communities. However, we also identified potential limitations to this approach. Our analysis of the interplay between resiliency and information accuracy also shed light on the potential drawbacks of adopting this organic defense strategy. Our research from testing this concept also compared the efficacy of resiliency mechanisms in communities where contributors engage in active learning versus those where contributors only generate information. Our results showed that the active learning community was more resilient against hostile instances

This discovery leads to significant consequences, allowing the calculation of stable and unstable manifolds for these surfaces. To leverage this insight, we develop a novel method for distinguishing between different types of surfaces, particularly focusing on structures supported by isolated saddle catastrophes. Essentially, we identify criteria for determining if a given dilation surface is homeomorphic to a dilation surface featuring an "asymptotic core" and an additional horizontal saddle, or if it is homeomorphic to a dilation surface featuring an "inverted asymptotic core" and a negative horizontal saddle. To illustrate the utility of this approach, we successfully classify and describe certain types of surfaces featuring specific dynamical behaviors, such as surfaces supporting two horizontal saddles and surfaces supporting a helicoidal structure. Furthermore, our results allow the solution of several open problems regarding the classification of certain types of surfaces, including smooth, compact structures that support a hyperbolic vector field and those that support a non-zero, continuous vector field with "horizon boundaries" and a specified topology. We prove that all such surfaces featuring a specified topology are either cylindrical in structure or support the described asymptotic core and horizontal saddle configurations. This outcome has significant practical implications, enabling the construction of various types of surfaces featuring specified dynamical behaviors, as well as confirming the existence of smooth, compact structures supporting a hyperbolic vector field and those that support a non-zero, continuous vector field with "horizon boundaries" and a specified topology. This study focuses on designing a sensor network consisting of strategic locations both on the ground and above the sky, with the goal of achieving seamless connectivity between these sensors. By analyzing the capacity in various scenarios with the aid of two key parameters - density and distance, we develop a systematic approach to determine the optimal sensor placement. By establishing relationships between ground and aerial sensors, we devise a ground-breaking algorithm that enables an efficient search for the optimal sensor placement. Additionally, our analysis also enables us to calculate the minimum number of aerial sensors required and their optimal deployment distance. By solving a simplified linear system, we are able to determine the inter-node link strengths. By incorporating these strengths into our algorithm, we are able to calculate the optimal sensor placement. Our research also demonstrates the conditions under which standard wireless models are applicable and unveil a surprising interplay between density and deployment distance. Simulation results show that our algorithm performs efficiently even in the most demanding scenarios. Notably, our work has practical implications in the development of wireless communication systems for autonomous aerial systems, with the additional benefit of providing valuable insights into the design of dense sensor networks. Based on the results of our study, we propose a new wireless link design, the Skyline, which enables seamless connectivity in densely clustered topologies. By the same token, we also introduce a new wireless link design, Groundline. By experimentally comparing the proposed designs with established benchmarks, we have found that the Skyline outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in the literature. Moreover, our algorithm has also shown impressive robustness even under the adverse effects of interference. By applying the Mouline algorithm while disregarding the effects of interference, we have found that the results show a relatively small error margin compared to the baseline scenario without interference, thereby implying that the proposed design is resilient to interference. Notably, the Mouline algorithm is capable of handling a wide range of interference intensities while efficiently calculating the optimal sensor placement. By combining the results of both algorithms, we have shown that the proposed design is applicable in the absence of interference as well as under various levels of interference. In addition to these findings, we have obtained a list of open problems that need to be addressed in order to further improve the design of the links. Notably, the designs studied in this work are known to be near-optimal under the standard wireless model, with the implication that the proposed designs are likely to be near-optimal as well. Mouline algorithm reveals that the optimal inter-node distance ranges between the distances achieved by the Line and Ray designs.

Replay has been a key component of several neural network-based reinforcement learning methods, but the existing techniques have not fully utilized the potential of replay. This study presents a new approach to replay, where the key idea is to regularly create a new experience and temporarily store it in a replay buffer. The novelty of our approach lies in using a non-constant sampling probability in the replay buffer that decreases the variance of the historical experiences distributed according to a theoretical model. This allows recent experiences to be more strongly emphasized than older ones, more rapidly forgetting less relevant data, and thereby facilitating faster training. Our analysis shows that experiences can be forgotten as quickly as $t^{-\alpha}$ for $\alpha<1$ in the worst-case scenario, thus accelerating exploration-exploitation trade-offs based on time. Our proposed algorithm, VR-PE, has been empirically validated on a range of test cases and has demonstrated significant improvements over the conventional online-learning framework, as well as previous replay-based methods. The source code for VR-PE has been made publicly available on GitHub. This novel replay approach has the potential to be widely applicable to a variety of reinforcement learning methods and problems. One potential direction for future research is to incorporate the findings of this study into the development of more sophisticated variance-decreasing replay algorithms that can effectively adapt to changing environmental dynamics. The approach could be adapted for use in constant-bandwidth settings, but achieving theoretical optimality in this setting may not be feasible due to the constraints of the replay buffer. Nonetheless, empirical evaluations suggest that VR-PE remains an effective algorithm even in constant-bandwidth settings. The identification of a gap in optimality in the existing replay framework, and the proposal of a more efficient algorithm that effectively decreases variance, represents a significant contribution of this research. The study also identifies an open question regarding the feasibility of online-adjustable sampling probabilities that could effectively decrease variance, and highlights several promising research directions. The approach could be extended to address multi-agent reinforcement learning problems by adapting the sampling probability to account for the actions taken by multiple agents. Potential applications of the algorithm could be observed in the field of autonomous driving, where the actions taken by a single agent may be influenced by a variety of factors. Overall, the analysis provides valuable insights into the feasibility of different sampling probabilities, and the proposed algorithm represents an important step towards developing a more efficient replay-based framework. The approach effectively decreases variance in a broad class of historical distributions, and the proposed algorithm represents an important contribution in this area. This research compares and contrasts the application of the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula to convert real Gaussian matrix models into complex ones.  We specifically examine the differences in the resulting interaction terms, complex phase matrix, and associated bosonic and fermionic commutator in the two methods.  A theorem proving the application of the superbosonization formula to the simplest non-degenerate Gaussian model is provided, demonstrating that it results in a unique and non-degenerate representation.  For the first time, the distribution of the complex phase matrix and interaction terms, as well as the fermionic commutator's zero mode and spectrum, are quantified for the non-degenerate model.  These results confirm our previous predictions about the distribution of the phase matrix's determinant and the interaction terms' expectation value for the non-degenerate model.  Non-zero temperature effects in the effective field theory and the distribution of the phase matrix and interaction terms at non-zero temperature are also explored.  A quantitative relationship between the distribution's width and temperature is established for the phase matrix.  A comparison of the distribution's width for the phase matrix and the determinant of a similar complex number matrix is discussed.  Based on the effective field theory's one-loop results, the ratio of the fermionic action's imaginary and real parts is evaluated, providing an explicit measure of the system's "complexity."  A discussion in the context of holographic complexity is also included.  All findings for the non-degenerate model are corroborated with numerical simulations, specifically a "complexity-entropy ratio" that increases with temperature.  Additionally, the research demonstrates that the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and superbosonization formula yield indistinguishable results in the limit of very small phases and certain interaction terms.  Furthermore, the research rectifies a mistake in the calculation of the superbosonization formula's interaction terms in a previous study, revealing a difference of one factor of two.  A proposed explanation for the discrepancy between the two methods, beyond the limit of small phases, is provided.  As a related outcome, the research establishes that the phase matrix's distribution, when derived from the superbosonization formula, differs from the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation's result by a factor of two. Future predictive learning in robotics heavily relies on the use of probabilistic models to forecast a robot's motion, but these predictions are often made without considering the fine details of a robot's motion, like its trajectory path and speed. This lack of detail leads to imprecise and overall predictions, not accounting for the intricacies of real-world robot motions. To address this limitation, we suggest a novel framework for generating highly precise future predictions in robotics, taking into consideration a robot's velocity, acceleration, and position. To create accurate forecasts, we introduce detailed motion insights derived from the fundamental principles of physics that can be used with various predictive models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through experiments conducted on diverse datasets, highlighting the need for precise future predictions in robotics, and the success of our method in generating highly accurate future motion predictions. Our research, findings, and code are freely available for the benefit of the robotics community. By leveraging detailed motion insights, we were able to improve the precision of future predictions made by the widely-used RNN-Gyro model from 43.8% to 74.1%. The fourth Industrial Revolution integrates advanced technology into production processes to greatly increase efficiency and productivity, but also creates unprecedented challenges for tackling unexpected events. One key issue in this context is the scheduling of production, where uncertainty is particularly problematic due to the potential for unexpected scheduling changes. While techniques such as uncertainty representation and analysis play a crucial role in handling such disruptions, they are often insufficient on their own. To address this shortcoming, we developed a novel method for representing both stochastic and non-deterministic uncertainties in the scheduling process. Our approach involves dividing the planning horizon into discrete intervals and using a conditional likelihood ratio to evaluate the likelihood of essential parameters within each interval. We compared this method against three alternative approaches and found that it successfully reduces computation time while maintaining or improving solution quality. By enhancing uncertainty modeling and analysis, this research contributes to the development of more robust industrial scheduling solutions. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we tested it on a real-world industrial use case and found that it yields superior outcomes compared to existing methodologies. To facilitate adoption in the Industry 4.0 ecosystem, we recommend implementing the proposed technique as a cloud-based multi-agent solution and outline the key requirements for such a system. Furthermore, the concept of "event-affected" (or E-affected) events may offer a useful new perspective in this field, where the type of event is determined by its dependence on uncertain parameters. While the scope of this research is generally focused on the ACO algorithm, the techniques and principles we've established provide a foundation for addressing broader challenges in Industry 4.0, particularly in the context of robust planning and scheduling tasks. To provide a more comprehensive understanding, it is necessary to consider the entire sequence of code snippets, prompting the creation of the $\mathbf{OMOm}$-definition, which represents the probabilistic properties of programs in an abstract manner. The constant advancement in location-based service technologies has made it possible for a person's location history to be accessible. Despite the convenience offered by these services, revealing one's location becomes an invasion of their personal privacy. Observed statistics, such as the total time and frequency of visits, are often disclosed unintentionally. Location privacy is perceived as the ability to conceal these identifiable location attributes. A privacy metric based on the difference between the actual and expected location expectations is proposed. Location expectations represent hypothetical expectations based on a user's suspected location profile. The proposed metric assesses privacy risks using a user's suspected location expectations and an estimated total time budget. The model can be used to determine the optimal time to hide one's location, thereby protecting location privacy. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed metric in measuring location privacy under different suspicious profiles and hiding locations periods. Additionally, the consideration of individual activities, such as work and leisure activities, further improves the accuracy of the privacy metric, as demonstrated by the results of the Monte-Carlo simulations. A case study illustrating the applicability of the proposed model in real-world scenarios demonstrates its usefulness in determining the optimal time to hide one's location, such as when visiting a doctor. Furthermore, the research reveals that location privacy is an essential attribute of privacy and can be used in conjunction with other privacy attributes to define a comprehensive privacy metric. The model is currently being developed to incorporate multiple privacy attributes. A comprehensive version is expected to provide more accurate results, although the methodology remains the same. The proposed metric has the potential to be implemented in a location-aware app, allowing users to automatically adjust their location privacy settings based on their suspected location profiles and time budgets. A corresponding prototype, 'Privacy Guardian,' was created as a mobile location-based service application that demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed metric in protecting a user's location privacy. The prototype showcases a user-friendly dashboard displaying your location history and suspected location profiles, enabling you to automatically adjust your location privacy settings using your suspected location profiles and time budgets. The application also sends notifications when your location privacy settings are compromised and suggests a solution to protect your location privacy. The results of the prototype's development illustrate its potential in creating a user-friendly interface for managing location privacy using your suspected location profiles and time budgets. The application of the proposed metric has the potential to enhance our understanding of your location history and suspected location profiles, enabling you to automatically adjust your location privacy settings. A point cloud-based localization technique known as PC-PL has gained popularity in recent times, but it still faces several hurdles such as compound motion and unregistered point registration. To overcome these challenges, researchers have explored the Normal Distribution Transform Representation (NDTR) from the field of 3D computer vision. The NDTR method captures a scene's geometry by registering 2D normal vector data. This allows for the generation of 3D point cloud data that is registered to a scene. To take advantage of NDTR, a novel deep network called NDT-Transformer has been proposed. This transformer-based framework re-embeds NDTR normal vectors to create a 3D point cloud. In point cloud-based localization, both the reference and current point clouds are represented using NDTR. A registration module then aligns these two point clouds. To address data discrepancies, a novel multi-resolution approach has been developed. To address the issue of compound motion, a motion model has also been developed. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in simulated environments and real-world scenarios. It particularly excels at registering deeply unregistered point clouds and overcoming geometric disparities. The proposed approach redefines PC-PL. Research has shown that the precise measurement of functional connectivity between brain regions, achieved through advanced fMRI methods, enhances the accuracy of individual brain models. This more detailed information can, however, be statistically insignificant and even insignificant in certain data sets. Consequently, methods for assessing multivariate connectivity are required to account for variability between different data sets. To address this need, a statistical approach called "statistical strength" is introduced to evaluate significance in multivariate neural connections. The method assigns a continuous value to each connection that is consistent across different data sets, thus providing a means to compare multivariate connectivity measures. Applying statistical strength to the analysis of large public datasets has shown that it yields statistically significant results for correlations involving 10 or more time series, particularly for intralobe connections and those involving frontal and parietal brain regions. To evaluate its validity, statistical significance testing was applied to the correlations derived from synthetic datasets. Results showed a 100% consistency in the detection of significant correlations when data signals were strong but a 0% consistency when data signals were weak. To evaluate its applicability, statistical significance testing was applied to the correlations derived from resting-state functional MRI data in 1000 subjects, resulting in a 72% consistency in the detection of significant correlations among high signal strength connections and a 0% consistency in the detection of significant correlations among low signal strength connections. Results showed that the method successfully captures the effects of signal strength on the correlations between brain regions. This was demonstrated by the observation that self connections and interregional connections within the same brain region have the highest and middle signal strengths, respectively. Furthermore, the method successfully captures the effects of spatial covariance on the correlations between brain regions, resulting in correlations outside the LOBEs to have the lowest signal strengths. Results also showed that the method successfully captures the effects of age on the correlations between brain regions, particularly by observing higher signal strengths in correlations involving the anterior LOBE and lower signal strengths in correlations involving the posterior LOBE. Results also showed a significant correlation between the method's scores and the accuracy of individual brain models, as well as a significant relationship between the method's scores and the number of sources in multivariate connectivity models. One of the major implications of these findings is that multivariate analysis methods for assessing multivariate connectivity should be based on data analysis methods that are consistent across different data sets in order to ensure accurate and significant results. In systems utilizing distinct signal outputs, known as beeping networks, a central concern is establishing a communication system that enables devices to determine if a message has been sent by other devices. These systems, characterized by the ability to query if a message was received within a given timeframe, facilitate the creation of a distributed clock and allow for message transmission upon receiving a positive response from all intended recipients. Existing research into beeping networks, based on the assumption that devices maintain an active connection to the network unless they send a message, reveals significant power consumption issues when a device's network status needs to be continuously monitored. To address this, the FastFT protocol was developed using only two signals to maintain an optimized, clock-based system, even across multiple layers of communication. FastFT achieves energy-efficient monitoring through beeping periods that match the network's clock cycle, allowing for energy-saving adaptations when a device intends to transmit a message a set time in advance. FastFT's optimized beeping periods allow for a substantial 25 to 38% reduction in energy consumption, surpassing the efficiency of protocols like Resonate beeping and Clocked beeping, and outperforming recent advancements in this field. Furthermore, FastFT protocol execution times for tasks like sending a message and performing timing queries have been shown to be comparable to recent efficient protocols, and in some cases even faster. Adding message transmission capabilities to FastFT results in a substantial 3 to 17% reduction in energy consumption, and implementation-wise it is one of the simplest such systems to execute, and one of the most efficient. Finally, FastFT has the ability to perform complex tasks efficiently, and one implementation was shown to carry out time-based calculations 3 to 9 times more efficiently than recent protocols during the execution of a parallel loop that performs a task based on the devices network status. FastFT protocol was demonstrated through the development of two different hardware test platforms, and one of its key components was also successfully integrated into a sensor-based project, where it was implemented and tested alongside other protocols in the same system. The results showed that FastFT protocol was superior to the other protocols in terms of power consumption efficiency. Due to its notable power-saving capabilities and efficient execution, the FastFT protocol was successfully implemented and tested on two hardware platforms: the Raspberry Pi model B and the T-arm based on a 32-bit microcontroller. One of its key components was also successfully integrated into the distributed clock system of a sensor, and the results showed that FastFT protocol was the most efficient among all the tested protocols.

Code-mixed speech is a blend of languages, typically spoken by young urban individuals as a form of communicative ease. It combines vocabulary and syntactical structures from two languages, creating an unique linguistic format. However, code-mixed speech presents significant challenges to automatic speech recognition systems, primarily due to its hybrid language structure that defies conventional parsing, making it unsuitable for standard processing. To address this, a novel approach relying on transition points in code-mixed utterances is developed to inform dynamic neural network design. A method is introduced to train transition point-encouraging neural networks, particularly Transformer models, using a large amount of speech data. By representing input sequences in terms of the relative positions of languages instead of language codes, a improved understanding of code-mixed utterances is achieved. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this framework, achieving notable improvements in speech recognition accuracy on two code-mixed speech datasets. Specifically, significant gains of up to 9.5% and 6.7% in speech recognition accuracy are observed over state-of-the-art models on the SMSSLP and MALWIR datasets, respectively. Further details on data preparation, model training, and experimentation procedures can be found at the project's webpage at \url{https://sanyamayek4.github.io/pesto}. Furthermore, the trained models and related code have been made available through the GitHub repository at \url{https://github.com/Sanyamayek/PESTO}. A pre-trained model for code-mixed Hindi-English speech is additionally provided on the GitHub repository at \url{https://github.com/Sanyamayek/PESTO/tree/master/hheld_pretrained}, inclusive of model weights for implementation of further research on code-mixed speech models. To facilitate such endeavors, a 1-hour, 6-hour, and 16-hour versions of pre-trained models have been devised through fine-tuning on the Librispeech dataset. These can be downloaded through the GitHub repository at \url{https://github.com/Sanyamayek/PESTO/tree/master/pesto_finetune}. This research explores the challenges of user selection and channel encoding in multi-user MIMO networks, where multiple users equipped with multiple antennas transmit data to a central node connected via multi-antenna cables. To identify the most relevant users with the best signal quality, we formulate a combinatorial optimization problem using a specific matrix norm, then develop an efficient algorithm by reformulating it as a machine learning technique-known "Group LASSO" problem. The selected users are then cross-linked to the central node using an encoding method called "graph coloring", where an encoding matrix is determined to minimize interference between users. However, this method can become computationally intensive for large sets of users. To counter this issue, we develop two enhanced algorithms that refine the encoding process, making the entire algorithm more suitable for practical implementation. Simulation results confirm that our method outperforms existing approaches in terms of performance quality and complexity performance. In specific, when the number of users doubles, the loss in sum rate performance with our method is about 1 dB, whereas with random user selection it's around 5 dB. Moreover, the complexity of the encoding matrix with our method is substantially lower, namely two to three times larger, whereas with random user selection it's about tenfold. Interestingly, the entire algorithm can be reduced to a single "Group LASSO" problem that simplifies implementation, potentially paving the way for integration with other approaches, such as resource allocation, in future work. The final algorithm provides promising results, specifically a sum rate of about 94% of the theoretical optimal value, in a practical context with six users, while outperforming other existing methods in terms of complexity and overall performance. However, further research is needed to explore other optimization methods and algorithms that may enhance the algorithm's performance. The study indicates that future optimization efforts should focus on reducing the size of the encoding matrix, among other potential enhancements. The algorithm's simplicity also presents an opportunity for future integration with other approaches, such as resource allocation, by reformulating the entire algorithm using different mathematical techniques. While the algorithm's performance still falls about six percent short of the theoretical optimal value, the study provides a step in the right direction in terms of simplifying implementation and improving performance, ultimately paving the way for potential applications in a wider range of contexts. Let L be a tropical curve and T its associated tropical semifield. Then the logical function semifield of L can be expressed as the union of a set of finite extensions of T. Specifically, the logical function semifield of L has a presentation with generators involving a countable set of variables, along with constants derived from the coefficients of L's edges and vertices, and relations stemming from positive rewrites in the semifield. This proof confirms Conjecture 1.2 from "Logical semifields of tropical curves," which claims that the logical function semifield of L is attainable through a sequence of finite extensions of T, for an arbitrary tropical curve L. Moreover, the proof offers an even more robust statement: every logical semifield of L can be expressed as the result of successively extending T, first through the edge semifields associated with each edge of L, and then through the vertex semifields associated with each vertex of L. This extension process must remain within the field of rational functions over T. The proof reveals the underlying mechanism driving the construction of logical semifields, which has further implications for their study, particularly in relation to tropical function algebras, as per Conjecture 1.1. It is shown that every tropical field is the result of a sequence of finite extensions of the tropical semifield T, with the added condition that the field of rational functions over T must be preserved throughout. This new understanding has the benefit of simplifying many validations from the paper "Tropical cycles with finite shape," which were previously based on case-by-case analyses. It is expected that further study will delve into the topological properties of these extensions, particularly in relation to the shape of tropical curves. Ultimately, the presented proof confirms the conjectures from the mentioned sources. Additional considerations and questions for future research are provided in the concluding sections of the paper. Specifically, further study is suggested on generating sets for logical semifields, on expanding the findings to arbitrary tropical schemes, and on extending the study to more complex objects, such as tropical networks and matroids. Moreover, an investigation of the connection between logical semifields and tropical algebras, which was initially proposed in the papers' conclusions, has yet to be conducted. An alternative explanation for this phenomenon is also provided. Finally, an analysis of the issue's original solution and an alternative solution from the paper "Tropical cycles with finite shape" are also provided in the concluding sections of the paper. The proposed solution has the benefit of simplifying many validitations from the mentioned sources.

In tatonnement process descriptions, prices are assumed to change based on an information measure $\xi$ in relation to optimal quantities $x^*$, with the Q-procedure offering a methodological basis for this type of description. However, the convergence of prices to $p^*$ that exists in some models doesn't necessarily apply to all, leading us to explore and prove consistent convergence to the Q-operators for specific product spaces and measurable information measures, resolving this issue. Furthermore, we prove the prices will consistently converge to $p^*$ for any information measure in certain product spaces carrying an economy to equilibrium, while also providing examples of divergent behavior for other types of spaces, highlighting the significance of the space's structure in this matter. Finally, we address and prove the prices will consistently converge to $p^*$ for any information measure in certain generic types of product spaces. 

This research draws from the fields of general economic theory and general equilibrium theory with general information. Specifically, we utilize elements of mathematical analysis and measure theory to apply existing theorems related to tenso and operators. Chiral gauge theories are increasingly being used to describe diverse phenomena 
such as the Standard Model's gauge sector, topological quantum gates, and anomalous 
gauge theories that participate in anomalies. The robust phase of an anomaly is 
identified through a broken $\mathbb{Z}_2$ flavor symmetry, and its realization requires 
two stages: initially forming the flavor basis by making gauge-dependent choices, 
followed by determining the basis in that flavor frame. In theories with multiple 
gauge groups, these choices can lead to various and intricate robust phases, which 
often involve intricate combinations of free, confining, and deconfined phases. 
Particularly within theories involving $\text{SU}(N)_L\times\text{SU}(N)_R$ groups, 
these choices result in unique robust phases such as a "quasi-free" phase and a "weakly coupled deconfined phase". A new framework is established to systematically 
analyze these choices and phases in general chiral gauge theories. Furthermore, 
it's demonstrated that these phases can be mutually stable under conditions 
affecting quantum anomalies. The study highlights an inherent property of 
anomalous gauge theories: the non-triviality of their robust phases even after 
considering the IR influence of quantum anomalies. With the standard understanding 
of chiral gauge theories, their robust phases can be modified or completely 
determined. However, this modification raises a problem because it conflicts with 
the generation of 't Hooft polynomials through the standard approach, but this issue 
is resolved within the context of quantum anomalies. Consequently, these phases 
can be generated by incorporating quantum anomalies into chiral gauge theories in a 
way that mirrors their formation in the strong coupling regime, but in this case, the 
process is governed by quantum anomalies rather than strong dynamics. Ultimately, the 
analysis sheds light on an additional capability of quantum anomalies: not only can 
they cause baryon number violation but also, in certain situations, they can drive 
the transitions between different robust phases. A theory overview, mathematical tools,

This research introduces two modifications for Loidreau's code-based cryptography system.
First, the public matrix $G^{\perp}$ in Loidreau's system is typically constructed using the extended Euclidean algorithm, which has a time complexity of $O(m^3)$. We propose replacing this algorithm with the Sieve of Eratosthenes, resulting in a time complexity of $O(m^{1.61} \cdot \log^2 m)$. While the underlying idea is not new, we provide a detailed explanation of the application method for the sake of completeness.
Second, to counter a potential attacker, we suggest introducing a random modification to several columns of the public matrix $G$. Specifically, we select $k$ columns with $q-1$ elements and modify them accordingly. This modification has no impact on the system's complexity, but it increases the likelihood of a random parity-check matrix $H$ having a low weight, thereby reducing the capacity of a random error-correcting matrix. Consequently, an attacker's ability to compute the shared secret key $s$ using the knowledge of $G$, $H$, and a small subset of $s$ is limited, as the fake $G'$, derived by replacing the modified columns of $G$, significantly lowers the weight of $s \mod q$ while preserving the weights of the unmodified columns. This fake $G'$ is used in the online phase of a generic key-recovery attack, resulting in reduced probabilities for the attacker's online phase. Given that the modified columns are random, the attacker's query set for the online phase corresponds to a random subset of $k$ columns in $G$. Consequently, an attacker may only launch a limited number of attacks, thereby reducing the system's complexity, which can be verified computationally. In this study, we explore the potential of dictionary-based language model 
pre-training to enhance the performance of BERT models. By integrating a dictionary 
with word embeddings, we can refine model performance, particularly in dictionary- 
driven applications. However, the conventional approach to dictionary-based 
language modeling suffers from a critical limitation: word representations derived 
from the dictionary are tied to the subwords of the BERT model. This constraint 
severely hampers the model's ability to capture context, ultimately limiting its 
capacity to accurately predict dictionary scores. To overcome this limitation, we 
have developed a novel method of dictionary-based language modeling that is adapted 
for BERT. DDBERT, our innovative approach, separates word representations from the 
dictionary from the BERT model, thus allowing the two to coexist and making the 
dictionary scores open to interpretation. Through experiments involving 
Chinese and English data sets, we have demonstrated that DDBERT yields a higher 
predictive accuracy rate of 92 and 84 respectively, while surpassing the BERT model 
in 14 out of 16 applications tests. Notably, in the Chinese evaluation, DDBERT has 
exceeded the dictionary-based language model, Dict-BERT-LL, by a margin of 8 
accuracy points. Our analysis through the lens of semantic analysis reveals that 
DDBERT's success stems from its ability to accurately recognize ch, ing, ion, king, 
un, uke, une, and unemployment as suffixes, thereby highlighting the significance 
of dictionary-based pre-training in the BERT model capability to recognize 
contextualized suffixes. Importantly, our innovative method has also facilitated 
the development of the first Chinese dictionary-based language models, thereby 
enabling the simultaneous development of both BERT and dictionary models to achieve 
the sum of their theoretical performance capabilities. The source code and model 
of DDBERT are available at the link: github.com/ghuifang/dict-bert-ll. Additionally, the 
dictionary used in the research study can be obtained at the link: www.api.ai.uq.edu.au/dictr.

Federated Learning aims to enable the training of a common machine learning model by multiple entities, known as "Aggregators," without compromising individual data confidentiality. Research has shown that models created in a "horizontal" federated setting, where participants contribute the same data features, can be vulnerable to sophisticated attacks. To address this, we have developed two novel attacks on "vertical" federated education, where models combine data from different sources to learn a complete dataset. Our first attack targets robustness by disrupting a model's performance on specific queries, while our second attack uses participants's hints to determine their local data patterns. By successfuly applying these attacks, we were able to achieve nearly perfect model characterization and retrieve approximately 85% of a participant's local image dataset from a popular benchmark dataset. Our study highlights the need for strengthened security measures in vertically consolidated data environments. However, the increased reliance on technology in urban settings makes cities more vulnerable to sophisticated cyber threats. Our focus is on developing effective city defense strategies against multimodal, high-tech attacks that combine social manipulation, malicious AI, and physical aggression. Unlike traditional defense games that rely on a single agent, our game model involves multiple entities defending the city, incorporating the city's physical and cyber infrastructure as well as its influence on citizens' social behavior. The game's objective is to develop a tactical resource administration framework for effective city defense against unpredictable and dynamic adversaries. Our approach involves leveraging Monte Carlo simulation to devise defense plans, leveraging the entropy of the adversary's action distribution to identify optimal defense resources and distribute them efficiently. We explored the gravitational influence of a spherical shell on a black hole's thermal radiance in a scenario described by the Rindler metric. The boundary of the shell defines a two-sphere with nontrivial latitude and longitude distribution. The gravitational field strength caused by this distribution is absorbed into the boundary conditions imposed on the black hole's surface by the Gauss law, ultimately leading to the emission of thermal radiation. The temperature of this radiation correlates inversely with the shell's angular displacement, and its power density varies as the square of this displacement, presenting an alternative model of black hole's thermal behavior beyond the holographic principle. Furthermore, we investigated similar problems in scenarios described by the Helmholtz and Kruskal parabolic and cylindrical metrics, and derived corresponding generalizations for these cases. The phase transitions in the temperatures of the radiation emitted, as well as the black hole's surface area and mass, were analyzed in relation to the shell's angular displacement. The results showed that this temperature exhibits a first-order phase transition at zero temperature, displaying infinite discontinuity at specific angular values, in addition to a smooth variation in other cases. The surface structures of the black hole undergo first-order phase transitions as well, exhibiting a decrease in the surface area and mass at certain angular values, while showing smooth variations in the surface density and mass distributions. These phase transitions and variations in the surface characteristics can serve as predictive indicators for analyzing gravitational effects resulting from non-trivial latitude and longitude distributions on the boundary of the shell's surface. These indicators also enable identification of thermodynamic universality and universality in the surface characteristics in diverse physical contexts. The indicative indicators include the temperatures of the radiation emitted by the black holes, the surface area and mass, in addition to the power density and the surface density distributions. This research aims to develop a ranking system that overcomes the limitations of human-annotated data prone to noise. Experimental results indicate that training a ranking model utilizing noisy data with optimized bag sampling and group-based loss techniques produces a ranked list comparable to one created using a fully supervised model, given the same amount of data. Moreover, our method allows the training of a ranking model using a significantly smaller amount of annotated data, resulting in only 0.31% of the required data for comparable performance, thereby saving both computation time and human effort. The ranked lists generated by our method based on optimized bag sampling and group-based loss techniques outperform those of traditional methods in terms of performance on both annotated and noisy datasets. Specifically, our method surpasses the baseline approach in three key metrics: the full set ranking loss, the MLE ranking loss, and MADA ranking loss. Furthermore, we found that our method improves the robustness of ranked lists against varying levels of noise from 10% to 50%. Finally, we observed that combining our method with other ranking models enhances their performance in comparison to individual training with either optimized bag sampling or group-based loss. Consequently, the research demonstrates the potential of combining these methods to develop a robust ranking system and explores the limitations of using pre-trained models in the presence of label noise. The research also reveals that a well-designed data retrieval strategy is crucial for the effectiveness of a ranking model as much as the design of the loss function. The research is further validated through the analysis of experimental results on two datasets. Graph Neural Network (GNN) pseudo-labeling has shown promise in cost-effective semi-supervised learning scenarios by expanding pseudo-labels to unlabeled nodes. Nonetheless, conventional pseudo-labeling approaches are hindered in their ability to incorporate graph structure due to computational constraints. To address this limitation, we introduce Insightful Pseudo-Tagging (IPT), a graph clustering-based framework that efficiently utilizes unsupervised nodes to generate precise pseudo-labels from labeled nodes through graph partitioning. IPT leverages soft clustering for both node and edge spaces to refine pseudo-labels across multiple iterations, ultimately enhancing the accuracy of its pseudo-labels using soft edge predictions. By grouping unlabeled nodes, IPT significantly reduces the scope of its pseudo-labeling exploits to only high-confidence nodes, preventing labeling noise from unfolding during training. Notably, IPT scores outstandingly without modification to pre-existing code for GNN models, making it adaptable to diverse types and configurations of GNN models. Moreover, IPT offers the capability to expand the scope of available supervised labels by taking advantage of its unlabeled nodes' grouping information. The analytical findings into IPT's behavior in conjunction with its performance on popular datasets (Citeseer, Pubmed, JJ) highlight the efficacy of IPT and validate its empirical results. The source code for IPT is publicly available at the repository https://github.com/ziplze/insightful-pseudo-tagging. The results demonstrate that IPT is capable of outperforming state-of-the-art models, achieving an improvement of 4% in edge classification performance over GraphCL on the PubMed dataset, thereby effectively integrating graph clustering into existing semi-supervised learning frameworks for GNNs. IPT even surpasses model pre-training methods, improving their performance by 2% in edge classification on the PubMed dataset. Notably, IPT's results on the challenging Citeseer dataset were found to be equivalent to those of state-of-the-art models, although the model still slightly underperformed these models after numerous iterations. By analyzing the behavior of IPT, the model's behavior in several distinct scenarios is explained: (i) sudden changes in the IPT's pseudo-labels, (ii) insertion of labeling noise, and (iii) extended iterations. Consequently, a variation of IPT, referred to as IPT-Noise Robust, was developed using analysis to design a regularizing mechanism that mitigates the detrimental effects of labeling noise, ultimately enhancing the model's overall accuracy by 1% on the PubMed dataset. In a superconducting phase that's triggered by kinetic energy, the impact of anisotropy is analyzed in terms of microwave conductivity. To be more specific, the conductivity of d-waves and s-waves superconductors with nodal and nodeless gaps respectively, are examined in the presence of an extended, A-vector dependent gap, where A-vector is parallel to the c-axis. It's findings show that in d-waves superconductors with nodal gaps, the impact of anisotropy on the imaginary part of the conductivy is reversed when compared to s-waves superconductors, while in d-waves superconductors with nodeless gaps, the impact of anisotropy on the real part of the conductivy is similar to that of s-waves superconductors with nodal gaps. Through numerical demagnetization, it's found that in d-waves superconductors with nodal and nodeless gaps, the critical temperature can be increased respectively by the introduction of isotropic scattering at the gap nodes and the Fermi energy dependence of the gap, but not through ordinary doping. On the other hand, in s-waves superconductors with nodal gaps, the critical temperature can be increased through both ordinary and chemical doping. Lastly, it's observed that in d-waves superconductors with nodal and nodeless gaps, the superconducting phase is stabilized respectively by high energy doping and the gap's dependence on the Fermi energy. To support these predictions, two possible materials are suggested. One, with transition temperatures of 48.9, 34.9 and 9.9 K respectively for H = 0, 2 and 20 ML of contaminants, is modeled after the high-Tc La2CuO4 while the other, with transition temperatures of 58.9, 43.9 and 33.9 K respectively for H = 0, 2 and 20 ML of contaminants, is modeled after the related superconductor Nd2CuO4. These predictions demonstrate that kinetic energy driven superconductors with extended contaminants have the potential to be realized. Furthermore, their radiation output could provide a solution to the cosmological lithium-7 problem by accounting for the production of lithium-7 through primordial nucleosynthesis being diminished. Our study evaluates the effectiveness of Transformer-based models in identifying generated headlines as authentic, comparing the outcomes of training on datasets comprised solely of genuine headlines and those mixed with fabricated examples. We believe that combining our results with suitable validation processes could efficiently detect synthetic headlines across languages. In our study, we investigate the emergence of a chiral spin fluid in disordered systems, which adapt to the arrangement of topological defects in their crystalline structures. Using discrete lattice models, we demonstrate that both polycrystalline and amorphous states exhibit the same statistical distribution of topological defects as long as the density of the defects is high. At high defect densities, the distribution follows the "unwinding law" first proposed by Janssen and Zanchini. Conversely, the time it takes for the system to reach a high defect density, known as the "reordering time," has a significant impact on the results. The high performance of pre-trained models in downstream tasks is due to their built-in capacity for complex distribution modeling, not their ability to adapt to new environments. The widespread success of these models, not only in natural language understanding but also in natural language generation, is largely attributed to their capability to produce probability distributions over tasks. We investigate the effects of extent distributions on synchronization and oscillation in networks composed of Binet-Scherrier type of neurons. Our findings reveal that the critical transition from synchronized to desynchronized states in these networks is profoundly affected by the characteristics of the extent distribution. Notably, the width of the distribution itself is found to be a critical determinant, as well as the location of the peak and the skewness of the distribution. This is seemingly counter to one's initial intuition, as the average extent is found not to be a crucial factor. These results are visually illustrated through related examples. Our study provides the basis for exploring sync and oscillatory states in more realistic neuronal networks, reflecting the varied sizes of individual populations within the brain. Binet-Scherrier type neurons have the advantage of being the simplest type of type-I neurons, facilitating numerical analysis, whereas more realistic type-I neurons (e.g., Wright type) do not lend themselves to such analysis. Therefore, understanding the impacts of extent distributions will also be crucial in exploring these more complex neuronal models. Moreover, a part of our study involves numerical analysis and visualization of oscillatory states in synch and out of synch regimes for various width of extent distribution that can be readily replicated. This research is well-suited for a course on computational neuroscience that can utilize the results of the research. Moreover, the related examples can be visually illustrated and presented in a course on practical mathematics. In advanced wireless communication systems, multiple devices interact dynamically to ensure reliable data transmission, which necessitates adaptive coordination among them. conventional solutions frequently rely on centralized control methods, which introduce delays and depend on the quality of global network connections. In contrast, decentralized control strategies allow edge devices to make rapid adjustments without relying on external support, utilizing local data exchanges to facilitate communication. Nevertheless, implementing effective decentralized control in complex communication networks can be challenging due to the limited visibility of local devices and abrupt changes in network dynamics. This study proposes a new decentralized control approach based on graph neural networks (GNNs) that enables effective feedback adaptations by allowing edge devices to integrate local and global data, thereby expanding their understanding of system dynamics. We present two variants of the proposed GNN framework: one for power control in multiple access scenarios and another for beamforming in coordinated transmission systems. Our theoretical and simulation results confirm that the proposed solution yields superior performance and robustness and outperforms existing decentralized control methods, particularly when operating in dynamic and uncertain environments. This research demonstrates the potential of GNN-based decentralized control to address real-world communication challenges, and its generalizability to various applications within the scope of wireless communication. Furthermore, this study provides a framework for applying graph neural networks to effective channel estimation in challenging contexts. It is hoped this research will inspire future investigations of AI-driven solutions to communication problems, bridging the gap between machine learning and traditional wireless communication techniques. Additionally, this paper outlines a pioneering framework for using neural networks to tackle complex problems at the edge of wireless communication systems. In the near future, edge computing may rely heavily on neural architectures like CNNs, GNNs, and other similar methods to analyze data, but such applications will depend on the speed at which edge devices can exchange data during training, leading to a need for novel unsupervised edge ML frameworks that can efficiently utilize local data, especially when 5G networks struggle with the limited visibility of local devices and external data exchanges. This concept could also be applied to the extension of unsupervised ML at the edge, allowing to combine various forms of edge ML in a unified framework: distributed ML, decentralized ML, and cooperative edge ML. This could also be a potential research topic that complements our primary communication-based control framework. Current machine learning-based robotic grasping rely heavily on large-scale datasets like the ITODD, which usually fall short of accurately predicting real-world grasps. These datasets also lack critical simulation components, like material and coating variations, which are crucial for simulation-based grasping methods. To bridge this gap, we've introduced the DexGraspNet dataset, a comprehensive collection of simulated robotic grasps. Our dataset features 518,528 precise hand configurations for 11,516 objects, including various factors such as 15 different materials, 12 different coatings, and five different object symmetries. Our experiments show that the integration of these additional variables enhances simulation-to-real world performance in grasp evaluation metrics. The full information regarding DexGraspNet's benchmarks and dataset is available online, and the dataset itself can be accessed through the following repository - https://github.com/AdvRSL/DRRL_DexGraspNet. Our large-scale dataset has been released under the license to allow for seamless collaboration with the community. To date, our dataset has outperformed leading competitors in simulation and real-world grasp evaluation metrics. We intend to expand upon the DRRL_DexGraspNet framework in future research by incorporating additional robustness techniques, specifically for grasping novel objects. We will also investigate novel techniques to further enhance simulation-to-real world performance and introduce a data-driven approach to analyze and identify the underlying causes of misalignments between simulation and real-world grasps. We will provide an in-depth analysis of the benefits and limitations of incorporating multiple object variables in real-world grasping and explore the application of these techniques to additional robotic skills.
