Continuous data collection enables the creation of a global respiratory cycle through automated processing of a subset of central slices. A multi-dimensional optimization algorithm constructs motion-adjusted volumes based on a four-dimensional data set, resulting in detailed anatomical images. In addition, we've created a user-friendly pipeline for enhanced quality and greater flexibility in post-processing images. Our pipeline includes a model for detecting reliable data and automatically filling missing information, which is particularly useful in clinical diagnostics. Deep model development often involves distinct processing stages such as detection, segmentation, and recognition that each require specific computational capacities. However, these different layers are often combined into a single, unified model to facilitate development and deployment. We introduce a new knowledge distillation technique called InDistill, designed to improve model compression by allowing the distillation of intermediate feature representations from larger models with fewer parameters. By leveraging adversarial examples to measure feature discriminability, our method ensures that the reduced model replicates the original model's data flow in addition to its output. InDistill can be applied to models with multiple processing stages and is effective across various types of datasets, demonstrating its ability to improve not only compression, but also robustness and accuracy in image classification and language modeling applications. In particular, our findings indicate that models distilled using InDistill for sentence encoding have higher accuracy and robustness than traditional knowledge distillation, and that compressed models using InDistill for detection and recognition have higher accuracy and more compact sizes than other distillation methods. This suggests that InDistill achieves a better balance between model accuracy and computational requirements for multi-stage processing tasks. The implementation of the InDistill method can be found on GitHub under the repository InDistill at https://github.com/asharakeh/InDistill. InDistill has also been made available as an open-source library through the PyTorch Lightning platform at https://github.com/feipos/thop. To facilitate research collaboration and knowledge sharing, these resources, as well as model checkpoints and demonstration code, are hosted on the following websites: GitHub under models-ids/InDistill at https://github.com/feipos/models-ids/InDistill and https://github.com/feipos/models-ids/tree/8f9b8b5/InDistill/dataflow_preserving_model_compression. Ultimately, the InDistill approach provides a foundation for compressing models in a way that respects their inherent data flow, paving the way for research into unsupervised learning strategies that identify natural features and improve model interpretability. A generalized framework, based on inverse kinematics, has been developed to address the issue of end-effector pose tracking in modular robotic structures. This solution is particularly adaptable to assemblies composed of basic mechanical components, allowing for the creation of diverse robotic architectures with varying numbers of movable limbs. The algorithm's flexibility is demonstrated through several applications featuring a modular robot constructed from 3D-printed parts, equipped with a 3D camera and a mechanical addition to enhance movement tracking and stability. The proposed solution achieves nearly 100% accurate pose tracking within 0.5 seconds, while maintaining an average position/reorientation error of approximately 50 mm/5.4 degrees after 20 seconds, thanks to a robust mechanical component attachment system. This modular design allows for the easy creation of new robotic creations from existing components, as well as the adaptation of existing robots through the addition of new modules. The capabilities of this algorithm are showcased by examples of both simplified and complex mechanical designs, highlighting its ability to effectively control intricate robotic structures featuring up to 7 degrees of freedom. The primary advantages of this solution include its efficiency (processing 8 poses per frame with a 30% error margin in 20-40 ms), dependability (trackable even when the 'inside' part of a module is obstructed), and flexibility (capable of handling movements inside or outside of modules with simultaneous tracking). The proposed method successfully addresses the computational challenge of calculating inverse kinematics for every module pose, pose error, and velocity and acceleration rates in real-time, as well as incorporating user-defined constraints to prevent collisions between modules and external objects. The algorithm's implementation code, along with 3D printing and mechanical specifications for the described modules, has been made publicly available. The proposed method achieves real-time performance by processing 8 poses per frame within a 20-40 ms time frame using a CPU power of less than 30W. Similar to how pharmaceuticals are regulated, there is a need for guidelines and regulations on the testing and evaluation processes for these AI models. A key challenge in AI model assessment involves comparing them with one another, a task known as domain adaptation. A second challenge in AI model evaluation involves determining how accurately they can provide reliable results and avoid biased outcomes, a testing process known as bias mitigation. At present, no system exists to support task-adaptable neural networks that can be easily understood by non-experts. We aim to create a compact, adaptable program that can be translated from a task-based graph neural network model by utilizing a formal translation framework. A new translator has been developed, based on a formal translation framework, which allows for an efficient and automatic translation process. Experimental results demonstrate superior parameter optimization methods to conventional hyperparameter optimization techniques. Furthermore, the flexibility of our translator enables the creation of complex graph neural networks as well as other deep learning models not covered by existing tools. We showcase its capabilities in areas like program synthesis and semantic analysis. Overall, our system presents a novel approach to task-adaptable neural networks. We demonstrate its effectiveness in optimizing the parameters of a GNN program by achieving a top-1 accuracy of 97.85% in graph classification. Additionally, our system allows for the program size to be reduced without compromising accuracy. Such flexibility and efficiency could potentially lead to new avenues in the research domain. The massive galaxy cluster, RXCJ0232.2-4420, is notable for its unusual layout and weak X-ray emissions, which suggest that the system still exhibits dynamic activity. The cluster's formation processes can be studied in detail by looking at the subgroups within it, specifically one subcluster that contains a radio source, 3C234, located right at the cluster center. A recently collected radio data set provided data on 34 detected sources within this subcluster, allowing for an analysis of the cluster substructure. It's found that the sources tend to lie within or near the cluster's equator, particularly near areas with large-scale density, such as the Morphonical Web. Some sources appear to be embedded within smaller-scale density areas, while others surround the cluster's equator. A few sources show signs of being morphologically distinct from the cluster, suggesting possible external origins. Overall, it's argued that the formation of radio sources within this subcluster is closely tied to interactions between 3C234 and surrounding large-scale structures. Additionally, it's been proposed that the cluster itself may have originated from a collision between 3C234 and a smaller cluster or group, which could explain the cluster's unique characteristics, such as its unusual layout and slow formation of radio sources. To support this idea, an analysis of the sources within the region showed evidence of a smaller-scale structure centered on 3C234. Moreover, it's been suggested that the cluster is likely home to a active radio source that predates its formation, which could explain its unique and distinct morphology. Finally, it's argued that the formation processes of the cluster can be better understood by looking at the distribution of its sources relative to large-scale structures like the CSO-CfA survey region. However, it's also found that the distribution of radio sources within this region shows very little evidence of cluster-scale activity, which could explain the cluster's unusual X-ray emissions. Further collection of data will help to better study the formation processes of the cluster. Importantly, it's found that the formation processes of the cluster are closely tied to the distribution of large-scale structures such as the Morphonical Web and specifically its filamentary components, rather than other smaller-scale features like the CMB. A detailed study of the formation processes of the cluster's subclusters, combined with the collection of more data, will help to further our understanding of the evolution of large-scale structures and their role in the formation of galaxy clusters like RXCJ0232.2-442

This issue is particularly pronounced when PINNs are used to solve PDEs with intricate details. Although training multiple iterations can mitigate the problem, each simulation is expensive and time-consuming. This paper explores the potential of using the momentum term in the gradient descent optimizer to reduce spectral bias. The introduction of momentum leads to a more smooth and continuous weight space, allowing the network to capture a wider range of frequencies. Our experiments demonstrate that utilizing momentum can significantly improve the performance of PINNs for complex tasks, such as solving the Sod problem and approximating solutions for Riemann problems at multiple interfaces. By leveraging momentum, PINNs are able to reproduce accurate solutions while requiring fewer simulations, consistent with theoretical expectations. Additionally, our findings reveal that optimizing towards intermediate frequencies can facilitate faster convergence. Ultimately, this research validates the efficacy of momentum as a complementary approach to addressing spectral bias in PINNs. The proposed method has significant implications for optimizing PINNs, enabling them to solve a broader range of difficult problems more efficiently. Importantly, this research provides a comprehensive understanding of the impact of spectral bias, the behavior of momentum in optimizing algorithms, and the factors influencing the choice of regularization methods, all of which are crucial considerations for PINN design. These insights can be easily extended to other deep learning architectures beyond PINNs, including other physics-informed networks such as those employing loss functions for volume-to-surface optimization. Moreover, our research demonstrates that bias-variance tradeoffs are inherent to neural network optimization, offering a valuable foundation for the future design of deep learning algorithms. Aging populations around the world face increasingly pressing healthcare challenges. To tackle these issues, novel treatments and strategies must be swiftly implemented. However, existing AI models are often unable to provide sufficient insight to inform healthcare decisions. Therefore, policymakers lack confidence in relying on their recommendations. We propose an innovative solution by integrating explainable model-driven learning into policy selection, leveraging the inducive power of logic programming to unlock AI's full potential.

We begin by developing two types of explainable models: one using rule-learning and the other through counterfactual reasoning, both designed to provide granular insights into policy recommendations. We extract underlying decision rules from data using rule induction and learn to evaluate the confoundability of policies using counterfactual inference. This dual approach allows us to uncover the combined effects of policies and their interactions.

We then incorporate these explainable models into a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework, treating them as transfer knowledge. By using the explainable models, we can determine whether suggested actions align with recommended policies, enabling us to assess action-based policies as coherent and intuitive. This approach also enables us to uncover the underlying decision rules driving the agent's behavior.

We implement our method using existing datasets, focusing on two problems: one selecting orthopedic surgical tools and the other policies addressing HIV transmission. Through experiments, we evaluate our approach's ability to provide policy insights and improve robustness and transference in the reinforcement learning process. We further validate the inducive power of our approach by learning general decision rules from diverse datasets using ILP, revealing the underlying mechanisms behind the agent's actions. This work contributes innovations to the field of transfer learning in reinforcement learning and develops a novel method for extracting granular insights from AI models. It also addresses pressing healthcare challenges by improving the understanding and transparency of AI-driven policy selection. Building on previous quantum compression experiments, our theoretical predictions indicate that further advancements in quantum optics and photonics can result in the generation and demonstration of highly nonclassical states, such as superbright emitters, within accessible optical systems. Quantum compression offers a flexible tool to reveal the nonclassical properties of light states across various applications. Nonetheless, our theoretical model indicates that these properties can be destroyed by conventional quantum compression methods. To overcome this limitation, researchers can develop novel asymmetric compression methods or exploit natural asymmetry found in certain light states, such as single photons, where their natural asymmetry prevents full compression and reveals their nonclassical properties. Additionally, our theoretical analysis shows that multiple natural asymmetries can combine to generate highly nonclassical properties in superposition states, as well as in states created by measuring a nonlinear medium in specific configurations. Ultimately, our theoretical framework suggests that these properties can be confidently confirmed using quantum compression without need for positivity criteria evaluation. Experimental validation of these properties can occur through low-photon-number correlations, a technique already established in previous quantum optics and photonics experiments. This paper presents an innovative solution to the blind image restoration problem. Typically addressed by generating numerous deconvolution pairs to create a "dictionary" of point spreads functions, our approach instead relies on a mixture of Gaussian kernels. The Gaussian kernel set can be limitless, yet training-based methods exploit these sets' limitations to fall short in real-world applications. In contrast, our framework leverages the inherent properties of these distributions to extract low-quality sensor images, which are then utilized as prior knowledge in a variational Bayesian deconvolution framework. Diverging from conventional dictionary-based methods, our algorithm generates priors tailored to each specific image without requiring extensive training, while also accommodating heterogeneous sensor phenomena. Through comprehensive tests on synthetic and real-world datasets, our approach consistently surpasses the current state-of-the-art in blind image restoration accuracy. The implementation code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/harshvee/BIR\_GaussianKernel.

Our framework shifts the focus from conventional program verification centered on a fixed logic to a more dynamic approach rooted in a set of predefined logical systems. Each logical system defines a set of axioms and a corresponding Hoare logic semantics, enabling us to express and validate programs through a Hoare logic logic semantics. To facilitate the automatic generation of program specifications from logical forms, we devise a new semantics called the crisp semantics, allowing for a direct translation of program specifications to their Hoare logic counterparts. We provide a soundness proof for NHR, demonstrating that, given correct program specifications, the resulting assertions guarantee program correctness. The challenge of constructing a quantum model based on the ADM Hamiltonian, which is fundamental in loop quantum cosmology, is being addressed. Leveraging insights from full loop quantum gravity, we develop a cosmological model that incorporates both scalar constraint-based models and vectorial models. By exploiting the discreteness of the quantum groupoid, we successfully derive the potentials driving cosmological evolution in the context of loop quantum cosmology. Additionally, we outline the general procedures for formulating loop quantum cosmology models derived from ADM-invariant Hamiltonians, including quantizing the classical potentials using the UV completion principle and defining dynamics based on the quantum Einstein constraints' implementation. As examples of these procedures, we derive loop quantum cosmology models for scalar and vector constraints, shedding light on their discrete cosmological implications. Furthermore, we establish that cosmological models derived from Hamiltonians with flat spatial geometry automatically include isotropic uniform spatial excitations, while those with non-flat geometry also include spatial excitations. Moreover, we explain the connection between our models and existing loop quantum cosmology models, particularly the chirally invariant ones, and demonstrate that cosmological potentials derived from Hamiltonians with non-negative energy are positive. Lastly, we elaborate on discrete cosmological implications, focusing on scaling relationships, a character associated with discrete cosmological evolution, and confirm that cosmological potentials derived from Hamiltonians with negative energy exhibit correct discrete behavior. Moreover, we demonstrate that cosmological potentials derived from Hamiltonians with negative energy have a correct discrete behavior as well. Specifically, we demonstrate that cosmologies arising from the scalar constraint have a natural cosmological bounce, and that this phenomenon can be tuned by adjusting the quantum Einstein constraints' implementation, and also reveal the connection between the quantum Einstein constraints' implementation and anomalous discrete behavior in cosmologies arising from the vector constraint. Our results provide a robust foundation for quantizing any ADM-invariant Hamiltonian, enabling a consistent loop quantum cosmology model with a built-in implementation of the quantum Einstein constraints. By developing this framework, we can systematically investigate and compare various quantum Einstein constraints' implementations and their discrete cosmological implications. Such a framework has the potential to extend to full loop quantum gravity and loop quantum black hole models. Moreover, our results validate the applicability of the chiral approach in loop quantum cosmology models and shed light on discrete cosmological implications using the UV completion principle's characterization of the quantum Einstein constraints' action. We introduce an object detection method called BayesOD. By representing the object and background probabilities as Bernoulli variables and combining them with a Poisson variable, BayesOD assesses the classification uncertainty in deep object detectors. The corresponding loss function and optimization backbone for uncertainty quantification are also formulated. The theoretical framework of BayesOD is built on two key probability assumptions concerning the distribution of objects in the scene and the number of visible objects in the image. Based on these assumptions, BayesOD generates an object probability map, a background probability map, and a classification uncertainty map. Our method is validated by comparing its loss functions with those of existing object detection models, demonstrating its ability to accurately simulate uncertainty for object detection. Furthermore, BayesOD is applied to the Cornell dataset, resulting in improved generalization and robustness, as well as enhanced data augmentation insensitivity. The "Lights Out" problem is a well-known graph problem where a player's goal is to turn off all lights in a graph by pressing buttons represented by graph vertices. By using an algorithm based on Hamiltonian Path, we have developed a solution strategy that effectively addresses the "Maximum Clicks Challenge" - a problem adaptation where a player must minimize the number of clicks needed to turn off all lights in a graph. This adaptation is equivalent to finding the shortest Hamiltonian Path in a modified graph. By utilizing an iterative depth-first search approach, we can efficiently identify the shortest path in this modified graph, where edge weights represent the number of clicks needed to traverse a path. Additionally, we have outlined the necessary modifications to implement this approach within a graph structure. By testing our algorithm with different graph types (complete and hypercubic), we have observed a notable exponential increase in the number of clicks required to traverse the shortest path in the modified graph. Notably, the complexity of our algorithm is influenced by the following factors: the level of the search (layers of the graph), the breadth of the search (number of vertices at each layer), and the density of the graph (its connectivity). Based on these factors, we have derived both upper and lower bounds for the number of clicks required to traverse the shortest path in a complete graph. These findings suggest that the complexity of our algorithm is influenced by a power of the product of these factors. This research presents a novel technique in Abstract Interpretation known as the
peak-reach paradigm that separates the upper and lower bounding phases during
approximate sound analysis. Typically, sound analysis combines both phases in a
specific order, which we improve by leveraging the sound peak-reach framework,
enabling us to identify and accurately calculate limits in individual phases independently.
We have developed a general algorithm for identifying such limits using the peak-reach
approach and have tested its applicability across various abstract domains, specifically
in the contexts of convex domains, such as polyhedra and exponents, and non-convex domains,
including lattices and monotone domains. The proposed method achieves tighter bounds
while reducing the overall analysis time, essentially achieving optimization in two separate stages. 
Furthermore, we have implemented a tool called Decoupler to verify our results, which can modify existing Abstract Transformers to operate in the peak-reach paradigm, thus identifying limits more precisely with significantly less computational expense. The presented tool facilitates the application of these insights to enhance the precision and efficiency of established domains in use today. This novel method leverages a complete graph and defines edge closeness using a measure that reflects the data point's deviation from the data majority, based on nodes' neighboring nodes' distances. The modified quantum harmonic oscillator with an increasing mass is analyzed using path integrals by employing a novel set of coordinates that simplifies the exponential potential. As a result, the propagation of paths in the modified potential can be closely related to that in the classical limit, with an increasing bias that mimics the thermal propagation in the canonical ensemble. Nonetheless, the quantization effect arises from the non-localization of the trajectory due to an increasing mass. These characteristics are leveraged by a Markov-Chain Monte Carlo method to compute the energetic state of the modified quantum harmonic oscillator. Employing a log-metric analysis, the efficacy of the algorithm is assessed through the computational evaluation of path integrals for the ground and first excited states at varying coupling parameters. Moreover, the algorithm is extended to analyze the propulsion of particles in potential landscapes that mimic these characteristics, such as nanoscale particle drive, with implications for future experimental studies. 

Key words: quantum harmonic oscillator, increasing mass, Markov-chain Monte Carlo, log-metric analysis, particle drive, nanoscale quantum propulsion.

Recent advances in evaluation information have greatly improved the performance of recommendation tasks. However, existing methods still overlook valuable feedback cues contained in fine-grained evaluation ratings and reviews, as well as the diverse information needs behind evaluation queries. To address these limitations, this work presents a novel approach, termed as SIFN - a Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network. Utilizing a pioneering dataset, we demonstrate that user-generated ratings and comments are highly relevant to evaluation queries, but are often disregarded by state-of-the-art methods. To rectify this, SIFN retrieves relevant ratings and comments through an end-to-end training process and integrates a context-sensitive sentiment tracker to capture diverse information needs. By incorporating a sentiment-sensitive module in the retrieval process, SIFN distinguishes between informative ratings and questions, thus enabling the recommendation of relevant items. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of SIFN and reveal the significance of explicit information needs and user-generated feedback in evaluation-based item recommendation tasks. Notably, the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on two public datasets without utilizing additional training data. Such training would necessarily alter data such that SIFN's performance on training data surpasses that of several baselines by large margins. While these results hold promise for public datasets beyond those examined here, further study is needed to fully evaluate how well SIFN generalizes to new, unrelated tasks. The proposed method is expected to enhance the performance of recommendation tasks on various real-world datasets in the future. Effective numerical methods, based on partial differential equations, aim to accurately depict physical phenomena while being computationally feasible. Traditional approaches, such as finite element methods, have gained significant traction, albeit with a potential drawback: when precise solutions are not attainable due to computational limitations, the method's outcome is a poorly conditioned large-system matrix. Consequently, the method's uniqueness property is breached, resulting in multiple possible solutions, and, as a result, post-processing operations become increasingly challenging and unreliable. To address this issue, this study presents an innovative filter operating under the principles of convex optimization. By retaining the underlying matrix structure, the filter ensures that the number of computations required remains manageable, even when the size of the system matrix grows. Furthermore, the method retains key performance metrics, including the time-step's numerical stability and the physical accuracy of the simulation's results, without compromising the solutions' feasibility or post-processing efficacy. To validate its performance, the proposed filter is implemented in the OpenFVM code, a widely-used open-source tool for multidimensional fluid dynamics simulations; through a combination of theoretical analysis, practical experimentation, and rigorous testing, the efficacy and advantages of this approach over traditional methods have been demonstrated. To show its applicability, the method is applied to a realistic simulation of the Rayleigh-Taylor instability, a fundamental process governing a range of explosive systems behavior. We introduce a novel method for localizing key points and determining region-to-region correspondences without relying on detectors. Determining the bias of a data recovery method or a comparison value is crucial when evaluating the accuracy of sunspot magnetic field data. To recover the vector magnetic field from photospheric intensity images, we use the least-squares inversion technique with different noise suppression methods. Since current automated error assessment techniques don't exist for magnetograms, we developed a novel method to calculate the bias of total magnetic field measurements. We evaluated noise suppression methods that incorporate magnetic field vector information to recover total magnetic field data, and compared the results with corresponding auto-correlation values. To simulate real-world conditions, we mixed total magnetic field data with Gaussian noise of varying intensity. We found that the error propagation method exhibits a high level of instability, particularly for sunspot regions with strong magnetic fields, whereas a suppression method that uses vector magnetic field information performs significantly better. This method demonstrates a low and nearly constant bias across various magnetic field intensities. Moreover, the results show a marginal enhancement in bias reduction of about 30% compared to existing noise suppression methods used in previous studies. We present a novel Bayesian evidence framework to establish and assess key exchange generation risks, offering a flexible and adaptable approach. To apply this framework, we examine and compare two decision tasks involving black-box distillation experiments, allowing us to establish a trustworthy key exchange generation risk assessment that's compatible with current standards. We apply the evidence framework to derive a risk assessment compatible with the NIST 800-171 standard, resulting in a tighter key generation risk limit than prior analyses, and one order of magnitude smaller than current standards require. This study presents an innovative reward learning technique that consolidates human guidance over feature spaces, combined with cluster-level policy evaluation. We develop a model-agnostic, visually-supported clustering approach to streamline this process, and propose using expert-suggested policy groups to initialize clusters. We evaluate our approach, dubbed C-RSL, and compare it to current fully-observed reward learning methods in both synthetic and game scenarios, revealing its superiority. A significant shift has occurred in the natural language understanding community, with pre-trained models gaining prominence.  Although many pre-trained models have been developed, none have effectively addressed the intricacies of conversational comprehension, which necessitates a thorough examination of contextual dependencies, perspicacity, and sentimental analysis. We propose a novel conversation comprehension pre-trained model called MeaningQuest, built on the Transformer architecture, that leverages contextualized semantic representations generated by the Simple Sentence Alignment and Meaning-Rich Modeling technique to augment input processing.  Our model is bolstered by an innovative utility function that aspires to capture the underlying meaning of the sentence by selectively omitting words from the sentence.  The applicability of the model's semantic representations was indirectly validated through an assessment of their association with human-annotated sentiment labels.  Additionally, our model performed an empirical analysis of the inherent biases within the language model. Firstly, many examples contain incomplete information, and responses do not necessarily follow from the provided context.  Secondly, the context often fails to provide sufficient information to yield a plausible response.  Given the existence of such flaws, we initiated an effort to develop a benchmark more accurately representative of the conversation comprehension task.  Our model demonstrated exceptional performance on the established benchmarks, and the proposed benchmark showed promising results in an initial evaluation. The typical outcomes are reduced accuracy and failure to converge. To address this issue, we developed TiWS-iForest, an isolation-based approach tailored for tiny model training in extremely limited-supervision and sparse data scenarios. TiWS-iForest consists of two innovative features: 1) a data normalisation method to handle significant data sparsity, and 2) an adaptation of the iForest algorithm to function effectively under limited-supervision conditions, which reduces computation time by 1/3 compared to iForest's. To further streamline model training, we incorporated online learning, initially evaluating TiWS-iForest on real-world Loosely Supervised Learning (LLS) datasets and comparing its performance to state-of-the-art one-class classifiers using classification accuracy as the metric. A new prototype, the Lyman-alpha Screen, is being developed to enable precise ultraviolet photometry by enclosing sensitive detectors in a hydrogen-like atmosphere. During a test flight in June 2022, the prototype was used with the Cubesat-based mission, Starling, which showed significant improvement in the photometric accuracy of the spacecraft's instruments. Using data from the Starling mission, a frequency-fluctuation algorithm was developed to analyze the hydrogen-like atmosphere's effects on the signal, revealing the atmosphere's properties in 121.56 nanometer radiation. Based on this data, it was estimated that accuracy of uninstrumented space-based photometry instruments could be around 10% lower due to the effects of the geocoronatmosphere, which was also compared to the hydrogen-like atmosphere generated by the prototpe's hydrogen gas. A new algorithm was also developed to automatically correct for the hydrogen-like atmosphere's effects, which was test in a flight of the technology demonstration, an astro-computer, in April 2022, which revealed its capabilities to correct for the hydrogen-like atmosphere's effects in real time. Through the testing of these technologies, it was found that the hydrogen-like atmosphere's effects on the photometric accuracy were almost completely eliminated in the Starling mission, resulting in an accuracy of less than 0.5%, which suggests the Lyman-alpha Screen's capabilities to facilitate precise ultraviolet photometry from space-based instruments. A possible application of the technology to the Joint Polar Satellite Demonstration mission, which is set to launch in 2023, is also proposed in the article. Physical keyless authentication protocols provide security without encryption keys by verifying the identities of participants in physical systems. We developed a unified framework to quantify the achievable authentication rates in keyless protocols in binary Gaussian channels, considering varied complex signal mappings and noisy transmission channels. Traditional keyless protocols often employ binary orthogonal mappings and receive theory-based analysis. Building upon this, we've expanded our framework to include non-orthogonal complex signal mappings, which can achieve higher authentication rates in multi-user scenarios. To illustrate the benefits of non-orthogonal protocols, we've introduced a novel keyless protocol, called "Linear Combination for Authentication," which utilizes multi-antennas and complex high-dimensional signal mappings to achieve higher authentication rates. We've also combined the LC protocol with state feedback control as well as differential methods to further improve its performance in variable channel conditions. These advances with the LC protocol have significantly outperformed existing keyless and key-based protocols in multiple authenticator scenarios, showing over 100 dB gain in noisy channels compared to the Northcott-Reinhardt protocol in binary Gaussian channels. Notably, the LC protocol's ability to use high-dimensional signals while transmitting at a relatively low data rate makes it an attractive solution for authentication in resource-constrained systems. The LC protocol's design also provides theoretical insights into the tradeoffs between authentication efficiency, transmission rate, and dimensional complexity in keyless protocols, which can inform the design of future physical authentication systems. These results suggest the LC protocol has the potential to significantly improve security for resource-limited systems, and its analysis can inform the design of future keyless protocols. Recent research has shown that hyperbolic space outperforms traditional Euclidean approach for semantic relations between words.  Building on this discovery, we have developed a framework, FGNET-RH, that takes advantage of hyperbolic space to improve named entity classification and ranking tasks.  Our proposal enhances the existing FGNET framework by introducing a new approach to feature enhancement, leveraging the geometric properties of hyperbolic space to increase the discriminability of the feature set.  Our results show that FGNET-RH achieves significant improvement in classification and ranking accuracy, and our framework has been successfully applied in fundamental (F) and relational (G) tasks.  FGNET-RH has achieved state-of-the-art results in named entity classification, and our research indicates that hyperbolic space can lead to improved performance in this domain.  Our work on FGNET-RH has the following key benefits: (a) enhances feature set properties without changing the underlying architecture, (b) is compatible with a broad range of architectures, and (c) shows promising results in hyperbolic space for all EEC tasks. Recent studies have demonstrated the potential of a generator-network architecture, in combination with perturbations, for predicting equilibria in Nash Equations and their extension, the Nash-Cournot model. Similarly, the Equilibrium Residual Framework has successfully applied unbalanced vectors to forecast equilibria. This research further develops the concept of Fixed Point Networks by integrating the Equilibrium Residual Framework with the current best-performing Fixed Point Solution Networks. Experimental results show that the combined approach outperforms FPNNs in scenarios with unbalanced vectors and maintains comparable performance for balanced vectors. Notably, the combined method exhibits an exceptional level of resilience, surpassing the affordability of having a smaller model while achieving similar solution precision. Historical analysis of solution costs and model size relationships reveals a fascinating pattern where the optimal solution quality is often attained at a specific ratio of model size to solution cost. This phenomenon presents an opportunity to establish a lower bound on solution quality based on the growth rate of model size. Moreover, the study's findings indicate that the combined model's precision can be predicted with high confidence from historical data in the Nash-Cournot context. Several areas are identified where the proposed method could be further developed, such as extending to larger Nash games and Multi-Agent Recurrent Q-learning models for more complex competition scenarios. Additionally, we have expanded on existing concepts of mutual information and conditional causal influence to create new measures for high-dimensional cases, illustrating the connection between these influences and the role of entropy in information theory. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the relevance of these influences to high-dimensional problems, specifically in the context of entropy regularization and entropy-based transportation costs. These concepts have practical applications in fields including statistics, physics, and engineering, as well as across multiple other disciplines. Existing examples in economics, astronomy, and biology highlight the importance of influential relationships in these domains. highly complex nonconvex problems derived from inference in probabilistic models, such as
Bayesian neural networks. Nevertheless, the existing nonconvex optimization research largely
relies on convex constraints. In our research, we identify nonconvex optimization techniques
that can be easily adapted to nonconvex problems lacking closed-form constraints. To this end, we
develop a new minimum square loss variational Bayesian autoencoder (MSVBAE) based on the
principle of squared loss minimization. The proposed MSVBAE is capable of learning disentangled
representations by leveraging a nonconvex analytical method with an intrinsic constraint.
MSVBAE utilizes an inverse autoregressive structure to impose a constraint on latent variables,
whereas its generative model employs a Gaussian distribution with learned parameters, such as
mean and variance, derived from the reconstruction residual. Through experiments using DSprites,
MNIST, and FashionMNIST datasets, we validate the disentangled representation learning capability
of MSVBAE, while demonstrating its superior generalization performance in unsupervised settings. For

Upward planarity is a type of planar embedding with directed components, suitable for various applications. Due to its significant implications and complex nature, it has been studied in depth for nearly two decades, yet it remains an open area of inquiry. Even simple upward planarity with crosses (upward crossing planarity) presents complex challenges, especially for planar upward drawings with constraints. In this study, we explore the upward planarity of bicolored series-parallel graphs, also known as upward planarity with color constraints. It involves additional constraints based on the colors of the edges in the graph. This problem is parameterized by the number of colors used; we demonstrate that it can be solved in quadratic time under certain conditions when using a specific parameterization but face intractability if two or more colors are used in another parameterization. To address this challenge, we develop an efficient algorithm for non-trivial cases by employing a more complex and involved approach based on the underlying structure of the graph. Specifically, we use a technique called the degeneracy ordering method in conjunction with the concept of contractibility in planar embeddings. In simpler cases (monocolored graphs), we develop an even more efficient algorithm that can be easily applied using the following key observation: a monocolored graph is upward planar if and only if its underlying black cluster graph lacks a specific directed cycle. This result enables us to develop a new parameterization, also based on the structure of the graph, which may be useful in other related problems. In particular, we show that a more complex and involved parameterization, also involving the number of cycles (or 'tangles') in the graph, is actually easier to solve than in other cases, also resulting in a quadratic time complexity. This particular parameterization also enables us to prove that a more complex and involved approach based on the underlying structure of the graph often results in a more efficient planar embedding, also in O(n) time complexity, for certain cases. Researchers have already studied methods to extract valuable information from noisy data, especially in cases where the class distribution is uniform or nearly uniform. However, existing techniques do not effectively account for cases where the class distribution is nearly uniform or moderately balanced. Our work addresses this gap by developing a method to derive meaningful information from noisy data collected through crowdsourcing, especially when the class distribution is not extreme. We achieved this by combining model ensembles, 'human softmax' probability distributions, and entropic measures of uncertainty. Our approach also allows for partial credit assignment in cases where the class membership is ambiguous. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach using synthetic datasets representing different scenarios and case studies involving two real-world datasets. A specific mathematical framework known as covering arrays aims to organize data within a grid, combining variables and experiments, to ensure all possible combinations are covered. To achieve this, each column in the grid must contain a unique set of data values that corresponds to a specific number of required combinations. Typically, the number of required combinations is calculated as the product of two values: the number of experiments and the number of possible outcomes per experiment. To expedite the creation of these grids, a specific type of arrangement is utilized, known as strength-$2$ covering arrays, which allow for the reduction in grid size through the use of a factor of $p+1$, where $p$ represents the largest prime number dividing the number of experiments. Academic researchers in the learning sciences focus on uncovering underlying patterns of how students learn, whereas educational engineers develop, assembly-line-style, teaching tools based on proven best practices. This study combines both perspectives to examine the effect of two learning strategies, knowledge-based feeding and conventional detailed feedback, on students' comprehension of testing concepts, using a experimental approach with a control group. The investigation looked into the interference of feedback on learning and the impact of timing and content on understanding testing. An online pre-test, immediate post-test, and one-week follow-up assessed students' initial, short-term, and long-term understanding of testing. Results revealed that students taught using knowledge-based feedback without feedback performed better in the marks they scored, and that there was no decline in the scores of the students who received feedback. Contrary to expectations, students taught using conventional detailed feedback showed no improvement in their testing abilities. The study also concluded that students taught using knowledge-based feedback showed notable improvements in their testing abilities. A subsequent investigation revealed that students taught using knowledge-based feedback showed increased critical thinking skills compared to those who received conventional detailed feedback. The study's findings suggest that knowledge-based feedback can be effectively automated, and that conventional detailed feedback may actually hinder students' development of testing abilities. Despite its widespread usage and fine-tuned distribution, none of the existing systems for computing answer sets in logic programs has been formally grounded in the theoretical foundations of logic programs. This lack has led to a proliferation of unverified assumptions and system-specific biases. To address this, we introduce a theoretical framework for understanding the role of 'giving meaning to symbols' in system design and outline the main points of groundings for answer set solvers. We then examine the groundings of publicly available solvers, reviewing systems based on decision trees, tableaux, and dipredicates, and highlighting the need for a universal, platform-independent characterization of system design. Furthermore, we clarify the potential for developing answer set solvers using reversible computations and reversible two-valued logic programs, and the main outcomes of our research on these topics. This paper aims to consolidate the theoretical foundations of answer set computing, promoting a deeper understanding of its current state and informing future research. It also serves as a companion to our video lecture "On the Grounding of Answer Set Computation," spoken by the first author at the school "Recent Advances in Answer Set Programming," held in Ghent, Belgium in September 2021. The lecture is now available on YouTube at the URL https://youtu.be/8cM-0o2fI1I. The discussion is based on our joint research with the answer set programming community on grounding as a category, and specifically on our joint work on the theoretical groundings of systems designed to compute answer sets, particularly the systemsasp, smodels, and, for completeness, systemv. The paper revisits these systems from a beginner's perspective, stressing that system design is not a one-size-fits-all topic but rather a highly specific area requiring a deep understanding of the underlying concepts. Systems design is typically grounded in Ph.D. theses; our effort here is to provide a concise, compact version of such an account, tailored to one-size-fits-all systems that compute answer sets. The paper shares similarities with the concise account provided by Martínez et al. in their answer set programming tutorial on the "Implementation of Answer Set Programming Solvers," particularly when discussing the grounding of systems based on decision trees, tableaux, and dipredicates. To this end, our research focuses on the theoretical groundings of systems designed to compute answer sets, raising questions and speculations on the design of future answer set programming solvers, ultimately identifying the potential for reversible computations and two-valued logic programs as promising research avenues. The distance-$r$ dominating set problem is a variation of the dominating set problem where each element of a graph's vertex set is assigned a distance value, indicating how many neighbors the vertex is closest to. For a given radius $r$, a distance-$r$ dominating set is formed by selecting vertices with the smallest possible distance value. Applying a specific weight function to these vertices weights them by their distance value, enabling a suitable dominating set to be identified through a greedy algorithm. However, this approach fails to yield optimal results for specific graph types, particularly for large $r$. To address this limitation, this study introduces ensembles of independent sets, later modified to form the distance-$r$ dominating ensemble, weighted by their minimum distance value. This hybrid approach combines the success of distance-based weighting with the capability to capture intricate ensemble patterns. Initially, the ensemble's effectiveness is evaluated on regular graphs and examined against various $r$ values to assess its change in behavior. Next, the ensemble is extended to weighted graphs, using weights derived from a graph's degree distribution to represent different neighborhoods. Lastly, the ensemble is scaled up to large random graphs created through an application of the Bar\'{a}teti and Albert (BA) model, weighted by vertices' degrees, to observe the ensemble's behavior as a product of its underlying graph structure and the weighting function. Using numerical methods, the ensemble's optimal size is determined for different Scalability=N^{\alpha} and Sparsity=\epsilon scenarios and compared against the mono-variable optimal size, revealing a distinct shift in the ensemble's optimal size for specific \alpha and \epsilon values, denoting a deviation from the graph's size, and sometimes an actual increase in the ensemble's size. The deviation and increase in the ensemble's size are attributed to a change in the graph's structure, from a sparse to a dense regime, and investigated visually. Lastly, the ensemble's optimal size for the complete graph is evaluated and compared against the mono-variable optimal size, denoting both variables as complementary, and forming the basis of a new parameterization. The proposed ensemble has also been applied to remove data outliers, exhibiting an exceptional performance in this task. The ensemble's behavior has also been investigated when used in the context of a bio-inspired algorithm, for instance, a distributed coordination algorithm, leading to a significant reduction in the algorithm's execution time. Neural radiance fields (NRFs) have made significant improvements in generating images of unknown objects, but they often require numerous images, usually over a hundred, to accurately fill in missing information. This limitation restricts their practical use in taking random object photos, resulting in incomplete views, as it's impractical to capture numerous images in the field. To overcome this challenge, a new method known as brightness field neural rendering (BFNF) is introduced to generate high-quality images of unknown objects from a single or few views. BFNF is built upon an ordinary differential equation that describes the variation in image intensity over the object's manifold, with a special neural system that captures and generalizes the light conditions, unlike traditional methods that just estimate missing data. This approach enables BFNF to accurately reconstruct and complete images, outperforming existing methods by leveraging real-world training data, and allows BFNF to synthesize high-quality views from minimal information, including just a single image, surpassing state-of-the-art methods by a notable amount, usually over ten times, in this capacity. Implementing BFNF in a webcam enables the collection of thousands of images per second, enabling real-time object reconstruction and image synthesis from a webcam, allowing the creation of interactive web applications for 3D reconstruction and image manipulation. This research was further validated through a quantitative analysis of the effects of image resolution, viewer angles, and the light source's geometry and position, revealing BFNF's robust and versatile nature. Extraordinary applications of BFNF were observed, such as its capability to generate highly realistic images with implicit light conditions, using the light's path in three-dimensional space, and its ability to effectively distinguish between a person's and a car's semantic segmentation even when semantic information is completely absent. Moreover, BFNF enabled the collection, interpretation, and visualization of big data, consisting of millions of images, from various light conditions, further affirming its capabilities. In this work, we tackle the weakly-supervised action detection problem, where our innovative spot-based model leverages key view identifiers to connect action videos to corresponding class labels and key frames. We treat action detection as a localized problem, mapping it to a category labeling task within a graph structure. Our graph convolutive network (GCN) is designed to capture the compact context around each key frame's features. We also introduce a new GCN variant, dubbed triple-GCN, to enhance context integration. Our system's main components can be easily extended to other weakly-supervised vision tasks. Comprehensive experiments conducted on ActivityNet, THUMOS-14, and Sports-1M demonstrate the GCN's effectiveness in enriching key frame features, with triple-GCN enhancing action detection performance on ActivityNet 20 by substantial margins. Specifically, our final system achieves an mAP of 20.1 on the ActivityNet 20 benchmark. The full implementation is available on GitHub under https://github.com/spot-gcn/spot-gcn.py.

In many mobile and sensor-based applications where data storage may be limited, approximate data search algorithms play a crucial role. Existing near-optimal approximate filter implementations require a memory overhead of a particular logarithmic order. This paper introduces a space-optimal linear filter called NPF, where false positives are not possible and allows for queries of logarithmic overhead as well. NPF achieves query processing in O(log n) time with predefined false positives and can replicate the performance of existing filters like VLF or LF with additional memory overhead. The paper also discusses how NPF can be integrated with other data structures like a hash table and a priority queue to enhance its performance in line with previous research by Papadimitriou et al. Telepresence systems allow users to control remote destinations with their preferred devices, enabling an optimal interaction between humans and robots. However, evaluating Quality of Experience (QoE) in these systems poses a significant challenge due to their interconnected nature, where various factors, such as visual and audio feedback, control methods, and human factors, simultaneously influence the overall experience. To tackle this issue, researchers have developed an innovative, human-in-the-loop evaluation approach for assessing QoE in telepresence systems. This solution involves rapidly switching a user's view with autonomous AI-generated 3D scenes and disrupting their control by simulating random input disturbances during interactions. By leveraging this approach, scientists can thoroughly analyze a user's response to out-of-theordinary situations, quantify QoE through the user's resulting actions, and estimate the time it takes for the user to recover from disturbances. Furthermore, by superimposing virtual objects on real-world images, researchers can analyze how visual distortions impact QoE, while also assessing audio feedback requires a simplified simulation of this component. The proposed evaluation framework has been tested with over 20 participants, who interacted with the test platform via a remote-controlled robot, showing that users do not normally deviate from their tasks, but are highly sensitive to out-of-theordinary situations, and quickly return to their routine behavior. Following these findings, scientists have tested various autonomous AI techniques to minimize users' disturbances and found that AI-driven measures can effectively reduce both the frequency and duration of these events. Moreover, by optimizing human-robot interactions, researchers have successfully reduced the time it takes users to recover from disturbances. Lastly, by assessing the impact of different factors on QoE, a quantitative model was created using the collected data, which was accurate within a margin of 1.5. This method successfully accounts for various factors, showing that human behavior is largely driven by visual and audio feedback, while human factors play a relatively minor role. By contrast, human factors have a much bigger impact on QoE in cases where users are engaged in unanticipated situations. Ultimately, the proposed QoE model was confirmed by having a higher correlation with the users' observed QoE values, showing that human behavior is largely influenced by these two factors. The QoE model is available at https://github.com/fateme-tajer/kqoe. The Mixture-of-Experts algorithm has been a highly influential tool in piecewise function approximation, underpinning numerous neural network architectures such as Gaussianization and autoencoding techniques, yet its practical implementation consistently yielded subpar quality in approximating real-valued functions. The main reason for this shortcoming was the absence of convergence guarantees in the algorithm's traditional version, leading to incomplete coverage of the input space and the propensity for overfitting. To address these limitations, we have expanded the algorithm to accommodate an infinite number of experts, thereby ensuring comprehensive coverage and transforming Mixture-of-Experts into a powerful method for approximating complex, real-valued functions. We have rigorously demonstrated the algorithm's convergence under mild conditions and confirmed its efficacy through empirical testing on various benchmark problems. Notably, our algorithm achieved notable success in image compression, yielding compression ratios of 40 and compression speeds of 2-3 times the state-of-the-art methods, while producing image quality comparable to the standard, codec. Moreover, the algorithm significantly outperformed competing techniques in approximating real-valued functions, as evidenced by its superior results in a fair comparison against established methods such as Gaussianization. We have released the algorithm's source code, known as MOE-Infinite, for the public at https://github.com/AsadP/MOE-Infinite. We have further developed an accelerated variant of the algorithm, known as Optimal MOE, which leverages its underlying Korneliussen optimality conditions to derive a distinct set of optimality conditions for the mixture coefficients. Consequently, the accelerated algorithm exhibits a time complexity that scales quadratically with the number of data points, as opposed to the traditional version, which exhibits a linear relationship with the data size. To our knowledge, the proposed algorithm represents the first instance of an accelerated version of the mixture-of-experts that strikes a balance between computational efficiency and algorithmic accuracy. We have rigorously demonstrated the algorithm's validity and provided clear evidence of its acceleration by establishing non-trivial lower-bound estimates for its time complexity. We have empirically verified the efficacy of the accelerated algorithm in a fair comparison against its traditional counterpart, solidifying its status as a reliable tool for approximating real-valued functions. Despite the widespread use of models for computer vision, there is a lack of clear understanding of how knowledge is transferred in deep learning. Current research in this area focuses primarily on black-box models, leaving a gap in the understanding of gray-box models, where the structure of the assisting model is visible. In particular, there is no clear explanation of how knowledge is adapted during the training process, making it difficult to create effective methods for transferring knowledge. As a result, the development of various knowledge transfer techniques has yielded limited success. In this paper, we challenge two widely accepted assumptions about knowledge transfer: the idea that the structure of the assisting model should be preserved and that knowledge transfer involves finding a common representation between the assisting model and the target model. By testing these hypotheses through experiments, we ultimately propose a new framework for transferring knowledge, allowing gray-box models to learn new tasks efficiently. Our approach, called knowledge-aware layer extraction, differentiates itself from other methods by identifying which layers of the assisting model contain which tasks and selectively copying these layers for the target model, effectively reducing the impact of introduced parameters on the target model's training process. As a result, our approach successfully addresses the challenge of overlapping tasks and promotes overlapping tasks learning, ultimately leading to improved model performance and transferability. Our approach achieved state-of-the-art results on three datasets: 91. 4% for back-to-back domain adaptation, 83. 9% for semi-supervised learning, and 83. 4% for unsupervised domain adaptation, outperforming previous methods on the same tasks. Our approach successfully promotes the understanding of knowledge transfer, allowing models to learn from one another in complex domains. Our code for knowledge-aware layer extraction is available on the repository https://github.com/damo-cv/RAXDL. As the first attempt to study gray-box model knowledge transfer, our paper has successfully applied the approach to models sharing the same backbone but differing in their heads, ultimately helping to develop more effective knowledge transfer methods. Ultimately, the paper was accepted for publication at the CVPR 2021 convention. As a result, the paper was selected for publication in the journal Information Systems, undergoing a revised review process, and ultimately published in the journal Neural Networks and Learning Systems. Ozy is a Python-based tool for managing and orchestrating distributed
computing jobs, supporting various execution platforms such as Slurm, PBS,
Lustre, and Globus. It enables users to run a wide range of file and job
operations, including uploading, downloading, copying, moving, and
removing files, as well as executing interactive command-line sessions.
Currently, Ozy supports integration with high-performance computing job
managers like Slurm and PBS, with upcoming development focused on adding
capabilities for other systems, including Ceph and Grid infrastructure. A
user-friendly web interface is provided for accessing Ozy functionality,
with the option to authenticate with credentials from remote systems or
specifically with Grid credentials. Ozy's design emphasizes modularity and
configurability, allowing for easy extension via a plugin mechanism for
adding support for additional platforms and features. A comprehensive set of
documentation resources and development guidelines are available to facilitate
community involvement in Ozy's development. This paper presents an overview of
Ozy's functionality, operations, and underlying design, highlighting its
current implementation and future development roadmap. Documentation and
source code for Ozy are accessible through GitHub under the MIT open-source
license terms, with development led by the University of Tennessee's Data
Integrity and Security group. Key design decisions and implementation details
are discussed, with a focus on the underlying architecture that enables
Ozy's current capabilities and informs its future development directions. A
detailed high-level architecture diagram illustrating Ozy's major logical
components and their relationships is included in the presentation. A related
paper discussing Ozy's performance and usability has been presented at SC19.

The dial-a-ride problem is a planning issue found in on-demand transportation systems, which requires determining optimal vehicle routes to maximize efficiency given a list of customer demands in a metropolitan area. Each demand is characterized by a pickup and delivery location, passenger count, and maximum travel time limit. In this problem, the goal is to minimize the total number of vehicles used while considering time windows for pickup and delivery. In this study, a branch-and-bound based solution approach is proposed to solve the dial-a-ride problem efficiently. Initially, a rigorous bound for the optimal solution is established by generating high-quality vehicle routes using a heuristic method, which in turn involves a best-first search to minimize travel time. In addition, the solution search is accelerated through the identification of viable solution branches utilizing a clustering based strategy, which in turn is enriched by incorporating lots of high-quality solution instances. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is evaluated using a comprehensive set of test cases from the well-known SiTra data set, which showed the method can solve problems with up to 30 demands within a reasonable time limit, but falls short of solving problems with 50 demands. In comparison to existing solution optimizers, the proposed approach could find exact solutions for 37 out of 40 test cases that had previously gone unsolved, which in turn allowed it to confirm the proven optimality of previously known solution instances while also allowing it to improve the reported lower bounds for another test case that had previously gone unsolved. It is noteworthy that the proposed solution optimizer utilizes a more complex and involved algorithm architecture in comparison to the previously tested solution optimizers. In order to further test and validate the proposed solution optimizer, the study also introduced a simplified and less demanding variant known as the simple dial-a-ride problem, which in turn allows it to solve 50 demand problems within a reasonable time limit, which in turn showed a significant improvement in comparison to the original dial-a-ride problem. In fact, in the simple dial-a-ride problem context, the proposed solution optimizer showed a significant improvement in that it could solve 50 demand problems that had previously gone unsolved by other solution optimizers, which in turn allowed it to confirm the proven optimality of previously known solution instances while also allowing it to improve the reported lower bounds for another test case that had previously gone unsolved. In addition to the proposed solution optimizer, the study also further developed the dial-a-ride problem by introducing a number of theoretical results that in turn allow it to minimize the number of vehicles used by dial-a-ride services

This research focuses on developing a pre-trained model that incorporates insight recognition and multi-modal pre-training to enhance product-based visual question answering performance. The proposed approach involves two pre-training tasks: one for learning multi-modal representations of products by leveraging product images and descriptions, and another for introducing insight recognition to model relationships between different product components and overall items. The insights derived from this method are then utilized to develop custom-designed transformer blocks that capture spatial information in images. Empirical results and ablation studies demonstrate the validity and efficacy of the proposed approach, leading to significant performance improvements in product-based visual question answering. Specifically, our model achieves mScores of 92.44% on fashionNet, 75.31% on clothing+ and 64.26% on clothing. Furthermore, our findings suggest that incorporating insight recognition adds value to traditional pre-training methods and highlight the potential of multi-modal pre-training for visual question answering. The proposed approach's strong performance in this context is particularly noteworthy as it leverages relatively simple insight knowledge compared to more complex and accurate sources, such as fine-tuned language models. Given that the quality of insight knowledge directly impacts model performance, we believe that more advanced and accurate insight knowledge could lead to even more substantial gains, ultimately transforming the use of pre-trained models from application-to-application to application-to-domain. The proposed approach was extensively tested using the public available open-fashion dataset. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/damo-cv/IR-MULTI on GitHub. Theories of dual processes, including the additive non-additive (ANA) model and analytic-availability model with analytic-ignorance (AMS-E), suggest that dual mental processes co-exist and that each has distinct mathematical representations.  Analytic-availability (A) is believed to be associated with precise analytical information, but only in a probabilistic form.  We validate the accuracy of the AMS-E by evaluating its ability to effectively reduce information using Shannon entropy on the results of 23 experiments supporting the dual processes theory.  In contrast, the Ana component of the model is unable to do so.  These findings provide empirical support for the two-part mental information structure hypothesis underlying the ana-ignorance part of the AMS-E, and also validate the ana-ignorance component of the model as a useful tool for evaluating the effectiveness of information reduction in cognitive processes.  We further develop the theoretical foundations of the ana-ignorance component, and demonstrate its ability to explain the negative entropy difference between uncertain and unknown states, as well as the difference in entropy for which measures can be predicted.  We also discover that the ana-ignorance component is able to explain the difference in entropy differences observed in the Stroop interference paradigm.  These findings provide the basis for a new theoretical module, the ignorance module, that can be integrated into the dual processes theory.  We also provide the basis for a new measurement protocol, Shannon entropy measurement protocol, that can be used to distinguish between the analytic and non-analytic mental modules.  We further show that the analytic module is able to explain the effect of temporal predictability observed in the temporal predictability paradigm.  These findings provide the basis for a new measurement protocol, prediction module protocol, that can be used to evaluate the effectiveness of information prediction in cognitive processes.  We also provide the basis for a new temporal module that can be integrated into the dual processes theory.  We further discover, however, that the temporal module is unable to explain the difference in entropy differences observed in the McGurk illusion paradigm.  Finally, we provide the basis for a new measurement protocol, integration protocol, that can be used to integrate the ignorance module and the temporal module into the dual processes theory.  We also provide the basis for a new fusion module that can be integrated into the dual processes theory.  We further demonstrate, however, that the fusion module is unable to explain the effect observed in the temporal predictability paradigm.  These findings provide the basis for a new measurement protocol

This study proposes a novel approach that enables online recognition of hand signs using dynamic feature extraction and linear discriminant analysis. Building upon this vision-based system, we explore its application in facilitating communication between a human and a swarm of robots. In a distributed setting, a human specifies task instructions for the swarm by executing a sequence of hand signs, which are received and interpreted individually by each robot. Our concept has been demonstrated through a series of experimental studies, starting with a basic design that involved designing a set of hand signals for basic commands like "go left" and "turn". In a more complex experiment, we investigated the recognition of swimming styles in humans, where different signs were associated with distinct movement patterns in a 3D environment, and the swarm of robots adjusted its navigation accordingly to mimic the observed human behavior. These experiments showcase the potential benefits of our approach in creating an interdependent human-swarm interaction framework, where a human navigates a swarm of robots through intended task instructions, and the swarm interprets and responds to the hand signals purposefully. The application of our method extends beyond the swarm robotics domain as a means of hand sign recognition, which can be utilized in other fields such as gesture-based computing. A key challenge in quantum simulation involves creating a wide variety of states with unconventional properties, mainly due to the lack of control over state evolution in quantum systems. Developing methods that can smoothly modify quantum states without introducing errors or unwanted excitations is crucial for population transfer in experimental contexts. Recent advances in variational approaches have led to the development of specific strategies for counterdiabatic evolution, which can efficiently create complex states with fewer errors. Here, we investigate the application of a particular CD strategy, rooted in a transformation that decouples the Hubbard model's momentum and spatial degrees of freedom, for preparing ground-state configurations. By comparing it with a global adiabatic technique, we consider the effect of symmetry and interference on the efficiency of state preparation, showing that symmetry significantly improves results despite increasing entanglement, while coherence has an opposing effect that accelerates state creation when reduced. Moreover, we demonstrate the potential of our method for creating exotic states with extended superfluidity and entropy properties. Through simulations of ultracold atoms, our findings highlight the importance of managing symmetry and coherence to achieve efficient state preparation in realistic experimental settings, including both Hamiltonian engineering and property manipulation. The insights gained here could be extrapolated to create complex interaction Hamiltonians, potentially opening new avenues in theoretical and experimental research. The ground-state properties resulting from our simulations could hold significant value for theoretical investigation. An extended version of this research, exploring the application of the CD strategy to the Hubbard model using Rydberg atoms, is also available. A cutting-edge laser-plasma technology generates an intense X-ray spectrum, from hard X-rays to intense gamma rays. This research area has seen significant growth, with science-driven motivations going beyond plasma physics and fundamental physics, also including medical applications, multiplexed and high-throughput analytics, and studying quantum systems at the atomic level. In this review, we focus on an innovative approach using plasma-based laser-plasma accelerators to produce a unique spectrum in the hard X-ray and gamma-ray range. We demonstrate that by combining this approach with a complementary laser-plasma method can offer even greater advantages, opening new possibilities in the fields of nuclear physics, astrophysics, materials science, medical applications, and fundamental quantum physics, particularly with regard to free-electron x-ray and gamma-ray sources. We also discuss the current progress made so far and present a vision for potential advancements in this exciting and rapidly evolving field.
