Measuring a firm's performance relative to its optimal efficiency level using input Optimization can be a powerful tool for decision-makers, helping to identify the minimum efficiency thresholds and evaluate the efficiency scores of companies in the industry. By leveraging a stochastic optimization framework, researchers can estimate a firm's efficiency using a sample of its optimization solutions, allowing for the analysis of both the efficiency of individual companies and the overall efficiency trends in the market. To achieve this, researchers can utilize the StoNED (Stochastic Non-orientable Data Envelopment Analysis) model, which provides a method for assessing a firm's efficiency in a multi-output environment. To simplify the use of this model for practitioners, we have developed a Python implementation, known as pyStoNED, which includes an implementation of the StoNED model and an efficient algorithm for computing the parameters, along with a series of tools for analyzing and visualizing the results. pyStoNED has been successfully applied to a dataset of French manufacturing companies. The implementation of pyStoNED aims to make it easier for researchers to analyze the trends and patterns in a firm's efficiency over time, as well as to compare a firm's efficiency with that of its peers. Furthermore, we have created a new dataset of French manufacturing companies, along with the code and procedures used to analyze it, to demonstrate the effectiveness of pyStoNED. The results show that, on average, the sample mean spectral efficiencies of French manufacturing companies have exhibited annual growth of about three percent since 1990. What's more, there is substantial variability in firms' efficiency over time, with some companies experiencing relatively small variations in efficiency across years and others experiencing more significant fluctuations. To achieve better performance, decision-makers should prioritize strategies aimed at improving firms' internal or external links with other businesses. The analysis of these results relies heavily on the developed analysis tools within the pyStoNED framework, without which it would be extremely difficult to achieve such insights from the data. What's more, the results highlight the significance of internal and supply-chain competitiveness in determining firms' efficiency and supporting policy-making efforts. The analysis demonstrates that policy interventions targeting specific value-chain nodes can have a major impact on firms' efficiency and overall productivity, and that achieving better efficiency in these cases requires more complex decision-making approaches. The developed tools within the pyStoNED library have proven particularly valuable in identifying trends and explaining the impact of interventions on firms' performance, and that is an area where further research is needed. In the era of expanding data demands, significant challenges arise, especially in the context of language processing. Firstly, the requirement for vast amounts of labeled data significantly hinders many supervised learning models. Secondly, the sheer volume of newly emerging texts makes real-time manual examination an impractical task, necessitating the development of more efficient methods for processing and analyzing language content. To address these concerns, this research leverages the capabilities of pre-trained language models, integrating them with data-driven approaches for extracting and refining structural components, such as named entities and dependency relationships. By exploring unified frameworks that combine the strengths of the GPT-family models and the BERT-family models, this work introduces new techniques for structure extraction, structure representation, and structural analysis, ultimately enabling the model to capture complex structural information without requiring extensive labeled data or human oversight. To demonstrate its efficacy, this research executes in-depth structural analyses on various datasets in medicine and cuisine. Moreover, the proposed framework is made publicly available through the Git repository https://github.com/guyan001/unfew, as well as the accompanying server https://server-unfew.gitee.io. To the best of our knowledge, this study innovates the development of the GPT-family models, particularly the GPT-2 model, in structured text analysis, as well as the adaptation of the BERT-family models, excluding RoBERTa, in the same field. Additionally, this research develops two novel techniques for few-example learning: entity extraction using the GPT-2 model and structured text analysis, and structure representation employing the BERT model and structured sentence decomposition. Ultimately, the results of the experiments show the superiority of the proposed unified framework over 20 existing baselines across four different tasks, achieving an average F1-score of 0.1456, an F1-score increase of 48.2% over the strongest competitor. By expanding the boundaries of the existing models, this research is believed to contribute to the advancement of the field. To improve text standardization, inverse text standardization approaches can be employed. During this process, a large database of standardized text is referenced to correct text that doesn't meet a desired standard. One significant challenge with these methods is the loss in textual characteristics after extracting words from their original context. Furthermore, as word usage evolves over time, there's a growing issue of word phrases that have become obsolete. Effective inverse text standardization requires not only comprehensive dictionaries but also a deep understanding of valid word sequences. To this end, we are introducing a data enhancement method to aid in acquiring a thorough description of current language usage. This technique analyzes a database of standardized text and generates various versions of each sentence to illustrate all its aspects. To facilitate standardization, a dictionary of the smallest textual elements -- words -- is supplemented with a database of significant phrases. This structural knowledge is then used to re-create the original non-standard text in a way that mimics the dictionary's description of the target standard. To optimize this re-creation, a specialized model is developed. Its structure is specifically designed to incorporate multiple versions of a sentence while preserving their internal consistency. To complete the optimization process, a neural network model is employed, trained on the structure of the sentence models. This network can recreate a valid sentence that accurately reflects the dictionary's description of the standard. To facilitate training, a large database of text examples is generated. To test the method's potential, a challenging standardization task was defined: correcting the text of the first edition of "Alice in Wonderland" without reference to its original meaning. To this end, a neural network model was trained on a database of the book's sentences. When applied, the model successfully corrected 94.7% of the book's text while preserving its original meaning. To further validate the method, a test was conducted using a challenging standardization task, comparing our approach with a competing method that re-creates a valid standard using a dictionary description. When applied, our approach re-created the standard text in a form indistinguishable from the dictionary description (KL divergence: 0.66). This paper demonstrates the Faber-Krahn inequality for the first eigenvalue of 
the Hermite operator when subject to Robin boundary conditions, with 
specific weights depending on $x$ and $\partial_x$, in one-dimensional space. 
A sharp inequality is proven in terms of the weight function $\omega(x)$ and 
its mean value $\bar{\omega} = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_{a}^{b}\omega(x)\,dx$. 
Moreover, when $\omega(x)$ is a constant, say $\lambda$, the inequality is 
proven to be tight; however, for general cases where the mean value of $\omega(x)$ 
is not zero, the inequality is found to be strict. Ultimately, some examples are 
utilized to confirm the accuracy of the newly established Robin Faber-Krahn inequality. 
The inequality is found to be analogous to its Neumann counterpart but is found 
to diverge from the Dirichlet counterpart. 
A useful application of this new inequality is found within the context of a study 
where the characteristics of a system's harmonic oscillator are investigated 
using specific cases of $\omega(x)$. 
To begin, two studies are adapted into three types: the Neumann, Robin, and 
Dirichlet cases, resulting in distinct eigenvalues in each; through analysis, 
it is determined that the Neumann and Robin cases share numerous similarities, 
while the Robin case surpasses the Dirichlet case. 
The proposed method may be leveraged in future research to derive tighter

Transformers' sequential nature limits their application in various fields. To address this, a family of transformer-based models with NFT-Core architecture has been developed, leveraging kernel methods to expand their capabilities and enhance their scalability. The core, designed to handle datasets without exchangeability, utilizes kernel elimination and generalized formula derivation to improve efficiency and scalability. By assigning a core to each group of sequences, NFT-Cores can process independent data sets, and our kernel-embeddings alignment technique ensures their alignment with established cores. This approach allows for the flexible integration of NFT-Cores, achieving optimal model performance. Through experiments and analysis, we validate the benefits of our NFT-Core architecture and kernel-embeddings alignment technique, demonstrating their superiority in various applications. Our findings indicate that multi-task learning via NFT-Cores can surpass single-task approaches in model scalability, and that kernel-embeddings alignment further improves the accuracy of deep learning models in low-data scenarios. Ultimately, our proposed NFT-Cores provide a versatile family of transformer-based models, suitable for a wide range of applications. -- Updated from initial submission -- Our exploration of NFT-Cores' potential has led to the discovery of an additional advantage: (i) pre-training NFT-Cores on random data results in an adversarial robustness of the model that cannot be easily attacked using standard approaches, (ii) due to NFT-Cores' ability to process independent data sets, the associated adversarial attack is highly computationally intensive, (iii) the increased cost of the attack is not a result of an overly complex model but rather an inherent property of NFT-Cores that cannot be easily understood via state-of-the-art explanations. This additional advantage has been incorporated into the updated abstract and paper. The updated version of the paper also includes two additional experimental results, demonstrating that NFT-Cores' associated adversarial robustness cannot be easily explained by state-of-the-art explainable models. -- Updated from updated initial submission -- Our proposed NFT-Cores has been successfully applied to the analysis of adversarial robustness, providing four distinct contributions that are not related to the initial final update: (i) the establishment of a new type of data-free adversarial attack, (ii) the confirmation of NFT-Cores' adversarial robustness through a theoretical demonstration, (iii) an analysis of the relation between NFT-Cores' adversarial robustness and its cost, and (iv) a comparison of NFT-Cores' adversarial robustness with existing approaches. Listeners identified the personalities of the synthetic voices based on characteristics such as agreeableness, emotional sensitivity, warmth, energy, assertiveness, and competence, and overall perceived them as effective in conveying these traits. However, controllers crafted with such artificial intelligence lack the transparency and adaptability required in unpredictable systems. In particular, the possibility of detecting and overcoming unexpected sudden changes in the system's dynamics cannot be guaranteed. To address this limitation, this research introduces a new model-based method that aims to develop robust and adaptable controllers using reinforcement learning. By incorporating a stochastic approach to model learning, the proposed algorithm is able to create multiple possible controller variants based on the learned model distribution, ensuring resilience to potential system changes. To defend against sudden changes, the policy learning algorithm utilizes the model distribution as a measure of uncertainty, combining simulated data with actual real-world data collected over time. Through simulation testing on a 14-subsystem system, the proposed method successfully created multiple adaptive controllers capable of navigating complex nonlinear dynamics, while equally protecting the controller from attacks and defending against sudden changes in the system's dynamics. Notably, the proposed method was found to outperform multiple existing controllers despite not utilizing expert-designed controllers or incorporating any form of regularization. Furthermore, the method was found to be more effective than traditional model-based methods which often struggle with identifying changes to the system's dynamics. Researchers have been studying the Larmor clock for over 60 years, and have successfully applied quantum theory to the Larmor clock in 2005. In this current research, a new quantum time measurement approach is presented, where the duration of a particle's tunneling event is directly linked to the frequency of oscillating spin within the Larmor clock. Initially, the study considered a non-tunneling particle, revealing that its spin oscillation frequency is zero. Based on this understanding, the study then examined a tunneling particle using the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, and derived an energy equation for the case where a particle undergoes tunneling. This energy equation is analogous to that of a non-tunneling particle, and its solution yields a particle probability density. When the particle undergoes tunneling, its spin oscillation frequency is found to be proportional to the duration of the tunneling event, and this duration is achievable through measurement when the particle completes one and a half oscillations. This research also demonstrates that the tunneling duration is defined by the particle being within a specific region, and this duration is proportional to the particle's mass. Experimenters can replicate this phenomenon using the Larmor clock with the conditions: particle mass of 1kg, tunneling duration of one second, and corresponding oscillation frequency of 0.6 Hz. Finally, the study considers the energy requirements for the particle to complete one, two, and three oscillations, and examines how these requirements compare to the energy requirements for a non-tunneling particle. Together, these results validate the application of quantum theory to the Larmor clock in tunneling phenomena. This research has significant implications for understanding quantum systems, and its results could pave the way for a new approach to quantum measurement. Researchers have achieved groundbreaking measurements in both non-tunneling and tunneling cases, and these measurements demonstrate that the frequency of oscillating spin within the Larmor clock is intimately linked to the duration of a tunneling event. This relationship allows for the measurement of the tunneling duration, and highlights the novel connection between spin oscillations and tunneling events in the Larmor clock. Continuous learning in real-world situations often involves learning multiple concepts sequentially from various sources. However, one major obstacle in advanced machine learning models arises when trying to adapt to new tasks quickly, especially when task similarities are minimal. To overcome this challenge, researchers have developed the Collective Continuous Learning (CCL) framework, which aims to separate task-specific interpretations from general representations by grouping similar tasks together and integrating them into a broader framework. Despite its initial potential, however, CCL has shown practical limitations in keeping state information for online learning conditions, particularly in large-scale training settings. To address these issues, this paper proposes a framework called Neural Framework for Online Collective Continual Learning (NOCL-NF) that uses a lightweight and adaptable neural network to manage state information effectively. NOCL-NF also incorporates a unique ensemble mechanism to improve its overall performance and stability. By combining multiple component models with minimal additional parameters, it achieves effective ensemble effects while keeping computational requirements low. Experimental results demonstrate that NOCL-NF outperforms other competitors in collective continual learning scenarios, both in terms of final performance and computational efficiency. To facilitate further research, the paper also makes available a comprehensive dataset collection containing 90 challenging tasks, dubbed NOCL-Dataset, which is accessible at https://nocl-dataset.github.io/. The source code for NOCL-NF can be found at https://github.com/argus007/NOCL-NF. The research also highlights potential issues related to data quality, label accuracy, and class balance, which are crucial factors to consider in collective continual learning. The study also showcases the current standard-based models' sensitivity to these factors, leaving room for potential improvements through data engineering approaches. The research ultimately points to promising collective semi-supervised learning directions that could enhance collective continual learning effectiveness. The study also examines the current standards in collective continual learning and proposes a more robust ensemble-based approach to overcome existing gaps. The research also evaluates its findings against baseline models, using a combination of diagnostic methods and detailed analysis. The study also shares its code and dataset through public repositories to facilitate further research. The research also provides a thorough review of related works in collective continual learning and proposes a novel online ensemble-based approach to overcome existing gaps. The study also evaluates its findings against state-of-the-art methods, using a combination of performance analysis and parameter complexity measurement. The research also shares its code and dataset through public repositories to facilitate further research. Using these counts, we further determine the Erdős-Ginzburg-Ziv type upper limits for the additive sums of four elements in a finite field of size $q^{3}$. Furthermore, we confirm that these values match the known lower bounds for the additive sums of four elements in a finite field of size $q^{3}$, as proven by Gao and Liu. The findings presented here are a direct consequence of our analysis on the permutation functions and complete permutation functions over a finite field of size $q^{3}$. In addition, we offer a straightforward evidence of Gao and Lao's result that shows the additive sums of four elements in a finite field of size $q^{3}$ cannot exceed the value of $\frac{4q^{3}+3q^{2}}{2}$. This proof is simpler compared to Gao and Lao's result, as well as other results established by Chen, Chen and Gao, and Chen, Gao and Lao. Finally, we conduct an analysis on the additive sums of four elements in a finite field of size $q^{4}$ and set up an upper limit for the counts of permutation functions and complete permutation functions over a finite field of size $q^{4}$. The path planning problem in unstructured environments is a critical challenge in unmanned systems, and solving it efficiently is a prerequisite for navigating through obstacles to reach a goal position. Our enhanced SDSM method achieves optimal results in a feasible space by incorporating a genetic filter to analyze candidate solutions and streamline the searching process, while introducing random guesses as an initial population to accelerate the convergence of dual simplex algorithms. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we've implemented a flight controller called PIDA, which demonstrates the feasibility of our method by applying dual simplex algorithms to optimize the path and trajectory of a feasible solution in a probabilistic environment, and using a genetic filter to filter and accelerate the convergence of feasible solutions in real-time. Our research shows that PIDA can achieve steady and stable flight in real-time, with the overall framework being termed as PIDA: Path Planning and Path Following. The results reveal that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of real-time path planning and real-time flight control, offering a level of robustness and stability. Additionally, the genetic filter and SDSM framework make it possible to achieve an optimal feasible solution in real-time, which can be applied to a wide range of Feasible Path Planning problems. Detecting distinct patterns in categories of data is a key objective in numerous applications. In the context of contagious diseases spreading across populations, non-parametric methods using graph theory have yielded substantial benefits. Prior approaches typically separate data into two groups, whereas detecting an arbitrary number of groups requires employing alternative algorithms. In this paper, we present a new geometric method for grouping data on a plane or surface, based on the K-means algorithm. By linking each data point with its nearest network connections and determining the center of the resulting geometric shape formed by these connections, our method effectively clusters data. Notably, our approach can automatically determine the optimal number of groups without needing to specify it. In addition, we present an analytical solution for clustering nodes closest to each other in a graph. By leveraging the Riemannian structure of the graph, we develop an algorithm with a time complexity of O(n log n) and demonstrate its efficiency through clustering exercises on graphs of up to 13,000 nodes and datasets of up to 43,000 time points. Our new method also outperforms existing algorithms in a comparative study using graphs of 4,000 nodes. Lastly, we illustrate the efficacy of our approach through a case study analyzing COVID-19 outbreaks in Scotland. In summary, our geometric method offers a novel K-means algorithm with a time complexity of O(n log n) that can automatically determine the number of groups and relies on standard geometric ideas. As a result, it can be employed as a standalone graph clustering algorithm or combined with existing methods for enhanced performance. With a user-friendly implementation available on GitHub, including associated COVID-19 data, our algorithm can be easily utilized. Furthermore, our method generates coherent, spatially-structured outbreaks that lend themselves to subsequent modeling and prediction. Specifically, we demonstrate that our algorithm is compatible with the SIQR model developed by Ke et al. in 2021. In the future, we intend to develop more sophisticated models by integrating our algorithm with the existing literature. In particular, we aim to analyze the detection power of diffusive processes using non-parametric methods and to develop models incorporating time series, behavioral parameters, and other relevant factors as part of a broader statistical framework. Ultimately, our research aims to contribute to a future Bayesian framework for analysis and prediction, much like the one proposed by Ke et al. in 2021. Although our current work remains largely methodological and experimental, it lays the groundwork for a more in-depth, theoretically-informed analysis in the future. Related files - 1909.

In reinforcement learning scenarios with changing objectives and unknown reward functions, agents typically receive suboptimal training data. This phenomenon, referred to as referential uncertainty, stems from the alignment of observers' and agents' understanding of task instructions. As a result, agents may adapt poorly to new tasks or rely heavily on human corrections, which can be an inefficient use of human resources. We introduce a cutting-edge method to address referential uncertainty through reference clarification. This innovative technique utilizes natural language processing to pinpoint potential ambiguities in human corrections and present them to humans for clarification. As an example, our method is applied to a real-world robot pushing domain, which requires agents to push objects into specified locations. We demonstrate that our approach effectively mitigates referential uncertainty and enhances learning outcomes, as supported by a quantitative user study. This research is expected to contribute to the advancement of reinforcement learning with changing objectives and highlight referential uncertainty as a crucial consideration in goal-conditioned reinforcement learning. We're exploring the shadow of quantum channels through the implementation of the shadow tomography technique. Shadow tomography offers a new approach to reconstructing the dynamics of quantum systems without requiring intense computational power. Our research involves examining the capabilities of shadow tomography in reconstructing quantum channels across varying degrees of dimensionality, channel types, and initial state accuracy. We discovered that shadow tomography effectively reconstructs quantum channels in resource-friendly scenarios but faces significant challenges in high-dimensional settings, particularly when dealing with quantum channels having singular values close to 1. These findings suggest that shadow tomography is best suited for applications requiring resource-efficient scaling, such as quantum diagnostics, rather than more complex tasks like optimizing quantum gate design. Additionally, we advocate for further research in developing techniques to refine initial state approximations for more accurate channel reconstructions. Our results also illustrate the utility of shadow tomography in reconstructing quantum channels of unique types, such as entangling quantum channels, and demonstrate its potential in constructing accurate channel families through randomized reconstructions. Finally, we've developed key mathematical equations underlying shadow tomography, specifically the average fidelity and mean absolute deviation, and have implemented them in cross-disciplinary applications to validate the feasibility of applying shadow tomography to analyze quantum channels. These equations can be found in the associated code repository. Through numerical simulations based on real-world experiments, we've confirmed the practicality of using shadow tomography to reconstruct quantum channels even under constraints of limited experimental data and low-dimensional quantum systems. Our work has implications for future research on channel reconstruction and may also inspire new approaches to quantum tomography. It's anticipated that these findings could lead to new developments in this area. In the context of learning generative models, a typical approach involves
examining the inverse Hessian matrix of the likelihood model, terms which
often contain invisible strings. To simplify this, we've redefined the
underlying representation by approximating negative Hessian matrices at a
specific point, resulting in a more manageable 'profound generative decoder'.
This decoder offers an accurate approximation of the true representation, 
allowing us to leverage white-box techniques and analyze its structure. 
Furthermore, we've extended this approach to the context of amortized
inferencers, developing a ProAD that approximates the reverse Hessian matrix, 
and showing its potential in accelerating variational inference. The code is
publicly accessible at https://github.com/andreabanti/profound. Our research 
is based on recent findings, specifically as documented in NeurIPS '21 paper, 
and an extended version is presented at arXiv:2201.05612. Additional insights were
also published at ICML 22, paper ID 211 in the Context-Aware Neural Hooking track.

The combination of autoencoders offers an effective sequence-to-sequence based solution for natural language tasks such as generating speech from text, yet their extensive training time and substantial memory requirements render them unfeasible for deployment on devices with limited capabilities, such as mobile devices and neural chipsets. To address this limitation, we propose an altered network architecture and training protocol that facilitates speedy and high-quality unsupervised speech generation. By replacing the standard encoder-decoder architecture with a simpler model that directly produces speech from text using a single pass, we significantly reduce the training time. Additionally, we employ the same encoder for multiple decoders to minimize memory usage and streamline the training process. Furthermore, we suggest using pre-trained models and fine-tuning instead of relying on a pre-conditioning period to save time, and implement the Swish activation function to boost model performance. Experimental results reveal that our method produces competitive outcomes on the LibriSpeech dataset, achieving a slight improvement in P/R ratio, and enables speech generation 2.5 times faster and with 50% reduced memory usage compared to the standard combination of autoencoders. Notably, the top-performing model requires only 20GB of GPU memory, making it suitable for deployment on devices with limited capabilities. Overall, our work aims to bridge the gap between cutting-edge unsupervised speech generation models and real-world implementation on resource-constrained devices. Recently, there has been an accelerated generation of diverse biomedical data collected from various experimental and simulation methods, causing a shifting imbalance between data availability and analysis capacity. Even though there are several data analysis tools, they often have limitations such as time constraints, user unfriendliness, and incompatibility with large datasets, causing a slowing analysis pace and hindering researchers' ability to keep pace with newly produced data. Furthermore, researchers face difficulties integrating and collaborating on cross-disciplinary projects due to differences in data analysis methods and software requirements, preventing data sharing and complicating reproducibility. As a result, there is an urgent need for a user-friendly, flexible, and scalable cyberinfrastructure framework that supports data exchange, workflow creation, and parallel computing to accelerate biomedical data analysis. We have developed the DataLab cyberinfrastructure portal from scratch to address these challenges, incorporating an advanced data exchange component that integrates data formats, ontologies, and workflows to facilitate user-friendly data analysis with various biomedical ontology terms. We have also created an interactive data exchange dashboard coupled with a state-of-the-art parallel computing engine that supports data analysis on local, remote clusters, and high-performance computing grids, demonstrating its efficiency by comparing it with leading data analysis tools. Our experiments show that our cyberinfrastructure portal delivers superior scalability, reliability, and serviceability, achieving up to 5 times faster results than leading data analysis tools, enabling users to run multiple data analysis tasks simultaneously, automatically detect errors, and receive timely service even during server downtime, validating our approach to developing cyberinfrastructure and guiding future development guidelines and best practices for designers and developers. Overall, our cyberinfrastructure portal enhances data sharing, collaboration, and reproducibility while facilitating large-scale biomedical data analysis, promoting data exchange and workflow creation. The intricate nature of aspect-based emotion analysis stems from its two-core tasks: aspect-term sentiment analysis and specific emotion detection. Effective training for both tasks is hindered by the'shared feature space issue'. To address this challenge, a novel approach called guided contrastive pre-training is proposed, leveraging the contrasting nature of positive and negative samples to create separate feature spaces for aspects and emotions. This leads to improved performance and distinct representations, particularly in sentiment analysis. Furthermore, a BERT-based model incorporating semi-supervised learning through self-training is explored, enhancing generalization and convergence in specific emotion detection tasks. Experiments on publicly available datasets demonstrate the efficacy of this framework, resulting in notable improvements of 5.38% and 3.28% in data-free specific emotion prediction, and up to 6.48% and 4.51% in aspect-based sentiment analysis. These advances significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art models and methodologies. The code and model weights are publicly available on https://github.com/autumn-fan/ABEA_GCP_SSL. In the Wild Internet Archive, a collection of deceased web pages offers a glimpse into the permanent nature of human information preservation. However, searching through the vast amounts of archived web content is a daunting task, akin to digging through a literary treasure trove. Despite the advantages of access-driven search methodologies, efficiently summarizing relevant content remains an unresolved challenge. To address this gap, a novel framework called Hindsight is proposed, designed to improve summarization by combining resampling and renaming techniques in a value-driven approach. Hightonst is the corresponding tool for Hindsight, featuring a comprehensive evaluation of existing resampling and renaming methods through benchmarking, followed by a value-driven evaluation of its results. Recent studies have demonstrated the capabilities of neural networks in solving partial differential equations with high accuracy, despite being trained with limited observational data. However, the network's ability to generalize depends on the nature of the PDE and available observations. In this research, we investigate the use of cell-mean based neural networks for elliptic and hyperbolic PDEs. These neural networks derive the mean outcome within a grid of cells based on the network's point predictions. We develop an innovative optimization method for training cell-mean based neural networks, specifically designed for PDEs. Our approach leverages an optimization groundhog to tackle constraints related to boundary conditions, volume integrals, and data adherence, which proves particularly beneficial for networks addressing hyperbolic PDEs. Notably, the technique can handle datasets with non-uniformly distributed observations. Through a range of numerical experiments, we validate the efficiency and potential of cell-mean based neural networks for solving high-speed elliptic and hyperbolic PDEs. One of the numerical test cases even surpasses existing state-of-the-art results by achieving a relative L2 error of 4.0% for the hyperbolic test case of a shock wave in a molecular gas. The success of these results stems from the ability of cell-mean based neural networks to accurately interpret data without literally replicating observed patterns. Moreover, the technique can also tackle inverse problems where underlying data is limited or non-existent. Specifically, the algorithm is applied to recover coefficients of an elliptic equation of a shock wave. The analysis of the obtained results sheds light on the role of measurements in reconstructing the coefficient profile. Ultimately, the technique demonstrates the capacity to accurately reconstruct the coefficient profile with a L2 relative error of 4.7% despite the absence of underlying data source. This study focuses on a previously unexplored topic, known as Occasion Extraction, which involves identifying the underlying reasons or contexts behind event occurrences. Events can occur for diverse reasons and understanding these underlying contexts is essential to grasp the event's meaning, making it a crucial component of natural language understanding. Unlike other related NLP tasks such as taking a medication, studying, or traveling, occasion extraction requires a more explicit context indicating a timeline, causality, or consequence. For instance, "she took the medicine at midnight to fall asleep." Here, the occasion is "to fall asleep" which signifies that the medicine was consumed for insomnia relief. Considering this newly emerging area, current NLU models still fall short in providing reasonable intelligence on this task and there is an overwhelming need for a comprehensive dataset to develop more accurate and robust models. To address this challenge, we introduce MEE, a multilingual dataset designed for Occasion Extraction, featuring 11,000 annotated text samples across three distinct domains, including scientific research papers, real-world web content, and real social media posts covering three languages, including English, Chinese, and Arabic. Our experiments not only showcase the effectiveness of models, including BERT and ELMo, but also highlight their limitations in handling occasions. Notably, while BERT-based models excel on samples that are closely related to the context, they struggle with samples that have ambiguous or reverse relationships with the occasion. Interestingly, even with extensive training, models fail to generalize to new and unseen scenarios even if the context is closely related with the occasion. The dataset and accompanying analysis are accessible via our GitHub repository at: https://github.com/ameerameer/MEGA.git. Furthermore, we also offer a competitively designed dataset called MEE-LT, which is specifically tailored to language pairs, available via https://github.com/ameerameer/MEGA-LT. This research not only opens doors for further language and dataset development but also paves the way for an extended multilingual approach to the Occasion Extraction task. A key challenge in natural language understanding stems from the necessity to access language independently in its universal semantic and syntactic dimensions. Although current techniques try to bridge this gap, they often struggle with diversity in training datasets, complicating the task with multiple possible semantic interpretations based on syntax. Recent advances in neural networks have successfully addressed some of these challenges, but still fall short of providing a robust general syntactic and semantic analysis. On the other hand, symbolic methods can easily synergize different language analysis models while addressing the diversity issue, but they are limited in automatically generating translations, unless additional heuristics are applied. To bridge this limitation, we suggest fusing symbolic and neural techniques and providing additional heuristics for translation. Our method is tested through applications in a variety of domains including subject identification, sentence simplification, and part-of-speech identification across different languages, showing promising results across all these applications. A significant component of this research was also conducted through user studies that highlighted the importance of high-quality syntactic and semantic annotations, a requirement our method seamlessly addresses through the proposed model. To support future researchers, we release our method, annotated datasets, and relevant toolsets. Researchers have identified some early-type galaxies that have extremely large scales within 0.46 Gpc by using data from Hyper Suprime-Cam, a Subaru telescope. These "giant E TGs" have distinct scales separated by a clear boundary, characteristic of massive galaxies. The large scales, however, indicate that they are still in an early stage of formation, which can only occur through the process of galaxy mergers. The data show a high ratio of outer galaxy mass to central mass in these giant E TGs, 0.26, which is significantly greater than typical massive galaxies, 0.07. The distinction between giant E TGs and normal galaxies cannot be solely based on this mass ratio. The researchers have found a strong correlation between the galaxies that contributed to the large scales and the luminosity of those galaxies. The inside outside flux ratio in these giant E TGs has a mean of 0.28 and shows a high degree of uniformity. The type 1 PGCs of PGc-IG have a mean of 0.28. This implies that the large mass outside the distinguished scales in these galaxies, 0.64 of total mass, comes from the mergers of smaller galaxies rather than through the accretion of hot gas. The merger of large galaxies results in a final total mass of 1.3 times the original mass, with 0.64 of that mass added to the black hole. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports anonymous transactions 
on multiple blockchains, showcasing its efficiency on the Bitcoin and 
Eclipse blockchain. The original RingCT, while effective, has a significant 
transaction size overhead due to the inclusion of an encryption layer. 
Our improved protocol eliminates this extra overhead, instead utilizing it 
for enhanced security features, including a more robust decoy transaction 
scheme. Previous RingCT transactions only included decoy wallet modifications 
in one layer, resulting in less effective noise. In contrast, our upgraded 
protocol leverages RingCT's encryption to incorporate decoy transactions 
in both layers, offering superior anonymity. The combination of these advances 
enables high-speed transactions, as evidenced by testing on the Bitcoin 
mainnet and Eclipse mainnet, alongside a comprehensive analysis of the 
trade-off between transaction speed and anonymity levels. The results 
demonstrate that our delegated RingCT protocol achieves these goals without 
compromising on anonymity, even when incorporating an additional 
unlinkable payment option. The success of these experiments confirms the 
usefulness of our upgraded protocol in multiple blockchain environments. 
Lastly, we acknowledge a critical timing-related limitation of our 
protocol, which may pose potential security risks in specific situations. 
Despite this, the benefits of our upgraded protocol clearly outweigh these 
potential drawbacks, making it suitable for deployment in most use cases.

the Eclipse GitHub repository at https://github.com/Chainber/ECLIPSE-RC2.

One such scenario is non-destructive testing for identifying surface defects in carbon-fiber reinforced polymers. Due to the inherent surface-to-volume ratio, conventional models often fail to effectively predict features such as notches, cracks, and manufacturing flaws. This proprietary technique utilizes an encoder to combine different data types, including images and point clouds, and then generates an encoded space-invariant map. Lastly, our work showcases the applicability of our method to various real-world problems, further establishing its practical utility. In planar graphs, researchers have proposed an efficient algorithm using distance labeling. This method assigns a unique set of integers to each vertex, known as a distance label, which determines its identity. This approach exploits the distances to all other vertices within a specific radius, which is typically much smaller than the total number of vertices. Although distance labeling offers superior performance in several settings, it suffers from vulnerabilities under malicious attacks that alter or remove vertices. To address this limitation, our study introduces an enhanced method called fault-tolerant distance labeling. This innovation incorporates error detection in the distance labeling scheme. Specifically, our FRDTK algorithm for general graphs requires a polynomial number of labels proportional to n^2, m^2, and delta^2, where n is the number of vertices, m is the edge density, and delta is the maximum degree. By restricting the graph to a planar layout, our FRDTK algorithm significantly reduces the label complexity to a polynomial bound of n^0.5358, demonstrating substantial savings in storage with this optimal solution. Furthermore, our results from experimental testing using various real-world datasets validate the polynomial tradeoff between the logarithm of the relative record size and the relative record density. We investigate the disciplinary loss of photons in the compelled single-mode Bose-Hubbard model, which incorporates both random gain and loss, as well as the associated phenomena of driven-dissipative Bose-Einstein condensation and non-equilibrium stationary states. In this study, we derive an analytical solution for the photon statistical distribution using the mean-field approximation, thereby accurately describing the influences of non-linear interactions on photon statistics, as well as the effects of random gain and loss. Unlike previous works, which have mostly focused exclusively on one or two dissipative processes, our theoretical framework is capable of addressing a comprehensive two-entity problem by combining compensatory techniques for arbitrary values of the non-linear interaction parameter. Our findings reveal that through the adjustment of system parameters, it is feasible to transition from the non-linear Lorenz-Stuart system to the conventional lossy Bose-Hubbard model, thereby facilitating comparisons between these two theoretically resolved and complex phenomena. Utilizing our moment method, which is based on the Pauli distribution, we derive closed-form solutions for first and second-order correlations of photon statistics, as well as the associated spectra and provide an in-depth analysis of non-linear photon interactions in the compelled lossy Bose-Hubbard model, which is complemented by the simulation results obtained from the quantum Monte Carlo method. By combining the moment method and the analytical solution obtained through the mean-field approximation, we are able to accurately describe and thoroughly understand the influences of non-linear interactions on photon correlations and spectra, thereby establishing a moment-spectrum of compound systems that combines the analytical solution and the moment method. Moreover, we extend our theoretical framework to investigate other disciplines, such as the compelled cubic Bose-Hubbard model, which is accompanied by the corresponding numerical results. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the complex relationships between random gain and linear or non-linear loss, which is facilitated by the moment method and the analytical solution obtained through the mean-field approximation. In addition, we are confident that the moment method can be extended to investigate and analyze other disciplines, such as the compelled cubic Bose-Hubbard model, as well as other complex phenomena at the quantum level. This study is intended to inspire further research into the moment method, which is an essential tool for understanding and analyzing a wide range of phenomena at the quantum level, particularly in the context of compelled systems, where the interaction between random gain and linear or non-linear loss is inherently fundamental. Specifically, dealing with dynamic network changes, implementation delays, and human intervention requirements in real-time SFCs poses significant challenges. The central part of the Milky Way exhibits a complex structure of bundled and tangled fibers consisting of rotating, star-forming cores, which are arranged in an arc-shaped pattern. A thorough investigation of these coherent units is crucial for understanding the core complex's development process. The primary objective of this study is to examine the physical attributes of these bundled cores. Through a detailed analysis of a core population dataset, which includes 55 identified fibers containing 315 cores, this research quantified the average diameter of these fibers ($8.0\pm 3.0$ degrees) and found that they tend to be shorter than expected based on their intrinsic scatter values. By assessing the angular separation distribution between neighboring cores within a fiber, this study found that only $11\%$ of cores in these bundles have a separation of less than $10^\circ$, indicating a significant gap in their arrangement. Additionally, this research discovered a lack of cores that are too close together, suggesting a minimum coherent structure extent of approximately $40^\circ$ in size. By interpreting the results through the perspective of a protostellar jet, this study found that the most likely cause of core proximity is due to the reexpansion of these jets from their birthplaces within the core complex. Notably, this research also points out a possible connection between the core fibers' appearance and the, currently observed, widespread protostellar group phenomenon. Furthermore, by comparing the protostellar core distribution with that of young stars in the area (as found in a separate study), this research found that only a small percentage ($0.2\%$) of these protostellar subunits show signs of dispersed star formation, which is much less common than expected across the entire core complex area. By considering the internal structure of these protostellar subunits, this research found that only a few subunits exhibit disordered star formation and that, in most cases, late-forming stars exist outside of these subunits, indicating an additional external process influencing their formation. The research concludes that early-forming stars within these subunits are densely packed and that late-forming stars, on the other hand, are more sparsely distributed, leading to a unique formation pattern of separate early and late-forming stars across the entire core complex area. To enhance the efficiency of distribution networks, reducing energy losses is crucial. One effective approach to this is the distributed Ideal Conservation Voltage Diminution strategy. This method fine-tunes primary voltage levels to minimize losses in networks with connected load devices. However, since these load devices' characteristics are unknown, the ICVD strategy must be compromised between optimal energy savings and voltage control feasibility. To improve this compromise, the paper proposes a distributed ICVD strategy that significantly improves performance over previous methods. For complex networks, the proposed method's computational complexity is analyzed and compared to its centralized counterpart, revealing a way to reduce complexity while maintaining improved results. Simulation data demonstrate that the new technique delivers substantial energy savings, up to a 35.6% improvement, while also being more robust to uncertain load parameters. Furthermore, the results show that the distributed ICVD method's energy savings are only about 0.9% away from the ideal conservative solution even in large networks. Finally, the paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the distributed ICVD method in modern network architectures with significant evidence. Current approaches to natural language learning in computational models are diverse and dispersed, leading to limited understanding of their individual benefits and combinations. To address this, we've developed a comprehensive framework, the LEARNING THROUGH ENvironment AND NATural dialogue with a Human under the Teaching regime (LEATHER), which standardizes and unifies the acquisition of natural language skills in computational models by incorporating a systematic approach to data collection, evaluation, and assessment. By establishing a structured model, we've investigated the effects of six fundamental principles underlying natural language abilities: syntax, semantics, vocabulary, context, intention, and approximation. To experiment with these principles, we've created two simplified language games that simulate human-like communication to demonstrate the teaching regime's efficacy in developing sophisticated language capabilities from fundamental elements. Although the initial results show that models learned under LEATHER outperform their counterparts on various tasks, such as intention detection and text creation, the experiments also highlight that combining multiple principles does not always lead to improved outcomes. Consequently, we suggest that future research acknowledge and explain the underlying assumptions of natural language learning in computational models and advocate for a dual approach, distinguishing between data-driven generalization and structured teaching methods in computational dialogue systems. The LEATHER teaching regime is applicable to various models, and we hope it will inspire similar initiatives in the field of natural language processing. To facilitate reproducible research, we've publicly released the code and data associated with our experiments at the LEATHER website.

During the early stages of an offshore wind farm's development, detailed load measurements are typically scarce, with limited prototypes subject to various environmental conditions. Nevertheless, researchers can utilize the available data to create a statistical model of turbine components' stresses, informing the optimization of design. By utilizing a Bayesian approach, a probabilistic proxy model can be developed to estimate the stresses of turbines, taking into account uncertainties associated with the meta-model. Recent research aims to expand the reach of machine learning to incorporate systems adhering to quantum mechanics, which necessitates adopting algorithms capable of processing data in accordance with both classical and quantum principles. To this end, we developed a novel version of the backpropagation algorithm suited for use in neural networks featuring quantum layers, which can efficiently compute gradients even in cases where the output differentiates in a non-analytic manner with respect to the input. Leveraging an existing explanation for the convergence of classical backpropagation, we proved its quantum counterpart's convergence, which in turn enabled us to derive an explicit expression for the rate of convergence for neural networks incorporating quantum layers. We further provided a comprehensive review of quantum circuits, which form the foundation of neural networks in quantum systems, discussing both the restricted and unrestricted variants. Lastly, we demonstrated through numerical simulations incorporated within a TensorFlow framework that quantum layers within neural networks capable of processing quantum data can yield outcomes consistent with current scientific knowledge. To date, the most effective approaches to integrating quantum mechanics into neural networks entail embedding classical layers within quantum circuits. By incorporating what is known as the backpropagation with the sign algorithm, which serves as an estimate of the gradient vector, we developed a quantum-enabled version of the Adam optimization algorithm capable of efficiently computing gradients in quantum systems to obtain optimal outcomes. The research validated the potential for leveraging quantum and classical layers within neural networks together to obtain accurate results. This research paper showcases a tool that translates ACL2 functions into efficient C code, and the generated C code can be seamlessly incorporated back into ACL2 for purposes of verification.  Key characteristics of this instrument include its capacity to impute absent ACL2 functions present in the target C code and its ability to accurately replicate ACL2's function behavior.  Underpinning this tool is a unique integration approach within ACL2, distinct from standard programming language embeddings in ACL2.  Utilizing ACL2's superficial execution model, the tool validates the correctness of the generated C code.  Validation is effectuated via a series of tests that reflect the tool's operational parameters, such as its reliance on the C code's recursive capabilities and the utilization of ACL2's mapsto function to determine memory pointer assignments.  To illustrate the tool's functionality, we detail its application in the creation of a C version of ACL2's list-data-structure function, list-elt, which permits the extraction of a specified list element defined by both an index and a total count.  Furthermore, we demonstrate the tool's production of non-trivial C code for a function designed to generate lists of random numbers, and the tool's verification of the tool's output correctness through the utilization of 500 unique test cases.  Key research outcomes include the demonstration of the tool's efficiency in terms of both processing speed and memory consumption and the determination of its processability test count.  Developed utility functions, including a data-structure comparison tool and a code processing speed diagnostic tool, were also introduced in the tool's documentation. In languages that distinguish gender through grammar, words are categorized based on their grammatical gender, which is influenced by semantic criteria. This paper investigates how a word's grammatical gender affects its representation in models, and we find that models trained on datasets including grammatical gender tend to learn inaccurate and biased representations of nouns based on their form rather than meaning. As a result, models are more likely to perpetuate social biases and inaccurate associations. Additionally, we show that these inaccurate representations can transfer to task-specific task representations, and we recommend developing guidelines and social guidelines to mitigate these issues when working with grammatically labeled datasets. Our study particularly focuses on languages such as Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese.  We've released our code and dataset recommendations for replication purposes.

Although words from the same category, such as animals, may share similar meanings, they may be mapped to different vectors based on their grammatical agreement class. For example, the French word for 'dog' in the masculine form and the feminine form are mapped to distinct vectors, and this separation also applies to other related words like 'feminine dog' and'masculine dog'. As a result, models trained on grammatically labeled data, such as the off-the-shelf French language model that we used, tend to learn inaccurate and biased representations of nouns based on their agreement class. 

We've discovered that these inaccurate representations can have a significant impact on a model's capacity to make incorrect and biased predictions on social issues, and we found that models are more likely to perpetuate these biases when trained on grammatically labeled data, and also when using form-based classifiers instead of meaning-based classifiers. By analyzing the impact of a word's agreement class on a model's representations and predictions, we've shown that these inaccurate representations can transfer to task-specific task representations, and more often result in incorrect and biased predictions. 

Finally, we've identified the agreement class of a word as an essential factor that affects its representation and predictions, and we recommend developing guidelines and interpretation guides to mitigate these issues when working with grammatically labeled datasets. 
This study is the first to investigate how a word's agreement class influences its representation and predictions, and we've chosen to study languages that distinguish gender through grammar because of their complexity and variability in how agreement classes are defined and the criteria that influence them.

Cyberphysical systems require a unique extension of cyber systems to manage the intricate interplay between physical and technical aspects in real-time. To achieve this, the concept of cyberphysical systems needs to capture the inherent properties of networked systems, allowing for decentralized control and localized decision-making. This must be complemented by a communication infrastructure that not only transfers data but also actively influences the behavior of system components, the physical world, and the interplay between CP and traditional networked control systems. 

This paper suggests a dual-layered cyber model to address these requirements. The upper layer represents the cognitive collective behavior of decentralized systems characterized by emergent phenomena. The lower layer is responsible for transferring data between centralized nodes. The study showcases the proposed model with three exemplary implementations: modeling collective behavior, the transfer of energy-like data, and the modeling of cyberphysical systems within the utility sector. 

Ultimately, the proposed approach is envisioned to facilitate the creation of formal cyber models that incorporate fundamental properties of physical systems, the inherent properties of networked control systems, and the inherent decentralization of cyberphysical systems, thus bringing the system's cognitive abilities to a state of near completeness. 

It is hoped that this methodology will enable researchers to formally express and capture the inherent properties of physical systems, the inherent properties of networked control systems, and the inherent decentralization of cyberphysical systems, thus bringing the system's cognitive abilities to a state of near completeness.

The notable advantage of federated learning is its ability to prevent data disclosure, ensuring the participant states' data security. However, once the trained model is shared with the federated server, it can be utilized to make predictions, which may lead to sensitive information exposure for participants. To address this concern, we aimed to develop a model where the trained model can estimate participant data while maintaining confidentiality, but our initial approach was unsatisfactory. Subsequently, we introduced a unique method, the categorical gradient barrier, to guarantee the trained model's differential confidentiality, and it can be optimized with participant data to enhance accuracy, specifically the participant's accuracy, at a reduced cost by minimizing the optimized model's training parameters. Our results show the potential of our approach to maintain a balance between model accuracy and participant data confidentiality. Recent research on intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRSs) has highlighted their potential in wireless communication systems, including their ability to improve the throughput of an energy harvesting network when assisted by a ground-laid IRS. However, real-world implementation of an IRS is hindered by the absence of precise phase information. This limitation can be mitigated with machine learning (ML), which recent studies have shown can effectively optimize IRS performance. Consequently, this study investigates the effectiveness of an unsupervised ML algorithm in enhancing the throughput of an IRS-assisted wireless energized network subject to disruption. To this end, a novel combination of ML and optimization techniques is developed, incorporating multiple deep neural networks (DNNs) to account for the influence of disruption parameters on the reflection coefficients of the IRS. Compared to existing solutions, the proposed approach yields considerable gains in throughput, with improvements of approximately $4.54$ and $6.05$ percent observed, respectively. Supervising learning in legged locomotion with basic reinforcement signals alone proves ineffective, as these creatures necessitate a combination of robustness, balance, and efficiency. Human intervention, typically in the form of pre-programmed control or trained neural controllers, is typically required to teach them to walk after collecting initial sensor data. However, supplementary information is often disregarded in such cases, such as the forces acting along the legs, which could also be part of the data gathered. We propose that these additional variables hold significant value in determining actions and maintaining stability, particularly in situations where limited data is available. We have developed an algorithm that leverages supervised learning by mapping leg forces to specific actions and control parameters, utilizing the forces from a few successful trajectories as a reference point to guide novel gaits. This method demonstrates exceptional adaptability, as evidenced by our experiments on a 13-Atlas robot, which successfully learns various gaits in under three minutes, even learning the ability to jump and balance while standing on one leg. We have further trained this model to locate its balance point by integrating ZMP-based supervisory signals, enabling it to walk along a straight path with minimal oscillations. These breakthroughs are built upon the idea of combining sensor data and supplementary information to design control strategies, which is presented in detail. We believe our work offers a new perspective on utilizing the wealth of supplementary information collected during data-driven control, and provides an in-depth analysis of the potential value in the actions and state of the system. Importantly, it challenges the conventional use of these additional variables, which has historically been viewed as noisy and irrelevant. We are confident that this approach will lead to the development of highly efficient, robust, and efficient legged locomotion systems, which will spur the creation of more robust and data-driven control strategies in the future. Object identification in written documents is crucial for both lexical and lexical-semantic analysis, yet existing dictionaries often fall short, leaving many words unaccounted for. To rectify this, a novel method using machine learning is introduced to enhance lexicon completeness, relying on training neural networks with pseudo labels derived from visual information about word appearances in documents' layouts. This approach leverages a type of convolutional neural network that excels at object detection within complex images, to quantify words within image-based representations of documents. Quantified words are then treated as distinct objects, enabling a ranking system to pinpoint individual words and demonstrating superior performance in comparison to a traditional machine learning technique that relies on text segmentation. Moreover, this new method easily scales to handle languages with a large vocabulary, such as English, and languages with a more limited vocabulary, such as Arabic and Greek. To facilitate replication and exploration of these findings, the associated code and a customized TensorFlow framework have been made openly available. By applying this method, it is now possible to identify both commonly used and infrequently used words in document formats, including various types of text - such as scientific publications, spoken dialogue, and written conversation - without relying on complex, human-driven approaches to text analysis. A collaborative effort led to the development of an extensive, 69-million-word open lexicon of individual words, encompassing a comprehensive range of vocabulary, and serving as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners. To ensure its continued development and expansion, a corresponding GitHub repository has been established, and multiple opportunities for future research have been identified. These opportunities include leveraging the lexicon and associated machine learning methods to facilitate a range of applications, such as improving word detection through visual and audio analysis, and refining the accuracy of machine translation. Importantly, the method and resources described in this dissertation are freely available to support a wide range of applications and research approaches. The Rho Ophiuchus cloud is situated close to the Sun, at a distance of just over 125 parsecs, making it an ideal subject for study in high resolution spectroscopic analyses due to its proximity. It is characterized by a prominent molecular core named S1 located centrally, surrounded by a photodissociation region (PDR) that is a result of external radiation sources. This area is seen to be compressing the PDR and, as a consequence, prevents it from expanding outward due to external pressure. High resolution spectra reveal molecular gas within 1 to 2 times the sound speed of neutral gas is observed, however PDR gas exists at approximately half of this speed. This suggests that PDR gas is contaminated with ionized gas originating from the S1 core. Furthermore, high resolution observations of CO, CN and CS molecules confirm that there exists inner regions lacking in molecular gas, characterized as'molecular voids', located at the heart of the S1 core, potentially influencing the surrounding PDR.  A PDR within Rho Ophiuchus has been estimated to be 0.5 to 1 parsecs in diameter, however in this study it has been found to be only approximately 0.25 parsecs in diameter, indicating that it is being overestimated. This study has also provided an accurate estimate for the Lyman beta continuum level, providing a potential explanation for the detection of ionized gas within the PDR. It is proposed that the detection of ionized gas within the PDR and the lack of molecular gas within the S1 core are a direct result of the'molecular voids', potentially produced during a core collapse, and the influence of an early stage magnetic field, however this requires further study.

Predictive models based on statistical analysis, such as linear regression and deep neural networks, often rely on an underlying factor structure to mitigate dimensionality issues and guide feature engineering in applications like mortality transference, financial analysis, and medical diagnosis. Given the versatility of factor models in addressing these problems, researchers have used Gaussian Graphical Models to represent relationships among variables and incorporate domain knowledge. However, traditional factor models assume a constant factor structure, which may be inadequate for applications involving continuous variables and driven by changing factor loadings. Following the success of time-varying extensions in areas such as topic modeling, researchers have developed a novel method for factor loadings that evolves over time, addressing constraints and leveraging domain knowledge to determine the factors' significance. The proposed approach, involving the selection of significant factors through optimization and regularization, effectively identifies and constrains the factors' state in time, resulting in a more accurate and efficient factor model representation. The method's efficacy has been validated through experiments on mortality prediction datasets as well as a medical diagnosis dataset employing expert domain knowledge, demonstrating the ability to capture time-varying factor dependencies accurately and resulting in notable improvements in predictive accuracy for mortality and medical diagnosis applications. The method's source code is publicly available.

Neural architecture search (NAS) is seen as a promising area for developing high-performing machine learning models automatically. Yet, a significant challenge for NAS lies in tackling the next step: model training. The issue arises due to the massive memory requirements and trainin costs associated with the traditionally employed training approach for nasnet architectures. Since most NAS methods rely on this approach, this trainin bottleneck significantly limits the scope and efficiency of their architecture search programs. In an effort to counter this problem, we are presenting two efficient model training methods called synthesis and apprendissage that yield substantial improvements in cost-effectiveness and model performance. Specifically, we demonstrate that our methods can train large nasnet architectures on GPUs like the V100, opening up previously inaccessible design spaces for NAS programs. The first method called synthesis separates the training process into individual components like layer rules and filter parameter initialization, thereby reducing its scale but not its overall number of parameters. In contrast, the second approach called apprendissage focuses on post-discovery model fine-tuning, aiming to diminish the impact of disruption on nasnet architectures. By combining these methods with a state-of-the-art architecture search technique, we are able to expand the scope of its design spaces while significantly reducing its training costs. Interestingly, our experiments reveal that nasnet architectures possessing smaller channel sizes exhibit greater resilience against disruption. Consequently, this discovery can be exploited to boost the performance of nasnet architectures possessing smaller channel sizes through either the synthesis or apprendissage method. Ultimately, our model achieves best-performance scores over various benchmarks, including CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet. Notably, our model sets a new standard for the ResNeXt architecture in the cross-space performance category, thereby validating our empirical findings. The source code for our methods called synthesis and apprendissage has been made publicly available on the GitHub platform. We intend to extend our methods in future research programs. The related hardware environment for our methods was supported by an NVIDIA V100 GPU. We will investigate other possible hardware setups in future work. The proposed initialization technique called synthesis has been successfully tested on various CPU and GPU systems. The proposed approach called apprendissage relies on supporting libraries like PyTorch and cudnn. We will explore other potential tools in future extensions of our methods. The synthesis method does not have memory requirements, but the apprendissage approach is sensitive to memory limitations. Time series analysis is now more accessible than ever due to the popularization of the ReStructuredText (R) programming language and the wide availability of time series data through the datasets package. Nonetheless, functioning expertly in this field demands not only a grasp of statistical concepts, but also proficiency in time series data preparation, including significant tasks such as data pre-processing, feature extraction, and visualization. A major shortcoming of the R programming language in time series analysis is the absence of a unified, all-encompassing package that addresses these fundamental tasks. In response to this shortcoming, we introduce the theft package with the aim of filling this gap. The theft package is designed to provide time series analysis functionality, supporting a comprehensive set of time series operations such as handling missing values, performing time series feature extraction, and creating time series-based dataframes. While t-SNE works well in many cases, it's not suitable for data that comes from sources like crowding experiments, where the correlation structure is more complex, particularly when neighboring points exhibit low correlation. Furthermore, applying t-SNE to such data can be inaccurate and inefficient, a problem that's particularly pronounced with partial data. Our main contribution is a new, spherical representation for t-SNE that utilizes the von Mises-Fisher distribution. This new model is an accurate reflection of the data's underlying structure, especially in cases with complex nearest-neighbor relationships. We've developed an efficient, GMF-based version of t-SNE that's particularly well-suited for partial data, maintaining good performance even when neighbors are far apart. This new method is an enhanced version of t-SNE and provides more accurate results than its predecessors, especially in cases with sparse data. Our experiments show that our technique provides more accurate recoveries of data from various, challenging sources. Furthermore, our technique outperforms other methods in terms of their ability to embed data from crowding experiments accurately. We've also provided code for our technique and shown that it's easier to modify the original t-SNE implementation to produce more accurate results. Our technique has many applications, particularly in cases with partial data, and we've provided numerous examples of its usefulness, starting from its simplest form, which sets a new standard for dimensionality reduction techniques that rely on t-SNE. Finally, our technique provides a more comprehensive understanding of the data's underlying structure, especially in cases with sparse data. We've also improved the t-SNE embeddings for data from crowding experiments and established a new, more accurate technique for this application, particularly in cases with partial data. Our work has many potential uses and sets a new standard for dimensionality reduction techniques that require accurate representation of the data's underlying structure. We've also improved the t-SNE implementation to produce more accurate results and have provided various examples of its usefulness, starting from its simplest form. Our embedding for data from crowding experiments outperforms other methods in terms of their ability to recover data from various, challenging sources. Our code and the original t-SNE implementation to produce more accurate results have many potential uses and sets a new standard for dimensionality reduction techniques that require accurate representation of the data's underlying structure.

The concentration of beauty hadrons was studied in Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC, specifically at a 5.02 TeV collision energy. A notable pattern was found where the concentration of beauty hadrons near midrapidity is lower in central collisions than in peripheral collisions and decreases as collision centrality decreases. This phenomenon was analyzed by comparing the electron yield with a non-charm lepton reference in different collision centrality classes and in various $p_{\rm T}$ ranges. In most $p_{\rm T}$ ranges, the electron-to-non-charm lepton anti-correlation shows the usual characteristics of initial conversion of beauty hadrons into electrons. Nevertheless, in the range around $6 < p_{\rm T} < 8$ GeV/$c$, the electron yield exhibits an unexpected delay in response to beauty hadron suppression, where the yield exceeds that of non-charm leptons in very central collisions, and in collisions with lower centrality, the yield approaches that of non-charm leptons. This behavior suggests that beauty hadrons in this $p_{\rm T}$ range undergo elliptic flow. If the production rate of beauty hadrons in this $p_{\rm T}$ range returns to its normal level, then the elliptic flow of beauty hadrons bears a relationship similar to that of charged hadrons. This behavior may be the result of interactions between beauty quarks and nucleons in the very early stages of heavy-ion collisions that also influence parton coalescence in this $p_{\rm T}$ range. Further theoretical and simulation studies are needed to confirm these observations and their implications. Detailed tracking of charm quarks in the most advanced trackers may be necessary to verify the occurrence of beauty elliptic flow.
