We introduce the concept of persistence within colored shapes, specifically developing persistent homology for colored alpha-complexes across various dimensions. Our work involves extending the existing homotopy theory to accommodate colored alpha-complexes, and we outline a comprehensive approach to defining persistence in this context. Based on this framework, we establish that persistent homology for colored point sets, analogous to uncolored sets, accurately reflects the temporal structure of filaments and surfaces defined by convexity intervals. Furthermore, our approach allows for efficient computation of persistence in all relevant contexts through optimization techniques. Our findings are demonstrated by applying them to a dataset of hand movements. Moreover, our theoretical results reveal an intriguing suboptimal relationship between the number of data points and precision, an intriguing discovery that may have further implications for high-dimensional contexts. Our work offers novel applications to surface mapping, and we show the effectiveness of our methods with a concrete example involving 3D object layout. Lastly, the accompanying software, developed using the JuJu Julia framework, is available online. Our approach has significant implications, especially in contexts where color differentiation is crucial, and it may also facilitate unsupervised geometric clustering operations. Through experimentation, we evaluate the scalability of our surface construction methods and demonstrate their practicality by mapping 3D objects with up to 2000 surfaces. Additionally, we measure the computational efficiency of our algorithms on large, 6D datasets, and finally, we highlight the visual value of coloring techniques in enhancing perceptual surface identification capabilities. To the best of our knowledge, our work represents a groundbreaking theory and practice of persistence in colored shapes, an area which up until now had no established theory or methodological framework. Our approach to extension has been guided by the principle of 'the simplest theory'. Precisely because we were looking for the simplest theory, we were able to leverage the power of automatic differentiators to compute derivatives for the uncolored approach, a feat not possible in the colored context. Similarly, the colored approach allows for efficient computation of distances, especially when dealing with dimensions greater than one. However, due to the combinatorial nature of these problems, the colored and uncolored surface detection algorithms exhibit different performance characteristics, an area of study that may be worth exploring further. Ultimately, the interaction between the theory and the automatic computation of gradients, and the sensitivity analysis, represents an area of study, and the extension of the theory to other dimensions remains an open question and possible future work. For the scenario with $K$ users and no more than two transmitters per user, we identify the GDoF gain achieved through optimal control as being proportional to the number of users, i.e., $\Theta(K)$. When there are multiple transmitters interfering with each user, for the "strong interference" scenario with at most two transmitters per user, we show the GDoF gain to be proportional to the square root of the number of users, i.e., $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. The management and analysis of vast amounts of stream and interactive data are becoming increasingly significant in the enterprise environment due to the growing use of IT services for data processing. To address this need, we've developed a new stream processing framework called H-STREAM, built on top of Apache Tez and secured through role-based access control. This framework allows for the creation of complex analytical pathways combining multiple data sources, including data records and high-speed streams, to create valuable business insights. To showcase its capabilities, we've demonstrated H-STREAM through a real-world application in the form of a web-based dashboard displaying integrated data from Facebook, Twitter, and Google Maps, all built into a single, secure architectural model. This research was presented at the 21st International Conference on Information Integration and Assurance in 2018.

The production of top and bottom quarks via the singular PoLP process is a prominent example of how final-state colliders detect new physics beyond the Standard Model. Unlike resonant signatures, which decline post-hadronization due to the Breit-Wigner form, the singular PoLP process remains unaffected by new physics signals after the LHC's collision phase, making it a crucial benchmark for new physics searches. Nonetheless, the singular PoLP process can be influenced by new physics, especially in the high-energy region, which is close to the threshold, via the new physics-determined phase. This is because, in this energy range, the amplitude is only partially new physics-influenced. To accurately determine the new physics effect, the phase must be calculated with the real and imaginary parts of the new physics-dependent loop function. In this work, the phase is calculated for the top quark pair production in the context of two specific new physics models: the gauge kinetic mixing and the scalar extensions of the Standard model. These calculations show that, for the gauge kinetic mixing, the new phase is about one to two orders of magnitude smaller than the standard model phase. Also, the calculations reveal that the new phase for the scalar extensions of the Standard model, specifically the type-X two-Higgs doublet model, is about one to two orders of magnitude smaller than the standard model phase at certain specific energy points. However, it is observed that the new phase for this model can be as large as the standard model phase at certain specific energy points. To accurately determine the new physics effect, the singular PoLP process is proposed to be measured as the difference between the top quark pair production cross sections at energies above and below the threshold on the real part of the phase, as well as the imaginary part of the phase, which could reach an accuracy of an order of ten times larger than the standard model phase. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the singular PoLP process could reach an accuracy of 0.05 (0.10) for the vector-like quark searches by introducing a mass-dependent interference effect due to the final-state strong interactions. In the last few years, significant advancements have been made in using deep neural networks for translating natural language to RDF and back again, a crucial component in various interactive systems such as virtual assistants and chatbots that rely on knowledge base components for language processing. However, replicating state-of-the-art results in this field is very challenging, mainly due to a lack of clear and concise abstractions to manage complex components, such as multi-modal training data preprocessing, and the need for large-scale hardware setup, such as GPUs, which many research groups may not have access to. Our paper focuses on replicating a top-tier neural machine translation model for expanding German to RDF terms, involving setting up a scalable training environment using TensorFlow and the open-source knowledge engine, Knowledge Base Muni. We provide a step-by-step guide on data preparation, distributed training setup, and deployment strategies, and replicate the results of our previous study with a full dataset, achieving an RDF exact match accuracy of 79.96%. We also compare the performance of our setup with the original one, particularly in terms of training time, pointing out potential issues and areas for improvement. Our entire project is hosted on a publicly accessible, reproducible research platform at https://github.com/ignomics/KBMuni-S2RDF.

The increased reliance on AI in regulatory decision-making poses significant
challenges for validating models, especially those in high-stakes environments.
The good continuations benchmark, originating from inductive programming, can be
utilized to evaluate neural networks used in regulatory applications, such as
predicting material defects in steel pipe inspections. However, applying this
benchmark to such tasks is difficult due to its dependency on a priori knowledge
of model inputs and outputs. To overcome this, we examine the properties of
models that utilize expert-provided input features, allowing us to link them to
models' confidence levels and output classes. Through a case study involving
X-ray steel pipe inspections, we demonstrate the feasibility of measuring AI
validability according to the good continuations benchmark. The analysis yields
insights into the process of grading neural network models for regulatory purposes. 
Ultimately, we explore the potential integration of the good continuations
benchmark into a formal validation framework in regulation. 
To that end, we propose a tiered validation approach comprising basic metrics
such as accuracy and explainability, intermediate measures like the good
continations benchmark, and advanced methods such as risk-based assessments. 
The proposed validation approach will feature an intermediate tier and FCA will be
one of the metrics within it. 
An alternative to relying solely on the good continuations benchmark is a
metric dubbed Risk Assessment for Validation (RAV), derived from it and other
conceptual network metrics. 
To test RAV's efficacy, we conducted studies in classification and reinforcement
learning and found that it accurately forecasts the performance of nearly 60% of
top models in a dataset. 
Ultimately, we recommend a balanced approach, combining basic metrics for low-
risk decisions, intermediate tiers such as RAV for medium-risk choices, and
advanced metrics like formal concept analysis along with an assessment of
uncertainty and model liability for high-risk applications. 
By partaking in a Delphi study, we gathered input from experts, including
regulators, from across the world, and obtained their feedback on the proposed
three-tiered validation approach. 
Our goal is for this process to be adopted formally, especially in the case
of software and AI products, in accordance with current regulatory guidelines.

Nonetheless, pressing real-life situations have compendiums of images and videos that undergo gradual degradation, like photo deterioration and video distortion. The existing tensor ring based restoration techniques are single-image based, which often fail to produce optimal outcomes for 2D visual data retrieval, such as those involving databases of images and videos. Moreover, they are uncapable of handling tensor ring structures that are susceptible to environmental changes, like light and visual distortions, without compromising the quality of pre-existing data within the tensor ring structure. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a novel method, Patch Monitoring-based Streaming Tensor Ring Restoration, that effectively maintains the quality of pre-existing data within the tensor ring structure by continuously monitoring the change in tensor ring structure and adapting tensor ring structure reconstruction. The experimental validation of our proposed method, using both image and video data, has shown superior results when compared to other restoration methods, such as those based on model propagation, mean squared error, and universal style transfer. The validation has shown our proposed method to be efficient, effective, and capable of handling large-scale data, such as those involving 2D visual data. This research investigates the behavior of rotating, disk-shaped fluids subjected to irregular boundaries, resulting in the generation of chaotic inertial waves. Unlike traditional fluid dynamics, these waves do not travel at distinct speeds and their energy is not dissipated in a predictable manner. Instead, it's speculated that the ratio of their energy at low and high frequencies remains constant. To test this theory, the researchers ran an extensive number of computer simulations under various conditions, and found the energy ratio fluctuating, but ultimately converging to a universal value, supporting Zakharov-Kolmogorov theory. By analyzing these results, they discovered that the energy growth follows a pattern first described by Kolmogorov, providing further evidence for Zakharov-Kolmogorov theory and confirming that the ratio of their energy at low and high frequencies remains invariant. These findings are particularly significant, given the diverse applications of these mathematical theories, which are found in various fields such as research into turbulent flows, study of chaotic systems and study of planetary rotation. Our observations of the flare star CR Draconis, lasting 5100 minutes, demonstrated the existence of a distinct low-frequency radiation phenomenon. This phenomenon, characterized by a variable and intermittent spectrum, was identified as an electron-cyclotron maser induced by the 103rd harmonic of the magnetic field. This type of radiation is a rare detection in the magnetized plasmas of stars. We observed a significant increase in flux density, by a factor of 20, as a result of a geomagnetically-induced disturbance, and further analysis revealed a bright radiation episode lasting 420 minutes with a distinctive rise-and-fall pattern. This type of low-frequency radiation is significantly contributing to the energy balance at the atmospheric interface of this type of star. We suggest that the ratio of non-thermal power to thermal power is in the range of 0.1-0.3, taking into consideration the interstellar medium magnetic field and physical parameters of the atmospheric interface. We observed a significant energy imbalance in the static equilibrium of the atmospheric interface of CR Draconis, and further research could determine if the observed discrepancy is resolved through dynamical balance, considering high-altitude wind and coronal mass loss. Moreover, the observed atmospheric interface of CR Draconis, characterized by a distinctive balance between non-thermal and thermal energies, might be especially sensitive to the influence of the Type II interplanetary stream, especially when it reaches its maximum intensity, as observed during the 2021 solar year, exceeding the background level of the stream by chance, as observed in the radio emission characteristics of CR Draconis. Building upon the insights from artificial intelligence and human cognition, we are exploring the parallels between machine and human learning. Machines, in particular, can be adept at ferreting out subtle patterns in data, but this ability makes them more susceptible to being misled by crafted distortions. Researchers have developed learning algorithms that can withstand such subversive images, but the effects of these images on both humans and machines are still poorly understood. To bridge this knowledge gap, we have conducted an extensive study on the impact of these distorted images on both humans and machines, with a focus on their ability to generalize knowledge. Our findings reveal that machines can be easily tricked by these images, but they are capable of withstanding the manipulation better than humans when generalizing knowledge. Conversely, humans are more resilient against these image distortions, but their cognitive biases make it more challenging for them to accurately generalize knowledge. Our analysis of these discrepancies between human and machine behavior has yielded four distinct patterns: 1) machines learning from flawed images exacerbate their susceptibility to these images; 2) machines equipped with remedies can effectively counter these image distortions; 3) humans learning from these images exhibit a consistent set of biases; and 4) humans equipped with various coping mechanisms shows a notable variation. Our extensive investigation into the inherent differences between human and machine cognition has laid the groundwork for a deeper understanding of these phenomena and opens the door for potential applications in multiple fields. The findings presented here incorporate the contributions of 45 distinct authors, detailing our experiments and analysis, and pave the way for future research to explore these fascinating cognitive disparities. Our code for these experiments and analysis can be accessed at https://github.com/fatecru/mis. Our study, encompassing over 2.5 years in the making, challenges the long-standing premise that machines and humans learning from flawed images share a common trait: a consistent set of biases. To date, no comprehensive study has adequately investigated these image distortions, leading to a notable lapse in the research community. Our study aims to fill this knowledge gap, yielding valuable insights into the world of flawed generalization and laying the groundwork for future research. Our work ultimately poses an intriguing question: what other cognitive disparities remain yet unknown? The study presented offers valuable insights to AI researchers and practitioners, emphasizing both the similarities and discrepancies between human and machine cognition. To facilitate future research, we provide an extensive list of potential investigation areas at the end of this report. The source code for our study can be accessed at https://github.com/albertot

Our study focuses on the quantum Monte Carlo sampling of periodic trigonal lattices, applying it to the analysis of the magnetic properties of 2D frustrated clusters as they thermally evolve from the ground state. The approach is exemplified by applying it to the simulation of the thermally-activated ordering in the Ba$_3$Yb$_2$O$_7$ compound and its implications for the presence of collective spin waves and a proposed'spin-liquid with a band gap' phase. Theoretical support for the method and its application is further provided by demonstrating that it accurately reproduces the ground-state properties of the triangular-lattice compound κ-Ba$_3$Yb$_2$O$_9$ and its behavior in the presence of an applied magnetic field. The method is also applied to the analysis of the magnetic properties of the dilute triangular-scanner, a trigonal-lattice structure composed of three individual spin-1/2 units. The study reveals that in the absence of inter-cluster interactions, the dilute triangular-scanner exhibits quantum spin-liquid behavior reminiscent of water, existing outside of any phase with long-range order. The presence of inter-cluster coupling, however, results in the formation of three-linked clusters of clusters and ultimately leads to long-range order at low temperatures. The study reveals that the inter-cluster interaction results in the formation of collective cluster-spin-density waves rather than an individual spin-wave, a discovery which may explain why ferromagnetism has not been observed in dilute triangular-scanner samples that have been cooled to mK temperatures despite the absence of inter-cluster interactions. The observer's performance is assessed through simulations of the SIR and SIS models, indicating that state reconstruction achieved a high level of accuracy, albeit with varying degrees of success depending on the initial disease parameters and total population size. Notably, the observer's performance was found to degrade as time elapsed after the onset of the outbreak, suggesting a time-sensitive approach could improve reconstruction in later stages of an outbreak. Building upon this observer, future work aims to develop an estimator capable of adapting to changing epidemic parameters and states. The proposed observer's design is generally applicable and can be applied to a wide range of partial differential equations describing individual or heterogeneous epidemic models, as well as models involving multiple infectious symptom categories and external drivers, exemplified by analyzing data from the COVID-19 pandemic in France and the United States. This work's innovative approach to observer design addresses the significant challenge of accurately reconstructing past states despite model inaccuracies, and its feasible implementation makes it widely accessible. The increasing prevalence of edge devices has propelled Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) and Federated Learning (FL) to the forefront. However, practical deployments of FL are hindered by system constraints such as non-linear regression problems, due to issues like significant label encoding delays and uneven training data availability across devices. As a result, asynchronous federated learning has emerged as a potential solution and is closely related to asynchronous gradient descent, which we draw upon from optimization theory to design an adaptive framework for asynchronous FL (AsyncFL). This approach is grounded in the findings of LaRocca et al. for nonlinear regression problems and is extended to the distributed environment. In this paper, we review the foundations of asynchronous FL and then propose a resource-efficient framework for AsyncFL, incorporating real-world edge computing constraints, including delayed communication, imperfect communications, and unequal training data. We then analyze the optical optical flow-based nonlinear regression problem on edge devices and provide a baseline solution based on the existing research by LaRocca et al., followed by the description of AsyncFL framework. Finally, we evaluate the proposed framework using real-world edge devices and demonstrate its ability to optimize local solution quality while remaining sensitive to network edge bandwidth, thereby providing a comprehensive framework for asynchronous FL. To enhance the absorption of thin silicon films, a setup with a 3D photonic band gap back reflector was investigated, whose design allowed the wavelength of the absorbed light to be tailored. Simulations showed that this setup could improve the absorption of a 100 nm silicon layer by approximately 60% compared to a conventional Lambertian structure. To experimentally validate these simulations, a photonic crystal reflector with a 125 nm silicon layer was developed and the resulting absorption measured as 79% rather than the 51% expected from a conventional structure. A major factor contributing to the disparity between simulated and expected results is the experimentally observed silicon layer doping loss. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed setup for thinner layers, a 50 nm and 25 nm thick silicon layers were investigated, resulting in measured absorptions of 56% and 47%, respectively, although these values are lower than the predicted 65% and 75% achieved by a conventional structure. Nonetheless, simulations suggest that the integration of a metal scatterer can optimize the setup's performance and minimize the doping loss discrepancy. Ultimately, the introduction of a metal scatterer enables the attainment of nearly 100% path-dependent absorption in thin silicon layers. Importantly, this increase in absorption does not come at the expense of forward scattering, the mechanism driving enhanced absorption in this setup, since the presence of a metal scatterer in the top layer actually preserves forward scattering in the system, resulting in its restoration when the metal scatterer is moved to an adjacent position. Consequently, this setup presents a versatile option for thin, ultrathin, and microstructured silicon layers across various thicknesses. Specifically, in 25 nm layers, the integration of a metal scatterer yields an absorption exceeding 98% in the narrow spectral range defined by the $\Gamma$-point and the first and second Brillouin zones' umklapp point, a range that can be manipulated through the metal scatterer's position to optimize absorption at the desired wavelength, in addition to facilitating light propagation at a customizable angle of 3.5$^{\circ}$. Large graph prediction tasks typically face challenges due to limited available information. The issue is more pronounced in sparse networks, where nodes lack sufficient context for accurate prediction. Existing models' approach to tackling this issue involves aggregating broader network properties such as structural or atrributual information. However, aggregating structural information can be inefficient and impractical for large graphs, while relying on attributes is only feasible when they're available, often not the case in operational networks. 

Instead of aggregating network properties, SSNE project node features into a lower-dimensional space, treating each node as an isolated entity. By doing so, SSNE enables direct prediction without needing to aggregate global network properties, making it more scalable and efficient than existing approaches. SSNE achieves this implementation by adapting the Structural Deep Learning (SDL) framework and optimizing it for cross-modal predictive tasks. 

The proposed SSNE approach consists of three modules: structure embedding, channeling, and classification. The structure embedding module projects node features into a low-dimensional space using an adaptive self-attention mechanism, critical in sparse graphs. The channeling module generates cross-modal signals that facilitate cross-neighbor signal sharing, allowing information exchange even among distant nodes. Finally, the classification module uses graph attention networks to aggregate node embeddings for prediction. 

To evaluate SSNE's performance, we conducted experiments using 16 real-world graphs across 5 link types, comparing its predictions to those of existing approaches. The results not only demonstrate SSNE's efficacy in sparse graphs but also its potential for improved performance, outshining existing models that often struggle to adapt to such networks. Furthermore, SSNE's cross-modal generalizability was validated through predictions on the North Atlantic Oscillation time series dataset and the Wikipedia graph, yielding significant improvements in accuracy. 

In terms of computational efficiency, SSNE's training and testing scalability were assessed on a large graph with 161 million nodes and 228 billion edges. The experimental outcomes illustrate SSNE's ability to adapt to various challenge scenarios and its potential in uncharted domains. Moreover, SSNE has been openly released at https://github.com/dataforkel/SSNE. The results of SSNE indicate that extensive structural information is not always necessary for accurate link prediction, and SSNE's ability to scale its predictions far surpass those of existing models. While performance and accuracy may decline in extremely sparse graphs, SSNE's design enables it to adapt to a wide array of challenge scenarios.

Wildfires pose a significant threat to global communities, and accurate monitoring is crucial for effective management and mitigation. This approach transforms infrared images, smoothing noise and amplifying fire patterns, and we have applied Generative Adversarial Networks to create a fire filter that differentiates fire and non-fire areas. Experimental evaluations using the CAMEO dataset have confirmed the efficacy of our infrared-visual integration technique in both filtering and image processing applications. However, traditional maximum principle methods include assumptions of complete

In the standard approach, matrices are compared on a relative scale, but we explore an adjusted BIC (ABIC) that considers an absolute threshold beyond which the fit is deemed inadequate. To establish this threshold, we determine the probability density distribution of a fit criterion under the null hypothesis and, through Monte Carlo simulations, define a fundamental score that marks the boundary between acceptable and unacceptable fits. By assessing the ABIC using simulations and real data, we investigate its performance and find that it offers benefits over the classical BIC in certain cases involving non-normal data. These findings also suggest that the ABIC is sensitive to the effects of outliers. Additionally, we propose a statistical test based on the ABIC that helps examine the existence of a non-degenerate matrix fitting the data perfectly, and this test shares similarities with the tests for moment-based population parameters. Furthermore, we derive an asymptotic distribution and conduct a power analysis for the test, revealing that it detects matrices fitting the data within a non-empty parameter space preferentially over those with zero-probability fits. Ultimately, we demonstrate the applicability and interpretability of the ABIC in real-world contexts by analyzing two related datasets. One such dataset involves modeling the expense structure of a finite number of finite-variance populations. To this end, we consider a scenario where each finite-variance group is distinct from the others based on its mean expense. We present a novel COVID-19 categorization approach that uses two phases and BERT attributes. First, a binary classification phase determines if a patient has COVID-19, followed by a secondary classification for individuals identified as positive. This secondary stage categorizes patients into COVID-19 victims or survivors. We examine various BERT models, including those optimized for medical text (BioBERT) and general English text (BERT), in conjunction with neural network and fully connected classifier architectures. Our experiments encompass 11 datasets, encompassing a total of 13,598 patients. Notably, the proposed system achieves an accuracy of 38.5% for differentiating between COVID-19 patients and individuals without the disease, and 85.1% accuracy for distinguishing between COVID-19 victims and survivors. This method demonstrates the ability to accurately utilize pre-trained BERT models as a dual-classification system. We further highlight that patients who are categorically misidentified are more likely to be female, with older demography and a lower level of medical report readability. Notably, the proposed system's secondary classification results demonstrate the ability to forecast patients' recovery, based on their medical record at the time of admission. This study showcases the applicability of transformers in medical settings, particularly for a wide-range of text classification problems. We release the source code on GitHub.

Our study examines real-world flaws in Python cryptocurrency applications by 
analyzing them under a single roof, across eight projects that deal with 
cryptocurrency parsing, transaction blocking, smart contracts, wallet management, 
electronic cash flows, and blockchain implementation. We discovered a total of 28 
new vulnerabilities, all of which have gone unreported in previous studies. 
Our analysis reveals that cryptocurrency-related Python software frequently 
involves outdated third-party libraries, leading to security issues. We have 
classified the detected vulnerabilities into five types and provide recommendations 
on effective cryptographic library use, as well as practical tips for secure 
coding, including bug fixes and patches. In addition, our research provides unique 
insights gained from in-depth code inspections that could aid developers in 
avoiding potential security risks in cryptocurrency-related Python software.

The investigation reveals that if the potential's saddle points are non-differentiable but still roughly convex in certain directions, it can still be treated as an integrability problem. Within this context, the usual concepts, such as motion characteristics and integrals of motion, can still be defined and explored. Ultimately, this study provides a method for calculating these concepts, provided certain conditions involving the potential's derivatives are met. An example involving the generalized Einstein system is included to demonstrate the applicability of this approach. Furthermore, this system also exemplifies how a non-differentiable potential can give rise to a novel type of integrability, specifically factorization. Moreover, this example highlights that factorization and integrability are distinct concepts, leading to novel, previously unsolved problems in the Einstein system. Specifically, it poses questions regarding the existence of additional integrals of motion beyond the maximally generated ones, as well as the novel factorization itself. Such questions remain unsolved for all the cases of the Einstein system that we were able to completely integrate. Lastly, this study also addresses a related query regarding motion characteristics in systems analogous to the Lie-Einstein system. Unfortunately, the method that we were able to develop for the Einstein system, when applied to its Lie-Einstein counterpart, fails due to a non-existence of certain Poisson structures possessing the desired properties in the Lie-Einstein system. This study introduces the concealed inverses protocol (CIP), a novel approach to error correction dynamically neutralizing errors without the need for predefined encoding methods. When applied to superconducting quantum circuits, CIP is capably handle errors induced by various decay channels, as experimentally verified. Furthermore, CIP is adaptable to be used in conjunction with other error correction techniques, thereby augmenting existing correction methods, and is compatible with contemporary quantum hardware. More advanced computer vision techniques could potentially enrich these collections by providing richer image features, but only when paired with refined text inputs. We investigate this possibility by introducing VT-CLIP, an innovative model that leverages CLIP's image processing capabilities in conjunction with sophisticated text processing techniques. By merging these capabilities, VT-CLIP achieves significant performance gains on 21 common vision-language tasks, outperforming predecessor models like FLiRTP by 11% and improving efficiency 3.9 times. Notably, VT-CLIP excels on visual reasoning tasks, such as VCR 3.15% and Charades 4.75%, while also excelling on other tasks without compromising speed. Our work provides new insights on strategies for quickly incorporating large pre-trained models to enhance vision-language capabilities. At the same that these models contribute to progress, they also restrict generalizability when their training objectives are at odds with our goals. We address this challenge by proposing techniques that separate visual and linguistic knowledge from specific text combinations, thereby refining these models to produce more effective cross-modal capabilities. Ultimately, the proposed visual-directed text approach yields the impression that sophisticated vision transformers can be directed by subtle text inputs to generate meaningful and informative visual representations. We demonstrate this capability through the creation of novel artistic compositions and the accelerated learning of visual concepts from natural language instructions. We conduct a series of experiments that start with the simplest vision-directed text generation protocol and gradually move on to more complex cross-modal training scenarios. Our results indicate that the proposed visual-directed text approach leads to more natural and semantically enriched visual representations, which can be leveraged for a range of vision-language tasks including image captioning, visual question answering, visual concept localization, and more. Importantly, our technique demonstrates the capacity to direct the development of large-scale models with rich semantic understanding of the world while remaining independent of specific training objectives and datasets. Mesh coarsening is a process that simplifies a fine mesh while retaining key features of the original geometry. In engineering design particularly, this procedure has a significant role in reducing computational costs associated with complex simulations. Unlike other mesh coarsening methods based on optimization, our novel approach creates high-quality quadrilateral meshes from complex designs using linear optimization, preserving important geometric details through the incorporation of strict mesh constraints. These constraints ensure that mesh vertices conform to design boundaries and that the resulting mesh has smooth, feasible coordinates, leading to a well-structured layout with favorable characteristics, such as small angles and short edges, making it suitable for various applications. Unlike methods that utilize sparse optimization to achieve a sparse mesh layout, our method creates quadrilateral meshes using linear optimization, resulting in a coarse mesh with favorable quadrilateral quality, especially suitable for models with complex features. In our study, we evaluated our method through comparisons with manually created meshes and other automatic mesh coarsening methods, demonstrating its effectiveness in generating high-quality quadrilateral meshes in a timely manner, in line with the requirements of the input design. Our analysis of the mesh quality showcases the superior quadrilateral quality of the resulting meshes, outperforming other methods in this aspect. In order to accelerate the mesh coarsening process, we successfully utilized the inverse-based mesh smoothing approach concurrently with the mesh coarsening process through the reuse of the same solving matrix, leading to significant time savings, ultimately resulting in a 30 times speedup in mesh coarsening time for large-scale models. Our method has been successfully demonstrated in its latest form through the mesh coarsening of the NASA Titanogear model as shown in the accompanying video. This research has been published in the June 2022 issue of the distinguished journal, Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering. Due to the distinct nature of our method, we registered two new patents in 2021, specifically addressing the creation of quadrilateral meshes and the simultaneous mesh coarsening and smoothing processes, leading to the presentation of our findings at two prestigious conferences, namely the 2020 Int. Conference on Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence and the 2021 Int. Conference on Advances in Hybridizing Soft Computing, in both cases, predating the formal publication in reputable scientific journals. By leveraging the S matrix, I demonstrate how quantum gravitational effects from general relativity and more advanced theories, such as effective field theories and loop quantum gravity, can be effectively modeled across diverse scenarios. Examples include ultra-peripheral heavy-ion collisions, particle scattering with a heavy nucleus, and quantum gravity effects in loop-space. Furthermore, applications to gravitational waves in scenarios like cosmic string collisions and monopole interactions have been successfully applied. Lastly, I will touch on the S matrix formalism's potential benefits and future directions of investigation.  Key to the methodology presented here is a conventional treatment of final-state interactions, incorporating the effects of weak channels and multiple final-state particles, as well as accurately accounting for non-analytic behavior, often seen in quantum gravitational phenomena. Crucially, the treatment enables the separation of real and imaginary components of the S matrix, facilitating the interpretation of various signatures, such as gravitational waves, in experiments. By providing concrete, numerically-verified applications, the S-matrix framework has been demonstrated to provide valuable, physically-meaningful results, complementing existing literature on the subject. Among the novel contributions included in this thesis paper, one significant finding stands out: the calculation of partonic montel space corrections to the vanishing S matrix, characteristic of general relativity in the weak-channel limit, which has significant implications for signature analysis. Due to these non-analytic contributions, the threshold behavior of the S matrix exhibits distinctive logarithmic and power-law dependences, as opposed to the classic analytic s-wave behavior seen in the classical Coulomb scattering, where the S matrix shows hydrodynamic characteristics via a complex scaling factor, given by (2ikT log(r)) and (2ikT log(1-r)) for one-particle and multi-particle final states respectively. Notably, the derivation provides an understanding of the magnitude of these corrections, as well as their dependence on the scaling variable, while indicating a missing factor in the Linder proposal, related to the Dulency ratio, in order to explain the observed signatures. Under certain conditions on q and the initial velocity, we demonstrate the exponential stability of the zero solution in a variety of Sobolev and Besov spaces. Our approach relies on manipulating the norms of the velocity v and its derivatives using certain inequalities, combined with the Galerkin approximation method. By locating a localized feedback control in a more regular space, we strengthen the stability properties of the associated semigroup in the original space. This achievement is further expanded to the study of the global uniform stabilization of the Navier-Stokes system, where we show the semigroup's exponential decay in a range of spaces, including Q2(p) and Bs(p, q) spaces for p ≥ 3. These results represent improvements on the existing literature, with broader applicability to various space frameworks and a more general range of initial velocity norms. Moreover, the study extends the applications of a prior work by many possible space frameworks. Our results will be exemplified through the investigation of a specific model representing a two-dimensional, incompressible flow within a 2π x 2π domain. By modeling the fluid's behavior under the influence of a localized source of force, we test the applicability of the study's results to a variety of such models. When exposed to an intense ionizing radiation flux, typical solid matter experiences a net forward force, or drag. This phenomenon can be described by a straightforward equation, as the drag's magnitude is equal to the radiation flux's magnitude, multiplied by the radiation's mean free path. If the mean free path is measured in units of distance, this result holds true regardless of the radiation being in the liquid or bulk phase. However, if the mean free path is instead represented as an angular measurement, or in cases where the radiation is highly scattered, the resulting drag force may be substantially reduced. Researchers found that the drag force on graphite exposed to high-fluence helium-I radiation increased linearly with the flux and meant free path, or angular measurement. Moreover, the drag force on graphite or polyethylene near sources of unmodulated gamma radiation increased linearly with distance, or radiation intensity. This increased drag force near sources was attributed to anisotropic backscattering of gamma radiation in graphite or other materials exhibiting high scattering powers. As a result, the drag force on such materials exposed to intense radiation fields can be substantial, as evidenced by experiments using unmodulated gamma radiation. In fact, the drag force on graphite or other materials exposed to high-fluence helium-I radiation can be several decades or even centuries ahead of their respective melting or vaporization points. This advance was as result of the drag force's linear relationship with flux, or mean free path, or as a result of the drag force's dependence on radiation intensity in cases of unmodulated radiation. Researchers speculate that the drag force on materials exposed to very intense or highly monochromatic radiation sources may be significantly less than their melting or vaporization points, or in some cases potentially reach their critical nuclear densities without melting. Such a prediction could potentially explain some of the anomalies associated with the nuclear structure of certain atoms and this could be an area of further investigation. Additionally, the drag force on materials exposed to intense radiation sources may be responsible for the formation of certain exotic dust or particle structures such as dust, or orifice dust, and this could be another area of further investigation. Researchers speculate that the primary result of the drag force on materials exposed to radiation fields can be significant changes to their structure and composition, and this could be an area for further study. The nearby neighbor classification technique, which uses nearest neighbor distances as a supervisor's decision criterion, is the simplest form of all supervised classification methods. Although the method's strong points include absence of sensitivity to irregularities in data and high simplicity of execution, largely optimal results can not be obtained from it, mainly because of its dependence on nearest neighbor distances which can not distinguish between different classes. This limitation leads to poor performance of the method near critical regions, where data from two different classes are very similar to each other. Unlike existing eternal view generation methods, which rely on supervised learning or adversarial training, Seq2CV learns subtle patterns of hidden objects through spatial attribution without prespecified object labels. By leveraging this technique, we create the first baseline for single-view eternal view generation and develop a dataset containing over 30,000 image triples that facilitate training and evaluation. When applied to real-world challenges in autonomous driving, Seq2CV effectively identifies and interacts with static objects on roads, demonstrating its practical utility. Furthermore, our model outperforms previous generation methods in quality and accuracy, and surpasses state-of-the-art object detection approaches in static object localization. Notably, we demonstrate our approach through in-depth experiments that reveal the interplay between hidden object composition and the perceived 3D geometry of the scene. Ultimately, our results validate the potential of single-view generation that is both scalable and effective. These findings have significant implications for the use of ultrasound scoliosis assessment, suggesting that robotic technology could enhance the consistency of measurements, ultimately improving clinical decision-making. Given these benefits, the technology could potentially be used in conjunction with manual scanning to provide more accurate and reliable measurements, and researchers propose specific protocols, such as combining modality with within-group and between-group repetition, for optimizing the use of ultrasound in scoliosis assessment. The research concludes by identifying and prioritizing future studies that can further refine and improve ultrasound technology, such as integrating it into clinical settings, and investigating its practical applications, such as in first-line scoliosis screening. Ultimately, the research aims to contribute to the development of trustworthy and accurate point-of-care tools for scoliosis assessment and treatment. Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) exhibit superior performance in image classification tasks, whereas Multimodal MIMO-DCNNs achieve even more impressive results by processing multiple images. In this context, MIMO-DCNNs strive to improve representation learning through multiple views of data. In addressing this challenge, we propose an innovative feature exchange method (FEM) that optimizes the sharing of spatial feature maps among individual MIMO-DCNN pathways. The molecular continuum model, known for its rigorous quantum description and extensive computational power, is explored in this research. This method employs a combination of quadratic functions on partitions of the three-dimensional space and a piecewise linear function on the partitions to create a collective set of points. However, standard procedures for this model involve evaluating functions at a finite set of points, typically based on the Newton-Cotes formula. But this traditional approach can be problematic due to a flawed point partition, leading to an overestimated space. We evaluate the performance of these oversampling methods in a realistic setting with a dataset of 76,000 articles from Wikipedia. Our results demonstrate that random oversampling leads to high classification accuracy but is plagued by class imbalance. In contrast, the incremental and Learn2Rank methods, which are designed to balance the class distribution, exhibit lower but more stable classification performance. We also observe that the Learn2Rank method offers improved accuracy in comparison to random oversampling as the training process progresses. Ultimately, we find that a combination of these methods results in the highest overall classification accuracy. Notably, our study contributes to the literature by expanding upon previous research, conducting an exhaustive evaluation of multiple artificial oversampling methods using a large dataset, and highlighting the importance of a balanced class distribution in machine learning performance, especially in data sets with significant information content. The spin maser offers a unique method for producing radiofrequency signals with reduced thermal noise and increased sensitivity. In contrast to conventional masers, the spin maser does not rely on a four-level system but can utilize a three-level system with specific characteristics. In practice, the spin maser effect has only been observed in narrow-line-width magnetic materials under extremely low temperatures and high magnetic fields. Nevertheless, the need for such extreme conditions might be avoided if a system with an inherently small line width could be used instead. The development of advanced solid-state devices to this effect has been hindered by the limitations of available single-crystal-line-widths, although the advent of nanotechnology and the utilization of individual nanocrystals or quantum dots have the potential to significantly lower the required thermal and magnetic field thresholds. The feasibility of producing high-frequency spin polarized maser radiation using individual nanocrystals of diluted systems, in which the crystal-line-widths are naturally minimized, is explored here. Our testbed consists of a diluted ferrite system with a very low crystalline line-width, which upon application of a sufficient external magnetic field and temperature, behaves as if it were a two-level system in the presence of a strong spin-orbit effect, thereby enabling the observation of the maser effect at a lower threshold than conventional temperatures. The ability to produce high-frequency spin polarized maser radiation using individual nanocrystals could thus revolutionize the development of high-sensitivity radiofrequency spin systems for scientific research and engineering applications. Our results also demonstrate that such individual nanocrystals could potentially be utilized in future quantum information technologies, including the development of magnetic monodomain CrO$_2$ nanocrystals as a potential alternative. Moreover, this technology could also enable the creation of extremely sensitive geophysical magnetometers for use on aircraft and in three-axis magnetometer systems for space exploration. Our research into these novel radiofrequency spin systems using individual nanocrystals is ongoing. The system described here offers a unique platform for investigating quantum effects in systems with high sensitivity radiofrequency spins, which until now have not been well documented. Our results also demonstrate that Gd$_{2}O$_{3}$-based nanocrystals exhibit naturally occurring nmr transitions at very low temperatures and in high magnetic fields, which could potentially be utilized in future maser applications. The development of high sensitivity radiofrequency spin systems using individual nanocrystals has the potential to enable the detection of quantum mechanical effects in these systems, which to date have not been observable at room temperature and in magnetic fields

Our research focuses on examining the performance of recurrent and fully connected neural networks in identifying hate-speech through text analysis, specifically within Hindi and Bengali languages, using a small dataset compiled from Twitter platforms. Our findings suggest that models encounter difficulties with hate-speech detection and classification tasks, primarily due to the dataset's limited size, leading to overfitting issues. Despite these challenges, our study demonstrates the effectiveness of various techniques in enhancing model accuracy, including the utilization of more sophisticated architectures, such as adding dropout operations to remedy overfitting, and the application of transfer learning from pre-trained models. Additionally, our research highlights the importance of manually classifying hate-speech categories to further refine model performance. Our study provides a comprehensive overview of the obstacles encountered and proposed solutions to facilitate effective hate-speech identification and classification processes in low-resource languages, particularly for the Indian subcontinent region. The research demonstrates through experiments that methods like transfer learning from pre-trained models, primarily from English-based models, can improve performance on tasks due to the leverage of weight from a more advanced model. Our research also showcases the effectiveness of combining manually labeled categories from a dataset through a multi-label approach in enhancing model performance, especially for the task of classifying hate-speech categories. Our study has been published in the International Journal of Advanced Networking Tutorial (IJANT) as volume 12, issue 2, pp. 01-09, 2021. Our related source code can be accessed via the repository located at https://github.com/SouravGC/Indian-Hate-Text-Classification. Our research based on the experimental findings suggests that there are several avenues to further improve hate-speech classification performance, particularly for the task of finding relevant neural network model architecture that could yield better classification results using a neural network, and the application of neural transfer learning from more advanced models that were trained with a larger dataset that could aid in the task of hate-speech classification, specifically for the task of finding relevant locations in a sentence that contain hate-speech.

In space exploration, there is a high demand for a gas time projection chamber (GTPC) that can accurately detect nuclear recoils while meeting stringent requirements. Achieving this necessitates not only low backgrounds, but also low intrinsic recoil detection limits above which signals become detectable. To exceed the reach of existing technologies on planets and asteroids, specialized chambers for direct dark matter detection must be surpassed as well. Consequently, a new figure of merit (FoM) called the Signal-to-Background Ratio for Dark Matter (SBR_Dm) is proposed to assess GTPC performance. This metric compares the rate of signal events to background events and can be expressed in terms of signal and background rates or signals and background yields. Using synthetic data, it is shown that SBR_Dm enables the evaluation of GTPC performance similar to that of clasic segmented detectors, using either rate or yield, with various scenarios such as using multiple variables to distinguish signals and backgrounds, accounting for varying ionization yields, and examining operations at different pressures. Furthermore, using synthetic data to test pressure, SBR_Dm values were found to increase with pressure between 1 and 3 bar, however this trend is expected to reverse at higher pressures due to increased ionization. Finally, using synthetic data to test pressure, SBR_Dm values were found to decrease with recoil kinetic energy, however this trend is expected to be mitigated at higher pressures. These results suggest the potential to detect dark matter at higher pressures than 3 bar, particularly in regions where the analysis threshold is lower than 100 keV, based on theoretical calculations of ionization yields. Based on this analysis, it is predicted that GTPC's ability to detect dark matter will be improved by an order of magnitude at 4 bar, another order of magnitude at 6 bar, and another order of magnitude at 10 bar. Ultimately, this novel SBR_Dm metric offers a valuable tool to assess GTPC's performance and guide research toward achieving state-of-the-art detection limits, ultimately surpassing existing achievements. To facilitate adoption across the scientific community, the SBR_Dm figure of merit and associated analysis code (in Python) and dataset (in h5file format) are made publicly available for sharing purposes. The SBR_Dm code is hosted at the repository https://github.com/JulianAguirre/Signal_to_Background_Ratio_for_Dark_Matter, while the dataset is saved at the repository https://github.com/JulianAguirre

Subsequently, the Transportation Safety Research and Engineering Laboratory created an advanced driver-assessment tool, which we tested on 600 drivers to evaluate various commercial driving practices. Our experimental setup included human and autonomous evaluators to assess the prevalence of unsafe behaviors. In this paper, we address this limitation by investigating to what extent the internal mechanics of the autonomous evaluator can be understood and thus safely deployed in practical environments. Our investigation reveals that, upon closer examination, the internal workings of the autonomous evaluator exhibit desirable properties but also introduce novel challenges. Ultimately, we propose a middle path, where some aspects of the autonomous evaluator can be modified while others remain unaltered, in order to ensure reliable and accurate predictions that can be applied securely in real-world scenarios. In doing so, we demonstrate how a variant of the original model, one that is informed by external contextual information, yields a more trustworthy and robust outcome that can be successfully deployed in a wide array of settings. Our findings support the notion that context equipping has a significant, positive impact on the performance of the autonomous evaluator. Moreover, a novel form of regulatory moderation significantly enhances the autonomous evaluator's abilities, thereby paving the way for its successful deployment in various application areas. Ultimately, in order to fully resolve these concerns, additional research is still required. We're reporting on our participation in the NLP-OOC 2022 challenge, which aimed to develop innovative methods for extracting and encoding unusual words, and subsequently assessing the performance of language models trained on these words. We present two key findings: first, there's a significant link between a word's frequency in the training corpus and its likelihood of appearing in the language model's outputs; and second, by incorporating non-traditional words into a word list; it is possible to boost the overall accuracy of language models in the task of replacing words with synonyms. We also outline a potential framework for further exploration in this area and provide a demonstration of our work at https://nlp-ooc2022.outoflexicon.moe/. In a typical investment, both the timing and length of a payoff period influence its value. Research has shown that a premature end to a payoff is generally unfavorable, but the impact of a prolonged payoff is still ambiguous. This ambiguous outcome poses a problem for numerous financial instruments, such as bonds and commodities. We develop a straightforward test to determine if the length of a payoff is an essential factor in its value. Our test focuses on the difference between the outcomes of two possible scenarios: a sudden interruption and a prolonged duration. We apply this test to examine commodity futures and show that, in most cases, prolonged durations result in reduced commodity supplies, but in some instances, they lead to increased levels of supply. We anticipate that in cases where the length of a payoff is an essential factor, it should result in differences in supply levels between interrupted and prolonged scenarios. Past research predicts urban dynamics will be altered due to the COVID-19 pandemic, and to study its impact, trip data from 11 major US cities was analyzed in this study. Countering previous assumptions, findings reveal a significant decrease in total trips and commuting, along with increased walking and cycling rates. Contrary to expectations, commuting trips recovered faster than other types of trips. Instead of universal demographic changes, income disparity in urban interactions was found to have increased. Factors leading to this disparity include urban residents' preference for walking and cycling over driving, as well as the limited mobility of lower-income individuals. To evaluate the effect of the pandemic on urban infrastructure, indicators such as interactions between different income groups and block-level density were examined across various cities. These metrics showed significant disparities, suggesting city planners' tasks have become more complex due to the pandemic. Furthermore, a simple microsimulation model revealed the increased separation of urban interactions within lower-income neighborhoods. Finally, it was discovered that the increased inequality in urban interactions largely resulted from the pandemic, consisting of 57%-66% of the pre-covid level and 22%-33% of the inequality that existed before the pandemic in cities like San Francisco and New York. This study provides empirical support for the notion that the pandemic amplified economic distinctions in urban design. It also suggests microsimulations of urban systems can be an effective way to develop and evaluate this type of policy intervention. And finally, the study advises city planners to consider the distinct needs of various demographic groups in recovery and rebuilding efforts from the pandemic.

Nevertheless, the limitations of current mapping technologies hinder their ability to support decision-making and navigation in all settings. To address these shortcomings, we propose HiTMap - a novel hierarchical diagram representation - designed to simplify the mapping of unfamiliar spaces and facilitate decision-making and navigation. By implementing a topological data analysis framework, HiTMap is capable of organizing spatial and attribute data from various sources, providing an interactive and intuitive framework for navigation through multiple scales. We ultimately hope that HiTMap will contribute to the development of future spatial cognition and human computation systems.

With the inter-group error detection capability, a proposed code set can identify single-bit errors and multiple-bit errors within a data byte. To achieve this, a binary number system is extended to a multivariable integer system with the inter-group error detection code set, which can detect errors within data bytes by utilizing different types of multivariable digits and redundant encoding. The 2-D array code set is created by combining single-dimensional codes in a vertical and horizontal manner, resulting in the ability to detect vertical and horizontal single-bit errors, as well as rectangular multi-bit errors, through the selection of appropriate precodes. The inter-group supplementary code set and 2-D Z-supplementary array code set have been validated experimentally and demonstrate superior error detection performance in practical digital systems. Furthermore, the study provides systematic design methods for the new code sets, enabling the design of practical digital systems with enhanced error detection capabilities. The proposed designs can be applied to develop various digital circuits, such as arithmetic circuits with inter-group error detection, array-based multiplier circuits able to identify rectangular multi-bit errors, and memory cells capable of detecting single-bit and multi-bit errors. The designs have been experimentally verified to showcase their efficacy in practical digital system design. The proposed code sets and designs were successfully demonstrated through practical experiments, highlighting their practicality and utility in digital system design. This paper presents a unified approach to reconstructing CT data using sensors with various types, eliminating signal noise, and distinguishing between different material groups. To achieve this, we developed a two-phase algorithm based on an advanced variational framework. The first step minimizes a spatiotally-dependent cost function that adapts to conditions at each sensor location, leveraging variance-weighted approaches to reduce noise in individual sensor data while maintaining data consistency across different sensors. The second phase leverages a hierarchical split Bregman technique to solve a simplified version of the reconstruction equation, allowing for the simultaneous removal of operator implications and weighted penalties through simple arithmetic operations. To identify material groups, we developed a dependent cost function that measures image intensity differences across sensor data. To test our approach, we used numerical simulations based on a polyenergetic CT X-ray tomography model as well as real-world data from a laboratory setup with dual-source equipment. To evaluate the effectiveness of our method, we employed a multi-criteria score that considers a combination of quantitative and qualitative factors. To demonstrate the sensitivity of our approach to the selection of parameters, we performed a parameter-sensitivity study using a pseudo-gradient optimization technique that assesses local perturbations in parameter values using a gradient-based approach. To further evaluate the reliability of our material separation approach, we performed a reliability study using a Monte Carlo technique that simulates the random movement of material groups across 1000 trials. To evaluate the accuracy of our reconstruction method, we used the root-mean-square propagation of uncertainty as well as a combination of quantitative and qualitative scorecards. The numerical and experimental results show that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and reliability, confirming our parameter and reliability sensitivity studies. The proposed methodology has been successfully tested on various experimental and simulated datasets, demonstrating its applicability to a range of applications. To facilitate future research, we provide step-by-step implementation guides as well as the relevant coding framework used in our experiments. To extend our approach to a broader range of applications, we propose an innovative time-dependent variational framework in our companion paper. In this study, we investigate the task of contextual NER without training data using
pre-trained language models as the sole training mechanism. Unlike other tasks,
contextual NER lacks traditional supervision methods such as label feedback.
Instead, we present a novel approach where we train a language model to provide
term importance feedback during concurrent constraint satisfaction based deduplication
processes in the pipeline. Our experiment on the standard Wikipedia dataset shows
that leveraging importance weights from the language model significantly enhances
duplicate identification and NER accuracy, surpassing performance with importance
feedback solely from the previous pipeline step. Additionally, our results demonstrate
that the two-step pipeline outperforms the recently proposed contextual knowledge
pre-training and copying approach, and even outperforms the strong benchmark context2Everything model in F1 measure, although the benchmark model includes training data. However, when training data is excluded, our modified pipeline yields an impressive F1 score of 89.95, a substantial 6.44 points margin over the nearest competitor. Ultimately, our findings highlight the utility of importance feedback in the context of contextual NER. This study examines the influence of temporal data dimensions on the engagement levels of visualizations, focusing on pinboard engagement tasks. We compare and analyze single-dimensional, two-dimensional, and three-dimensional time sequence datasets, along with one-dimensional linear data sets, to understand the impact of additional dimensions on user interest and the types of interactions that occur. Our investigation suggests that, generally, users are more engaged when exploring three-dimensional temporal data, but specific applications may benefit from the advantages of linear or two-dimensional visualizations. We identify key pinchboard engagement characteristics associated with different dimensionalities and highlight the types of interactions they facilitate. Based on our findings, we provide practical suggestions for designers to enhance engagement and optimize pinchboard interaction experience. The study also sheds light on the capabilities of pinchboard for three-dimensional visual exploration and reveals interesting and somewhat unexpected patterns of user interactions, such as the creation of cylindrical shapes. These results and user behaviors can serve as a foundation for future research exploring three-dimensional data visualization and visual exploration. A comprehensive mathematical framework for a specific type of localized state, known as the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov state, is developed within the context of relativistic many-electron theory. Theoretical considerations and comparative analysis with experimental findings demonstrate the validity of this framework, particularly in the context of magnetically impure superconductors. Theoretical evidence suggests that CRYSI-like states, characterized by distinct electron and hole components, emerge only under specific symmetry conditions, implying that Nb(110) is not suitable for producing CRYSI states. On the other hand, structures such as Mn adatoms and manganese dimers on the Nb(110) surface meet the required symmetry conditions, leading to the prediction of a strong and distinct magnetic response in local measurements of magnetization. Theoretical findings also indicate a significant and reversible shift between superconducting and normal states for Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states in response to external magnetic fields, with the field orientation dependent on the specific geometry of the system, potentially explainable by the recent experimental observation of a distinct zero-field state in Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface. Theoretical considerations also validate the initial assumptions of a previous study reporting the observation of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states in Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface. Theoretical analysis of the magnetic response and charge distribution reveals a strong and complex relationship between these two properties, with the magnetic response of manganese increasing in response to the geometric arrangement of the system, while the charge in the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states is localized to the impurity site. Theoretical findings also provide an alternative explanation for the absence of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states in the orientation perpendicular to the plane of the Nb(110) surface, with the theoretical predictions showing a gradual and predictable decline in the magnetic response of individual manganese atoms and manganese dimers as the external magnetic field approaches the critical threshold for superconducting phase transition in the vicinity of the impurity site. Theoretical consideration of the reversible magnetic response in the presence of external magnetic fields also validates the predicted magnetic response of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states to the in-plane magnetic field, while the theoretical analysis of the clean and impure surfaces of Nb(110) reveals a contrasting magnetic response to the perpendicular magnetic field, with the theoretical predictions showing a gradual and predictable decline in the magnetic response of clean surfaces in the vicinity of the impurity site. To measure prejudice, we've developed a set of labels based on various definitions, including (with a particular emphasis on) LGBTQ+ identity. While deep learning has excelled in this area, drawing physical edge representations offers several advantages, such as the ability to be executed on devices with limited resources, fine-tuned within a restricted set of parameters, or even entirely manually. In this research, a method for extracting edge representations is presented along with a specialized processing pipeline that utilizes a combination of shared, sparse computational resources via Google's TensorFlow framework. While this approach may lack the speed of deep learning-based solutions, particularly for large-scale datasets, it focuses on delivering accurate results and a compact, interpretable outcome rather than processing speed. The proposed edge extraction algorithm has been tested on 30 satellite images and compared to a deep learning-based approach, showing its capability to identify and represent boundaries similar to the performance of its more advanced counterparts despite being trained on a significantly reduced subset of the data. The research presents several techniques for rendering the training and inference processes more efficient and scalable. Finally, the edge representations extracted through this approach have been demonstrated to contribute to the enhancement of a geographic database with added precision in identifying buildings and other man-made structures. Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions in brain MR images plays a pivotal role in diagnosing and monitoring diseases. Recent studies highlight the performance degradation of models trained on established datasets due to out-of-distribution data. Given that training models from scratch on new datasets is computationally expensive, especially with large datasets, this study investigates the potential of continuous learning to adapt a pre-trained model to new datasets. We compared the performance of continuous learning and data augmentation techniques on a cross-dataset MS segmentation task, covering three different datasets. While both methods showed promise, data augmentation was found superior, yielding a significant improvement in DSC score, a substantial 16.75%, 11.55%, and 5.30% for training with SUMSDB, DESDB, and DESDB respectively, without requiring training from scratch on new datasets. For more details, refer to our paper at the Medical Imaging with Deep Learning (MIDL) 2022 conference. The code and trained models are available at https://github.com/RTGKCL/MS_segmentation_continuous_learning. This research aims to bridge the gap between deep learning and continuous learning in medical imaging applications. Furthermore, it highlights the potential of a well-designed data augmentation pipeline in achieving comparable results to continuous learning, reducing the need for retraining models from scratch on new datasets. Ultimately, this study contributes to the development of more robust and adaptable models capable of handling a wide variety of medical imaging datasets across different distribution zones with minimal model redesign and an abundance of low-resource data. To address this issue, researchers are developing novel techniques to quantify and assess dynamic system models, which go beyond traditional measures such as correlation coefficients to assess residual model behavior. A new approach to modeling error in non-linear systems is presented, which uses a linear representation to determine the impact of observed variable omissions on unobserved state variables and their first-time derivatives. This approach, based on solving a dual linear problem, provides a comprehensive understanding of the models' limitations, aligns model behavior with physical constraints, and offers a practical solution for intelligent machine diagnostics in dynamic systems. This method is showcased through its application in diagnosing a well-documented failure in the path following control of a unicycle. Current preference learning models, excluding set augmentation approaches, assume individual preferences are non-contextual and independent, whereas recent studies utilize set augmentation to model complex interactions between preferences. This concept has been widely applied in real-world problems, but its fundamental meaning remains unclear. To bridge this gap, this study introduces a novel set augmentation model, where a user's preferences over a collection of items can be expressed as a combination of individual preferences and interaction-based preferences. Additionally, this research provides theoretical analysis of the conditions under which set augmentation models work and proposes a practical method for learning interaction-based preferences. Extensive experiments conducted on diverse datasets demonstrate that set augmentation models often yield superior performance than conventional models. A subsequent analysis reveals that a key factor contributing to the success of set augmentation models is their capability to capture contextual dependencies between preferences, which is theoretically confirmed. These findings underscore the importance of considering contextual dependencies in preference modeling. Ultimately, this research presents set augmentation as a powerful tool for uncovering such dependencies and highlights its potential for modeling a wide range of real-world preferences. Children begin learning language rules from the sentences they encounter, but they also learn to reject incorrect hypotheses to avoid confusion. Despite the importance of learning to discard flawed assumptions, most existing language models are based on architectures that do not permit this capability. To address this limitation, we have developed innovative architectures for neural networks, specifically transformers, that can efficiently reject suboptimal language patterns. These approaches are grounded in cognitive developmental theory, which suggests that children periodically re-evaluate and discard suboptimal hypotheses as they accumulate new information. We have conducted computational simulations verifying the effectiveness of these architectures, both individually and collectively, in mimicking this developmental process. Furthermore, we have successfully applied these architectures to state-of-the-art transformer models, which results in improved performance on semantic parsing tasks using the HTL dataset. To facilitate future research, we have publicly released the associated code at https://github.com/raz3112/rejection-processor. Lastly, we hope that this study serves as a foundation for exploring other cognitive biases in the context of machine learning. We intend to explore this further in the coming months.
