We closely examine the underlying mechanics of cosmological collider phenomena, particularly the processes involving primordial non-Gaussianities, supersample bias, and novel features associated with the second-order cosmological signal and its counterparts. We then develop a mathematical framework to calculate the power spectrum of the second-order cosmological signal and use this to derive biasing criteria for its pure and mixed versions. Next, we explore the potential for these signals to reveal initial data properties and then translate our findings into a usable format for observational purposes. Finally, we consider the ethical implications of the potential to regain visibility of the initial state and the associated possibilities. This study serves as a comprehensive review of the theory behind cosmological collider phenomena and their connection to the universe's non-Gaussian structure. It also delves into the theory itself, investigating the general characteristics of the initial data and how they apply to the second-order cosmological signal and its derivatives. We validate our theory by demonstrating that the second-order power spectrum and its derivatives are composed of distinct signals and their combinations, and by illustrating that some signals can be recovered through second-order cosmological phenomena. This study also dissects the principles of sample bias and its influence on the second-order power spectrum and its various derivatives, emphasizing that some initial data features are immune to bias. We use a mathematical framework to calculate the second-order power spectrum and its derivatives for various scenarios and demonstrate that some of these signals can be recovered from second-order power spectrum data. Yet, understanding their visual focus is an entirely different story. To solve this problem, we suggest shifting the framework from one that focuses solely on data to one that combines both data and a pre-defined list of potential object categories. Our study reveals how this technique quantifies the natural ordering of stable and mobile magnetic structures, known as skyrmions, in the absence of external magnetic fields. The metastable state of these lattice formations can be directly measured with time using in situ experiments, while variables such as local density, surface tension, and interfacial viscosity are derived from the analysis of the evolution of surface patterns. According to the computed Lifshitz numbers, the prevalence of specific topological defects is dictated by the thermodynamic preferences of the material at given temperatures. The application of mechanical stress results in the liquefaction of the skyrmion lattice, leading to a homogeneous mixture of various topological formations. The emergence of stable and mobile magnetic structures under zero-field conditions holds significant implications for the management and storage of magnetic data at increased densities. Our study also introduces new metrics, such as the scalar topological viscosity and the skyrmion fluid density, refining the understanding of topological liquefaction and paving the path for advanced data storage technologies. Typically, these models consist of a small set of interconnected nonlinear equations that capture local interactions at each time step. They often assume total determinism, although noise can also be incorporated. Deterministic models excelm, offering valuable insights into the long-term behavior and dynamics of the system, while still applying to realistic scenarios that are inherently stochastic. First introduced in the context of graph dynamics, these models have expanded to cover complex processes like the spread of information, disease, and information filtering. Despite the creation of numerous models addressing diverse topics, researchers have made significant progress in understanding the underlying mathematics, particularly for systems with a limited number of dimensions and their connections to other areas of mathematics and physics. This review will focus on a selection of these models, exploring their mathematical underpinnings and the underlying complex physics that they reflect. It will also discuss the many open questions that remain, offering a perspective on where this field, which connects graph theory, nonlinear systems, and stochastic processes, may be headed in the future. Simply put, it uses a neural network to transform encoded data and an Slepian-Wolf encoder to encode the original data, thereby achieving the reversibility of steganographic communication. Our research explores the benefits of employing Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) in U reversible steganography over conventional deep neural networks (DNNs). BNNs provide certified uncertainty bounds on their predictions, allowing the sender to tailor the level of distortion and hiding capacity according to the receiver's requirements. Our framework supports a wide range of steganographic tasks, including image and audio communication. We conducted an experiment using Bayesian convolutional neural networks for image steganography in U reversible steganography, demonstrating an advantage over DNNs based on various metrics, such as the mean squared error of reconstructed images, visual quality scores, and the resulting secret key generation. Our findings confirm the potential of BNNs in U reversible steganography, especially in applications requiring uncertainty estimates. Furthermore, the integration of BNNs and SW encoders yields highly enhanced steganographic capabilities, exceeding those obtained with DNNs and SW encoders. These outcomes underscore the value of using BNNs in U reversible steganography. The development of convection-based dynamos in global-scale worlds including Earth and other planets is still not fully understood. The impact of convection's complex effects varies when analyzing a planet's rotation and convective dynamics, making it challenging to reproduce in global simulations. Our study uses the Global Mean-Field Dynamo Model to explore global dynamos in 1-D, taking into account the spectrum of convection's complex effects and turbulent influences. We tested various models of convection and turbulent influences against each other to see how they stack up. We found that when convection's complex effects are highly dependent on rotation and direction, they produce more energy in the outer planets and stronger dipole fields in the long-term. The global dynamo model's predictions about how these processes change with variation in certain parameters align with the results of other studies conducted in 3-D simulations. This model provides a useful framework for understanding how various parameters influence global dynamos, even when certain assumptions don't hold in 3-D simulations. It also provides useful tools for exploring global dynamos in various astronomical settings, including planets and stars. The Global Mean-Field Dynamo Model was written in Python using widely available tools and code, making it easily shareable and modifiable by others. The code and a step-by-step explanation of our analysis are both publicly available at public repositories, including magnetosphere.dynamo.org and astrodynamo.github.io. The dynamo model's predictions about how various processes change with different parameters were visualized using Graphical Python (pyglet). The effects of geostrophic beta-diffusion, anisotropic small-scale magnetohydrodynamic (MSMHD) turbulence, and kinematic magnetization were explored in detail, revealing complex interactions between these processes at different scales that were not previously noted. The presence of MSMHD turbulence and kinematic magnetization were both found to amplify the Earth's dipole field in the long-term and change the shape of the outer magnetosphere for certain parameters. The earth's dipole field was found to be strongest in models that included MSMHD turbulence and shortest-scale magnetization. The effects of geostrophic beta-diffusion on the outer magnetosphere were found to be the least significant. These results were found to be consistent with the results of other studies of the Earth's magnetosphere conducted in 3-D simulations and aligned with the predictions of our model. The effects of complex convection and turbulent influences on global dynamos were found to be more extensive and interconnected than previously understood, revealing new connections and processes

Investors often evaluate portfolio performance in relation to the market's instead of their individual worth. This relative assessment can be compromised by the benchmark's quality, which may be flawed and not accurately reflect an investor's true wealth. On the other hand, using absolute return as the sole measure of performance can overlook an investor's liquidity needs. To address these concerns, a paper presents a model based on a specific function that combines an investor's net wealth and the ratio of their wealth to the market's, enabling a more nuanced balance between growth and liquidity. This paper then derives the optimal portfolio allocation under certain conditions of elasticity and analyzes how different parameters impact the investor's behavior. Notably, the model's properties exhibit similarities with those observed in absolute return models when the relative wealth ratio is negligible, and several theoretical models and empirical studies confirm that an investor's optimal portfolio consists of an equal mix of stocks and bonds. The model's equations also reveal that an investor's taste for risk decreases when their market beta, liquidity needs, and information quality increase, while their market share influences their optimal portfolio allocation in a non-linear manner. This paper also uses data from U.S. investors to verify that an investor's optimal portfolio consists of an equal mix of stocks and bonds, and their risk preferences are impacted by their market beta, liquidity needs, and the quality of the benchmark used for evaluation. These results provide an explanation for the observed equity bias in optimal portfolios. The model's suggestions for an investor's optimal portfolio allocation are validated through several robustness tests. The combined theory and empirical analysis presented in this paper provides an in-depth and precise understanding of an investor's optimal portfolio allocation when evaluating performance using a specific function that combines an investor's net wealth and the ratio of their wealth to the market's. This analysis is the first to derive an optimal portfolio allocation for an investor with a power utility of absolute and relative riches, and provides an analytical solution for an investor's optimal portfolio allocation in the presence of a specific type of absolute and relative wealth function. The diminished scale of dwarf galaxies poses a question regarding the mechanics behind their star formation processes. Various theories have been proposed to explain their star-making abilities, such as the role of molecular gas in low-mass clouds and the impact of cold molecular gas brought in through galactic winds. The central question in this research inquiry is: What fuels the star formation processes in dwarf galaxies? The methodology for the study involved collecting existing data on CO emission levels in dwarf galaxies from the literature, followed by the determination of the mass of molecular gas in those galaxies. The accuracy of the data collection was verified using dummy models. The data was then plotted against the mass of their parent galaxies, with the mass of their parent galaxies calculated using their stellar masses, with further errors accounted for in the data. The resulting data was compared to predictions based on a galactic feedback model. The study found a nearly perfect correlation between CO emission levels and molecular gas mass, with a measured exponent nearly identical to predicted. The study suggests that gas brought into galaxies through galactic winds is the primary driver of their star formation processes. The study did however reveal a discrepancy between measured star forming material and that predicted based on the data, with the difference found to be comparable to the amount of material brought into galaxies through galactic winds. The study did not account for the role of supernovae explosions in the process. Findings from studies on MTurk users can be elusive, much like needles in a haystack. In particular, developers of summarization systems may struggle locating skilled workers with a strong understanding of language who also possess specialized knowledge or expertise. In this research, three distinct assessment protocols are explored to identify MTurk workers capable of producing high-quality summaries. A gold-standard-based approach and two automated evaluation systems are examined, each employing unique criteria for selecting qualified workers and summary samples. By evaluating human performance using various metrics, including completeness, accuracy, and summarization skills, as well as MTurk workers' task-specific abilities, this investigation reveals which protocol is most effective in producing high-quality summaries. Furthermore, an analysis of the summary samples highlights distinct characteristics of skilled MTurk workers and provides valuable insights for developers, such as optimizing task completion times, selecting eligible workers, and refining summarization protocols. In terms of summarization skills, while fluency and coherence show little variation among qualified workers, content knowledge significantly differentiates skilled MTurk workers, with some demonstrating a deep understanding of specialized topics and others only surface-level knowledge. A key challenge is then identified: while exceptional workers produce top-notch summaries despite working faster, average performers struggle even more with the task. In other words, the gap between top-notch and subpar workers widens when they slow down. A potential explanation for this phenomenon is offered by investigating the distribution of task-specific attributes, such as completion times, fluency, coherence, and comprehension requirements. In order to produce high-quality summaries, then, developers must strike a balance between working with MTurk workers possessing specific characteristics. In practice, this means selecting workers having either high completion times or specific qualifications, such as being experts in the field. In fact, by evaluating an advanced summarization system trained using annotations provided by these special experts, it is observed that such a model can achieve notable improvements over its baseline version trained on unselected MTurk summaries. In particular, when given a choice, it demonstrates greater understanding of the task in terms of content knowledge and also produces summaries that closely mirror those created by humans. In the end, then, while finding and working with qualified MTurk workers may be a challenging and time-consuming process, especially when dealing with task-specific abilities, developers of summarization systems can, in fact, improve model performance and generate better summaries with the cooperation of experts who have the necessary knowledge and fluency. A potential solution to reduce costs associated with finding and evaluating MTurk workers is then proposed.

Text clip retrieval, which emerged as a more efficient and accurate alternative to text encoding, has a notable drawback of limited support for very long and highly complex text documents, as its storage requirements are no longer directly proportional to the text length. Yet, in various domains like law and literature, there is a pressing need to support long and irregular text inputs. To address this, we propose the Token Shift and Selection transformer model (TS2-Net), specifically designed to process text clips of arbitrary lengths using a shifting mechanism that enables token navigation across the text domain. Furthermore, we introduce a novel selection attention mechanism to prioritize relevant tokens based on dynamic similarity calculations, effectively condensing lengthy text into compact yet informative text clips. Our extensive evaluations on 14 different retrieval benchmarks demonstrate that TS2-Net significantly surpasses state-of-the-art performance limits, while also successfully applying our method to retrieve full-length documents from pre-trained language models, thus recovering up to 40% of previously missed information. The related code and models for TS2-Net can be found at the repository address https://github.com/whuiye64/TS2-Net. Additionally, we have also established an open-source text clip retrieval dataset repository https://github.com/whuiye64/LongTextRetrievalData which is designed to facilitate the development of more advanced text clip retrieval models capable of supporting long and complex text inputs. Our research aims to fill a critical existing gap in the text clip retrieval domain, thus paving the way for the widespread adoption of this strategy in comprehensive text understanding frameworks. Experimental results indicate that TS2-Net outperforms all existing models on all 114 retrieval tasks, with an overall average 37.6% enhancement over the second-best performer, leading to a 67.4% reduction in the average gap to the ideal theoretical perfect score, thus demonstrating the substantial improvement offered by this approach. A related video is also available at the following address https://youtu.be/GAaLH7iU0lo. The derived model can be successfully applied to retrieve compact and meaningful text clips from extremely lengthy texts in various domains including law, literature and science, thus effectively addressing a critical existing bottleneck in the text clip retrieval strategy. Our research is specifically designed to fill this critical gap, thus significantly advancing the development of text retrieval models capable of supporting long and complex text inputs. Existing methods relying on optimization or approximation techniques introduce biases or penalties that can negatively impact performance. In response, we've developed Spartan, a novel approach that applies a straightforward differentiation to achieve sparse training, relying on either dropouts or pruning techniques. By introducing a regularization mechanism, regulated transportation, it deterministically determines the level of sparsity for each layer. Our empirical results demonstrate improved accuracy and faster training times for various networks and datasets, including FSD, ImageNet, and the MNIST/Theorem dataset. Additionally, we've successfully demonstrated zero-shot pruning of the spatiotemporal cerebellar neural model, revealing distinct pruning patterns for the cerebellum's homogenous layers. Finally, a detailed explanation is provided for the failure of previous methods to further reduce sparsity in deep models, explaining why our approach yields better outcomes. In the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, widespread contact tracing across entire populations turned to targeted case-specific contact tracing. As economies and societies reopened, new transmission dynamics prompted an optimal search for an equilibrium between tracing scope and practical limitations. Engaging in regional tracing efforts can enhance the efficiency of contact tracing, but may not be a reliable substitute for other strategies, especially when applied broadly. Here, we evaluate the potential benefits of targeted tracing efforts in specific regions of England, analyzing data from the Test and Protect scheme in Scotland, including demographic factors and density of residential areas. Our study also considers additional factors such as local compliance with public health guidance, as well as the influence of existing lockdown measures. Ultimately, a multi-criteria decision-making approach is applied to evaluate the effectiveness of different contact tracing strategies in various regions. Based on our findings, we recommend region-specific customization of contact tracing strategies, with the added advantage of regional collaboration. We further investigate how regional collaboration can enhance the overall efficiency of contact tracing, by either increasing its effectiveness or by reducing the need for additional measures. Through analysis, we find that a multi-regional collaboration involving the North East and North West regions can increase the total effective reproduction number threshold, necessitating further contact tracing measures. Similarly, regional collaborations involving the South West and other areas, or the entire North East and North West regions, are also likely to require additional measures. Conversely, collaborations involving the South East and other areas, or the entire country, are likely to render contact tracing less necessary. Additionally, a regional collaboration involving the entire country is expected to increase the total effective reproduction number, rendering it distinguishable from the baseline scenario, but ultimately, a scenario not evaluated in this study. Before making any recommendations to policy makers, we assess the validity of our findings by conducting several key analyses, demonstrating that our approach is robust and reliable. Specifically, we derive mathematical expressions for the total effective reproduction number, Rt, under different collaboration scenarios, and validate the consistency of our model set-up and interpretation in a posteriori analysis. In conclusion, our model is highly versatile, allowing for the evaluation of both regional collaboration and other tracing strategies, with the added advantage of applications to demographic and density-related factors. In robotics, training an eye-in-hand camera to reach objects is a fundamental challenge that we tackle in this paper. The conventional approach of utilizing image sequences to train robotics algorithms is not feasible when dealing with unknown or changing environments. Considering that learning algorithms require diverse data for generalization, we developed an innovative training method utilising a single image to instruct a robotic arm the optimal pose to grasp a object for an eye-in-hand camera. A novel network is employed to learn a correlation function between these projections and camera poses, facilitating the acquisition of essential visual and spatial knowledge. We've proposed an innovative approach that tackles the challenge of automated speech transcription in languages lacking substantial writing data, relying on only brief audio clips and limited transcripts initially. Our method relies on both a cycle-consistency constraint-based training technique and a novel inter-domain penalty to ensure the generated transcripts align both in terms of their acoustic characteristics and linguistic content. Experimental evaluations using the WSJ, Librispeech, and TED-LIUM datasets have shown that our approach significantly outperforms conventional methods in producing transcription. Furthermore, we've also investigated the efficacy of our technique in comparison to state-of-the-art transcription models, demonstrating its ability to enhance transcription accuracy by up to 10% in scenarios involving limited data. Notably, our study highlights the ability of our method to improve transcription results in languages for which there is an increasing amount of parallel data becoming available over time. In addition, we have made our source code accessible via the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/djeco/cgan_asr. Our goal is for this work to facilitate the advancement of research in automated speech recognition in under-resourced languages. We anticipate that in the future, the additional training data will become available for these languages, allowing the models to continually improve and thereby aligning the generated transcripts with their corresponding labels. In such a scenario, our technique is anticipated to be particularly beneficial in mitigating unwanted shifts in the model's decision boundary, thereby ensuring that the generated transcripts remain within the feasible space. We have also conducted an additional set of experiments aimed at investigating the efficacy of our technique in addressing domain-adaptation for speech-to-text applications through both a general investigation of its performance across multiple domain-adaptation settings and a more in-depth analysis of its applications in enhancing the transcription accuracy in specific domains (such as broadcast news, TED talks, and Librispeech). Our results indicate that our technique is highly effective in domain-adaptation settings in a wide range of scenarios. Supervised Learning for object detection tasks often falls short when applied across different environments due to a discrepancy in the training and testing data. This is particularly true for tasks like pedestrian detection where learning a generalised feature space proves challenging under changing data conditions. Domain adaptation for pedestrian detection typically involves adjusting the training data to match the characteristics of the testing data, although this process can be costly and time-consuming. Our novel contribution reorders the bounding boxes in the training data to create multiple domain-adapted datasets, which can then be used to train a single model that performs well on different environments. This method requires no additional labels and relies solely on an iterative process of labeling a small number of false positives in the testing data. Our experiments show that our approach reorders the training data to a degree that closely matches the testing data's features, resulting in a significant reduction of false positives in our testing data and outperforming state of the art methods in our experiments. Virtual characters' ability to simulate realistic throwing motions depends on various factors, especially the dynamics of the movement. While many studies have explored the impact of forces and velocities on throwing trajectories, little is known about the effect of the point of release on motion dynamics. To bridge this gap, our research aims to investigate how throwing characters perceive an artificial increase in the point of release in arm motions. Through participant feedback, we evaluated the perceptual and movement-related responses of 18 participants as they observed simulated throwing gestures from 6 different viewpoints. Our results show that distortions in arm motions affecting the point of release can go undetected in certain viewpoints but become apparent in others. Moreover, these distortions do not necessarily correlate with the perceived throwing force or trajectory. Notably, even slight distortions near the end of the throwing motion can create significant and unrealistic arm movements. Our findings suggest that characters may intentionally introduce errors in arm motions to convey more realistic throwing gestures. Based on these insights, we present guidelines for generating authentic throwing motions and create a new dataset, FauxThrow, that illustrates various distortions in arm motions to aid the development of realistic arm motions. The research was implemented and tested on a character named "Nineteen", producing accurate and realistic throwing gestures that are indistinguishable from those of humans. Overall, our research demonstrates that the impact of the point of release on motion dynamics is worthy of investigation and that our findings have the potential to enhance the realism of throwing simulations. Our method starts by generating translations based on syntactic analysis, then refines these outputs using a reverse process that starts with the sentence and works its way downward. This bottom-up review enables the system to identify flawed translations earlier, resulting in improved outcomes. Building on the versatility of linear models, we explore transforming raw images into a representable, linear form, then developing a universal set of parameters capable of accurately capturing various linear representations for multiple image categories. Focusing on adversarial training methods, we create a universal classifier for linear representations across diverse datasets, resulting in a unique parameter set applicable to unseen datasets. Importantly, we advocate for a transparent, explainable artificial intelligence approach where the internal linear representation is easily interpretable. To the best of our knowledge, this method offers the first instance of a self-supervised, end-to-end, adversarial training procedure for AIX (explainability), alongside exceptional performance benchmarks. Notably, our approach achieves explainable models for recognizing objects in the ImageNet dataset with high accuracy, as well as universal, transferable models applicable to multiple datasets with negligible performance loss. Furthermore, we successfully apply this method to the recognition of med objects in the  aID challenge, achieving state-of-the-art results. The code for our approach is publicly available at https://github.com/alexk43/axlinear. 

Importantly, this research answers three fundamental questions:
1. How can we linearize images?
2. How can we develop a universal set of parameters capable of accurately capturing various linear representations for multiple image categories?
3. How can we measure the optimal parameter set?

Our research provides the first demonstration of a fully self-supervised, end-to-end, explainable artificial intelligence procedure for uncovering the underlying structure of visual information. Importantly, our approach has been successfully tested in three distinct contexts: (1) recognizing objects in a widely used dataset, (2) applying to the medical field, and (3) achieving state-of-the-art performance in a highly competitive challenge. Language models are becoming increasingly popular, but their substantial size makes them impractical for low-capacity devices to use during translation. Two techniques to mitigate this problem are weight quantization and model distillation. This research is focused on creating lightweight translation models that require low capacity, specifically for low-resource machine translation. We analyzed and identified key factors that influence the performance of both techniques under various conditions, particularly dealing with small MT datasets. Interestingly, our results suggest that model distillation is more sensitive to changes than weight quantization. This is because small MT datasets can easily distort the distillation signal, causing significant performance degradation. On the other hand, weight quantization faces issues primarily with large and high-variance model weights, which are common in NMT architectures. To address these challenges, we explored the use of training techniques, such as representation learning and regularization, that improve the robustness of both methods. Additionally, we developed a new approach to model distillation that combines knowledge useful for predicting the given context. Our findings demonstrate that there are effective methods to make distillation more resilient, particularly when combined with data augmentation and constraint optimization. In practice, these techniques enabled the full utilization of large MT datasets during training, ultimately resulting in translation results comparable to models trained with extended datasets. In light of this, it's proposed that the notion of causal effect be employed to refine the hypothesis-relevance criterion and provide a more satisfactory definition of harm, ultimately making the revised hypothesis-relevance criterion better suited to meet its intended purpose. Low voltage grid management efficiency relies heavily on accurate load forecasts, which necessitate short-term and long-term prediction capabilities, particularly measuring daily peaks and off-peak periods. Failing to distinguish between these peaks and bases can result in over-forecasting, ultimately leading to inaccurate low voltage grid load predictions. We analyzed hourly load data from the low voltage network, decomposing it into off-peak and peak periods to assess forecasting performance. We found that combining short-term and long-term forecasting models, specifically up to 6 hours and 3 days in advance, yields the most reliable results during peak hours, with the largest uncertainties. We evaluated the effectiveness of peak-target and base-target regression models, as well as a unified model, and discovered that models aiming to predict both peak and base values outperform those focused solely on peaks. We further discovered that the strength of these models lies in their ability to adapt to the distribution of daily peaks, which is inherent in their design. We analyzed the effect of the number of samples on our models and the impact of atypical days, finally proposing an adaptation mechanism to compensate for the imbalance between samples to guide future researchers. We evaluated our models' performance using three common loss functions: mean absolute error, coefficient of variation of time series, and the Shannon entropy measure. Specifically, our analysis of aggregated load data from the low voltage grid showed that the combined model's error is generally under 5.8% and the coefficient of variation is around 0.24 throughout the day. Moreover, the combined model significantly reduces the standard error of its forecast compared to the short-term only model, although this gain largely stems from the properties of the Shannon entropy analysis, which may not be extensively used, and further analysis showed that the combined model performance could be improved during peak hours if it could better capture these peaks more accurately than the short-term only model, finally pointing out that the need for more accurate short-term forecasting models to enhance the overall combined model performance. The presented findings and analysis could contribute positively to generating more accurate forecasts of low voltage grid loads. COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, has become one of the most significant global health threats since 2020. Due to its high contagiousness, the disease has put pressure on healthcare systems, emphasizing the need for identifying COVID-19 patients promptly to facilitate early treatment, isolation, and disease prevention. Chest X-rays have emerged as a convenient and cost-effective diagnostic tool to diagnose and monitor respiratory diseases, including COVID-19. Researchers have proposed various machine learning methods for detecting COVID-19 and distinguishing it from pneumonia caused by various agents; however, a significant challenge lies in accurately localizing and segmenting COVID-19 lesions, particularly due to overlapping lesions and the absence of large, clean datasets. To address these issues, we developed a novel dataset and a new learning framework to identify COVID-19 lesions with minimal human supervision, leveraging the capabilities of convolutional neural networks. This approach combines semi-supervised and unsupervised learning to identify COVID-19 lesions from both annotated and non-annotated data, respectively, ultimately demonstrating its efficacy with satisfactory validation accuracy. This method exhibits improved robustness and performance compared to traditional supervised learning, and it can function effectively without requiring time-consuming annotation processes for fine-tuning. Notably, given the rapid spread of the virus, the importance of contact tracing has increased, making this research highly relevant. The versatility of elastic actuators in locomotion systems makes them an attractive option due to their reduced power consumption, decreased weight, and enhanced mobility. However, the increasing demands on lower limb actuation necessitate novel design approaches and learning techniques to capitalize on their potential. Current elastic actuator-based quadruped robots rely heavily on human-designed movement strategies and fail to optimize their performance. To overcome this limitation, a reinforcement learning framework utilizing an elastic actuator-based locomotion system has been developed, starting from a basic model derived from a traditional RSA system through inverse dynamics. When paired with an optimal control strategy, the phase variable trajectory can be obtained and further utilized to compute joint angles and actuator lengths. When the phase variable trajectory is used as the reward target in the reinforcement learning algorithm, the learned policy demonstrates superior mobility capabilities using an elastic actuator alone, without any predefined trajectory. With the integration of two elastic actuators in the hip, our quadruped robot can maintain a stable gait on various terrain types, including hard and soft surfaces, fueled by a diverse set of behaviors obtained from random searches. To expedite the learning process, we also developed a new variant of reinforcement learning, the Random Scan Trajectory Search, which seeks to balance the exploration-exploitation trade-off and has been proven to converge to an optimal policy in theoretical models. To facilitate future research, we have publicly released the code for our framework at https://github.com/verg-epfl/ELaMo/. Through our research, we have demonstrated that a comprehensive learning framework is a crucial element in unlocking the full potential of elastic actuators in quadruped mobility systems. The findings presented provide a foundation for the development of future generation, elastic-actuator-based quadruped locomotion systems. The measure of the non-separability of a quantum system, known as the quantum discord, can be calculated using the principle of minimum interaction. This approach allows us to derive a divisible form of quantum discord in certain situations. Furthermore, by applying a specific correction term, the derived divisible quantifier aligns with the original non-divisible quantum discord in all cases. In addition to its divisible form, the proposed method also yields a tight lower limit of quantum discord, along with a specific correction term needed to achieve equality. These new results provide insight into the relationship between quantum discord, compression of quantum states, and equilibrium conditions. They specifically enable the derivation of an optimal compression rate for maximally discordant states, along with a specific equalizing term. Moreover, the proposed method has broader implications, allowing us to develop general tight lower limits and divisible forms for certain one-way classical correlations in quantum systems. Examples of quantum discord in Bell-like measurements, continuous-variable quantum discord, and multipartite quantum discord are also considered. Finally, the proposed method has the potential to be extended to the most general mixed states of quantum discord. Researchers studied a mini-scale tearing mode in a lab-created slab plasma using a scale-down experiment, known as the Miniature Magnetic Test Facility (MMTF). The experiment used a small, curved current sheet to analyze and observe the properties of a tearing mode, which the team achieved by manipulating electron fluid dynamics using a current sheet geometry that drives specific modes of motion. By observing the scale-dependent behavior of various properties in the current sheet, such as magnetic fields, plasma density, and electron temperature, the researchers identified key characteristics of the tearing mode and distinguished it from other instability types that occur in a collisionless environment. Specifically, the team analyzed and compared the cross-helicity and energy contents of the observed modes to determine their source of energy, finding that the tearing mode exhibits unique properties in a collisionless setting. These results will inform theoretical modeling and experimental studies of collisionless environments, such as magnetic reconnection events and solar storms. Furthermore, the researchers demonstrated that the mini-scale tearing mode can be achieved using a small, intricate coil design that the team also utilized in a separate experiment. Specifically, the team linked the tearing mode to an electron-scale coherent structure observed in an MMFT experiment, known as the electron beam instability. Lastly, based on the results of their study, the researchers constructed a coherent framework for distinguishing between reconnection, standing modes, and electron Bernstein waves in a collisionless setting. As an added benefit, the team's findings also provide valuable insights for interpreting solar storm and magnetospheric phenomena observed from space using in situ measurements. These insights extend to various other phenomena, such as sawtooth oscillations in a stellar X-ray source, and they provide general guidelines for distinguishing between torsional modes and others in a general plasma setting. Finally, the researchers attempted to observe the mini-scale of the tearing mode by conducting an MMTF experiment with a freely evolving current sheet, an approach to which the team is able to return in a separate experiment. By analyzing this experiment, the researchers aimed to further elucidate the role of the z-pinch mode in a collisionless setting. However, the details of this experiment, along with the results, have been left for a separate description. In the world of fashion, where images of outfits are abundant, retrieving images with similar styles can be a daunting task, especially when styles keep evolving rapidly. This paper presents a novel approach to fashion image retrieval by editing images at the feature level, which allows for the retrieval of style-similar images. By extending a baseline model with our proposed semi-supervised editing method, we can enhance retrieval accuracy without needing significant updates to the model's parameters. This editing model is unique because it focuses on modifying individual image attributes while being computationally efficient and adaptable to datasets. Empirical results validate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming existing methods in accuracy and overall retrieval performance according to metrics such as average precision and Inception score. This paper marks a significant advancement in fashion image retrieval, making progress towards applications such as automated fashion design and style transfer. Our code is available at https://github.com/wz2017/FashionFLAM.git.

Evaluating the light field quality is crucial in various applications like visual navigation, object manipulation, and image rendering. Notably, occlusion issues significantly affect the light field's quality and should be taken into account during analysis. Existing methods focus primarily on analyzing the overall depth, but a novel approach has been developed to uniquely assess occlusion levels. This new measure evaluates an image's ability to prevent other views from providing valid depth information in the given light field. As an application of this new metric, an "Occlusion-Responsive Evolution of Depth using Kernels" (ODEK) algorithm was created. ODEK leverages the proposed measure and utilizes kernel-based techniques to quantify the overall amount of occlusion present in each image. By applying ODEK, it has been possible to identify images with the highest levels of occlusion, as well as understand how occlusion evolves throughout different datasets. Experimental results indicate that ODEK successfully captures the intuitive notion of occlusion and outperforms existing depth assessment techniques. ODEK's effectiveness has been further validated through its successful use in developing an occlusion-based active depth generation algorithm, as well as its capacity for informing active light field collection procedures. All necessary code and datasets have been made publicly available on the 'Occlusion-Responsive Evolution of Depth using Kernels' GitHub repository. This work presents a unique contribution to the field of light field analysis through the proposal of a reliable occlusion-based depth assessment approach. As such, it has significant potential for application in areas like object manipulation, image rendering, and occlusion-based techniques for light field depth assessment. By examining the action principle, we identify and categorize the non-standard gravitational actions that remain consistent with general relativity when applied to manifolds without singularities. Our analysis also covers the behavior of these actions when applied to manifolds with boundaries and explores their connection to dual field theories. By examining these theories in the context of two-dimensional gravity, we have gained insight into the characteristics of their duals, particularly those that exhibit non-hierarchical properties. It has become evident that duals of actions that include a volume term also possess this non-hierarchical property, whereas the duals of actions that include a surface term do not exhibit it consistently. Consequently, theories with a volume degree of freedom that have a surface-based action component, when transformed into their dual forms, naturally display non-hierarchical properties. In recent years, the deployment of Battery-powered IEEE 802.11n Extenders has become a vital component of Home WiFi networks, ensuring seamless connectivity across indoor and outdoor areas. These Extenders, often installed by customers in areas with optimal signal coverage, are chosen based on performance rather than actual network load. Since Battery-powered devices usually runs 24/7, selecting them based on performance criteria rather than traffic can be quite inefficient. For instance, an outdoor Extender might be chosen over a faster but indoor one due to higher outdoor performance, leading to sub-optimal configuration. This article presents a straightforward solution to mitigate these issues in Home WiFi networks by leveraging the feedback provided in IEEE 802.11k/v standards to always opt for the most loaded but efficient configuration, thus enhancing overall network performance and quality of service, particularly in densely configured networks. Our results validate the effectiveness of this solution by comparing it to the current standard configuration provided in IEEE 802.11s. Moreover, our findings demonstrate that the given solution can be efficiently applied not just to IEEE 802.11n but also to next-generation IEEE 802.11ac/ax technologies. Finally, our solution facilitates passive channel load monitoring, thus allowing operators to evaluate and improve their network configuration and quality of service without interrupting the network operation. Our research validates that the network performance and quality of service can be quite robust even in case of partial faults in monitor data. These results showcase that the given solution scored high on three key evaluation metrics: network performance, quality of service, and configuration overhead. Our results reveal that the given solution provides around 2.5 and 2.1 times better network performance and quality of service, respectively, compared to the current standard configuration provided in IEEE 802.11s. Moreover, our solution scored a 43% reduction in configuration overhead, thus validating its effectiveness and utility. This research and validation present a solid ground for integrating the proposed solution in next-generation of IEEE 802.11 standards. Such integration will benefit various real-world applications such as Air Quality Sensor Networks by providing robust network performance and quality of service. Finally, our research validates that the given solution can be easily extended to multiband white space technology by defining load and utilization metrics for each sub-band and applying them to AP and Extender choice problem. This extension will facilitate the utilization of feedback information for optimizing the performance of IEEE 802.11 networks during dynamic channel changes.
